Chapter 4

The Fatlands

There is no word in our dialect for full. We had one. We ate it.
— Fatlands joke, told at every table
Thank you, Long Acre. Thank you, Granny Hessop’s Rise. Thank you, Father, who is on the plate.
— a wake-grace from Low Tilth, as recorded by the Cutwrights’ College, 588 A.G.

The fat was the first thing. Mam always said so, and Mam was right about the fat: you start a man at the fat, because the fat remembers the fire best.

We laid Da on the big board at noon, the day after he went, with the shutters wide so the neighbours could see we had nothing to hide and no meanness in us. Hob Gristle came out from Sated to do the jointing, because Da had been a weighty man and a deacon of the Weighhouse and you do not let your cousins hack at a deacon. Hob kissed the knife. He kissed Da’s brow. He said, “Sorry, Wilm. Sorry, old lad. Sorry,” every time the blade went in, under his breath, like a man saying a grace he did not believe but could not stop.

Da came apart beautifully. That is what everyone said after. The skin lifted off the shoulder in one sheet, gold underneath, the fat as thick as three fingers laid flat and white as a new cheese, marbled with pink threads like a map of rivers. There was a smell from him even raw, a sweet one, grass and warm butter and the inside of a barn in Plenty, because Da had eaten Long Acre his whole life and Long Acre is famous. You could see the field in him. Everyone said so. They pressed in at the windows and said so.

We rendered the belly first. It went into the big copper over the yard fire and it sighed when it hit the heat, and the yard filled up with the smell of him, rich and brown and bottomless, and the dogs all lay down flat in the lane and whined. My sister Petty skimmed the dripping with Mam’s wedding ladle. She cried the whole time and kept tasting it. You could not blame her. Nobody could have blamed her.

The legs went on the spit. The hands went into the pie, with onions and the little purple turnips that grow along Granny Hessop’s Rise, because that is the custom for a man who worked with his hands. The heart was mine to cook, as eldest. I seared it in its own fat until the outside cracked like toffee and the inside was the colour of a plum, and I sliced it thin and laid the slices out on the blue plate that came from Mam’s mother, overlapping, like scales, the way he would have wanted. When I cut it, it was still warm in the middle. When I put the first slice in my mouth it was so good that I sat down on the floor.

I am telling you the truth. It was the best thing I have ever eaten. It tasted of being twelve and being lifted onto his shoulders at the Weighing. It tasted of his pipe. It ran down my chin and I did not wipe it.

By dusk there were sixty at the board and the yard was slick with drip and the copper had been refilled twice. The Bailiff came round to see the Feasting Laws were kept and there was nothing for him to do, so he sat and ate a rib of Da with tears on his big soft face and said Wilm Callock was the finest-marbled man in the parish, and he would know. Petty had stopped crying and was eating with both hands. Mam was eating with both hands. I was eating with both hands. The children were under the board, sucking the knuckle-bones, which is what the knuckle-bones are for.

And I was hungry. That is the thing nobody tells you before your first wake, though they all know it. I ate my father from noon until the Plate came up, and every mouthful was the best mouthful of my life, and I was exactly as hungry at the end as I was at the start. Hungrier. Because now I knew what he tasted like and there was no more of him.

Late on, when the board was down to bones, I went out to Long Acre on my own. The field was sweating in the dark. I knelt and put my face to the soil and it was warm as a cheek and it moved, slowly, up and down, like something sleeping. I said, “Thank you, Long Acre.” I said, “We are giving him back to you, we are, what’s left, I promise.” The furrow under my mouth opened a little. Just a little. Just enough for me to feel the teeth in it, small ones, wheat-teeth, rows and rows of them, all along the ground, all through the dark, as far as the Plate could light.

Then I went home and had the marrow, because the marrow had been saved for me.

— from the commonplace book of Abel Callock, Low Tilth, Carving 639 A.G.; given to the Board’s physician “as evidence of nothing in particular”

The Meal

Every land on the Table remembers its Gorging as something done slowly, in shame, with stops for vomiting and prayer. The Fatlands remember theirs as a party.

That is the first thing outsiders find unbearable, and it is true. In the ninth winter of the Long Lack the southern plains were a grey crust of dead clay from the Brawn to the sea. The people had eaten their seed, then their oxen, then their boots, then the thatch, and by the last Tablenight they were eating the clay itself, baked into flat cakes that cracked teeth and stopped the bowels. Their god had come down out of the hills to lie among them in the field called the Trencher, because there was nowhere else for it to go. Ummer, the Laden, the Harvest Walker, had once been so vast with plenty that the furrows bent toward it like grass toward a wind. By that winter it was a long grey heap of sagging hide, a hill of skin on a frame of ribs like a collapsed barn, breathing a little. Its belly, which the oldest carvings show swollen with sheaves and calves and fruit, lay empty and folded on the earth like a dropped sack.

The Fatland chronicles, which were written down in the Sweet Reigns by people who had been told by people who had been there, insist that nobody gave an order. A girl named Wenna Strake, aged about sixteen, walked out across the Trencher at dusk with a flint sickle, and the crowd watched her go, and she knelt by Ummer’s flank and looked into the one great clouded eye that faced her, and said, “Lack keep away.” Then she cut. The god did not move. Its eye, every account says, was wet and kind and pleased, the way a mother’s face is pleased when a child at last takes the spoon.

They ate it in a night. They ate it fastest of all the peoples. The chronicles linger on this with a horrible, unashamed relish that the College has never managed to edit out. They describe the hide, which peeled away in sheets the size of sails and was found to be lined with a layer of golden fat a hand deep, still faintly warm, smelling of cut hay and new bread and the inside of a dairy. They describe how the people, who had eaten clay for a season, tore at the fat raw and wept as it melted on their tongues; how the meat beneath was dark and dense and so full of juice that it ran in the furrows; how whole families crawled bodily into the cavity of the ribs to get at the organs, and came out painted to the shoulder; how fires were lit all over the Trencher and the smoke rose so thick and sweet that birds dropped out of it, gorged on the air alone. There was singing. There was dancing in the grease. Old men who had buried every child they had danced with their mouths full.

Ummer’s bones were cracked on the field-stones for the marrow before dawn. The marrow was yellow, and sweet as honey, and it is said that those who sucked it never afterward grew old in the face, only in the body. The skull was split with mattocks. The brain was shared out a spoonful each to the elders. Nothing was wasted. Not the hooves, not the hide, not the eyes. That is the Fatlands’ founding boast, still carved over the doors of the Weighhouse in Sated: NOTHING WAS LEFT.

The families who reached the middle first, and took the stomach, the paunch, the long coils of the entrails, and the great swollen liver, became the Gut-lines. Some say they won those portions by strength. Others say the god’s insides came to them, sliding out of the opened belly toward particular hands. The chronicles record, without comment, that the stomach was still working when it was eaten. It had been empty for nine years. It was digesting whatever it touched.

The famine ended the next morning. The clay of the Trencher was black and soft and steaming by sunrise. By noon there were green shoots across the whole plain. Within a week the wheat stood shoulder-high, and that was the Week of Rising, and nobody asked what it was wheat of.

One detail is preserved only in a single fragmentary song, sung in the Bleeding Orchards at pruning time, and the Board has twice tried to forbid it. It says that when the feasters had finished, and lay on the Trencher in the grey light, too heavy to move, every one of them woke at the same moment with the same thought. It was not guilt. It was not grief. The song gives it in four words, and the Orchard-keepers sing them very softly: Is there any more?

Ummer in the Old Carvings

Before the Gorging, Ummer was carved on every granary lintel on the plains: a broad, stooping, many-handed figure walking ahead of the plough, with sheaves sprouting from its shoulders and a belly like a full cart. In the few carvings that survive whole, it walks in procession with the other Providers. The Gut-lines prefer not to display these. One reason is obvious: Ummer is shown feeding the others from its own body, breaking off pieces of its shoulder and handing them along the line. The other reason is less discussed. In every surviving procession, there is a figure walking just behind Ummer, very close, with its hand on the Laden’s back. That figure has been chiselled away to the bare stone. In the oldest carving in the Fatlands, over the root-cellar of a ruined granary at Dimble, the chisel slipped, and a little of the hand remains. It is very long, and it is open, palm up, the way you hold out a hand for more.

The Rule of the Land

Everything here is meat, and nobody is ever full.

Those nine words are the whole of Fatland law, Fatland faith and Fatland misery, and every child can recite them before it can count. What they mean in practice takes longer.

Everything Is Meat

The soil of the Fatlands is Ummer’s flesh, scattered and buried and grown back, and it grows flesh in turn. Nothing that comes out of the ground here is entirely vegetable. Wheat stands in the field in golden ranks and looks, from the road, like any wheat on the Table; split an ear and you find each grain sheathed in a little moist pink gum, and in the gum, a tooth. Toothed wheat has been the only wheat for four centuries. Milled, it makes a heavy, sweet, faintly salty flour that bakes into bread with a crust like crackling and a crumb that tears in long fibres, like pulled shoulder. The teeth are sieved out at the mill. Most of them are milk teeth. Not all.

Orchard trees bleed when they are pruned: a slow, dark, clotting sap that scabs over in a day. Their fruit has a skin, a layer of soft white fat under it, firm pink flesh beneath that, and at the core a pit that is unmistakably bone, ridged and porous and full of a sweet grey marrow children suck out with straws. Root vegetables have veins. A beet pulled from the ground pulses faintly in the hand for a minute or two before it stops. Onions have a membrane between every layer, and if you cut them too slowly they flinch. Cabbages are warm in the middle. Potatoes, the poor’s food, grow in clusters joined by gristle, and when the clusters are pulled apart the cut ends sweat clear lymph.

Dig a well and you strike something that flinches. Every Fatland well is lined with salt-glazed brick, and the water drawn from it is warm, slightly cloudy, and tastes of broth. Drive a fencepost too deep and the ground around it will be bruised purple by morning. Ploughs do not so much turn the soil as open it, and the furrow behind the share is red-brown and glistening and smells, in the heat, of a butcher’s block.

The livestock is the strangest of all, because livestock should be the one thing that was meat already. The cattle of the Fatlands are enormous, sleek, docile and silent. They do not low. They watch. Drovers say a Fatland steer will follow a man anywhere if he walks ahead of it eating, and the Renderers’ Union does not employ anyone who has spent too long looking a steer in the eye. Pigs are hairless and pale. Chickens lay eggs with a heartbeat. Nobody asks what the cattle eat in the far pastures when they are out of sight, because the answer is grass, and the grass here has teeth.

And all of it, every mouthful, is delicious. This must be understood or nothing about the Fatlands will make sense. There is no bad food in the south. The poorest gristle-potato boiled in well-water is better than a lord’s feast in Oathen. Fatland bread, broken hot, is so good that foreign travellers have been known to weep at the first bite and refuse to leave the inn. The Fatlands are the breadbasket and the meat-locker of half the Table, and every land that buys from them knows, at some level it does not visit, that it is buying the Laden god by the pound.

Nobody Is Ever Full

A Fatlander can eat until the belly splits, and some do, and still feel the hunger exactly as before.

Hunger here has no connection to the stomach. It is not a signal that the body needs food; it is a presence, the god’s own nine-year famine, inherited and shared out through ten thousand bloodlines like the meat itself. It sits beneath the breastbone and gnaws. It wakes children in the night. It interrupts weddings and funerals and sermons and acts of love. Eating soothes it the way scratching soothes an itch: wonderfully, for exactly as long as you are doing it, and then not at all.

The Fatlands have therefore built a civilization around eating constantly. Five meals a day are mandatory under the Feasting Laws, and the poor fit four more around them if they can. Field-hands chew strips of salt fat as they work. Clerks keep bowls of cracklings at their elbows. Every inn and every house keeps a pot on the hob at all hours, and it is never allowed to empty. Waste is unthinkable. Refusal is sedition. A thin Fatlander is either sick, criminal, or one of the Thin, and in the eyes of the law these are the same thing.

The people are, accordingly, huge. A healthy labourer of the Scrapling class might weigh three hundred pounds. A prosperous merchant, five hundred. The Gut-lines nobility begin at a thousand and do not stop. Fatland architecture is wide, low, and ramped. Fatland chairs are benches, Fatland doors are double, Fatland floors are joisted like bridges. In Sated there is a profession, the Carriers, of men and women employed to lift and turn the great, and another, the Washers, who clean the folds.

The Land Also Eats

The god was the god of harvest, and a harvest has two halves. The land gives. Then it takes.

Each Carving, as the fields come ripe, people go missing from every village. They go out in the field at dusk and are not back by morning. They leave no footprints going anywhere but out. Sometimes a boot is found in a furrow, standing upright, laces still tied. Sometimes a hat in the wheat, or a sickle with a polished handle, or a set of clothes laid neatly in the shape of a body, flat and empty, with the soil beneath them dark and wet and freshly turned. More often there is nothing at all. This is called the Reaping.

The official explanation is wolves. Every Board proclamation since 300 A.G. has said so, and the Board employs a Wolf-Warden in every district, who files a report each autumn describing tracks, sightings and depredations. There are no wolves in the Fatlands. There have never been any in living memory or written record. Nothing in the Fatlands is anything but crop.

Those who have watched a Reaping happen and kept their minds describe it with a terrible consistency. It is always dusk. The light goes amber, then red, and the heat lifts off the soil in a haze that smells of hot fat. The field goes still; the wind drops; the wheat stops whispering. The labourer is usually alone, or at the far end of a row from the others, bent to the work. And then the field leans. Every ear of wheat for fifty yards turns toward them at once, slowly, like a congregation turning to look at a latecomer. There is a sound one witness compared to a crowd of people chewing with their mouths shut. The soil around their feet softens to the consistency of warm suet and they sink to the ankle, and then to the knee, and they do not, by most accounts, struggle much; their faces go slack and grateful, the way a tired man’s face goes slack when he lowers himself into a hot bath. The wheat closes over them. The ears move against the body, in and out, all of them, all over. There is a wet, comfortable, rhythmic noise, which goes on for some time. Then the field stands up straight again and the wind comes back and the wheat whispers, and next year that strip of field yields half again what the rest does, and the bread from it tastes, faintly, of the person.

Families know. Everyone knows. You can tell a Reaped man’s row by the colour of the ears: a little redder, a little heavier, nodding lower. The widow of a Reaped man will often ask the miller to keep that strip’s flour separate, and bakes it into a single loaf on Tablenight, and the family eats it together, slowly, in the dark, and says his name.

The Reaping in Play

The Reaping is not a monster to be fought; it is weather, and it is the god. A character caught alone in a ripe Fatland field between sunset and full dark in Carving may be Reaped. The GM should make it a slow, sensory scene, never a surprise kill. First the stillness (Eye + Search, Routine, to notice). Then the leaning (Dread 3 to witness; Dread 2 for a Fatlander, who has grown up with it). Then the softening ground: the victim must succeed at Caul + Resolve (Hard 14; Grim 18 if their Hunger is 6 or more, because the field smells like dinner) or stop wanting to leave. A character who fails may be dragged out by companions with Gut + Labor (Grim 18), but the field holds on: each round in the soil deals 1d6 Flesh as the ground begins, gently, to digest. A character who is Reaped is gone. What is pulled out after full dark is not a corpse, only a shape of clothes and a smell of bread. Fatlanders of Cut 3+ can sometimes feel which fields are hungry on a given night (Caul + Godsign, Hard 14).

The Regrowth in the Fatlands

Ummer is growing back, and what grows back is a field.

Every land’s Regrowth is a return of the god’s nature. Ummer’s nature was abundance: the slow, rooted, generative patience of soil, which takes in what dies and gives it back as food. In the Fatlands the god does not wear its people so much as plant them. The Cutwrights’ College calls the southern Regrowth “the most orderly on the Table,” because its stages arrive in strict sequence and never skip. Fatlanders call it simply getting heavy.

The Taste

Hunger that wakes you. Every Fatlander has the god’s hunger by day; at the Taste it begins to come in the night as well, a hollow ache that drags you up out of sleep with your mouth already working. Children chew their sleeves into rags, then their bedding, then the soft wood of the cot-rail. Mothers sew bone rings into nightshirt cuffs to give them something better to gnaw. Adults wake with the taste of soil on their tongues and cannot remember the dream. The breath begins to smell faintly of the fields, of grass and dung and rising dough. It is considered a healthy sign, and courting couples are told to look for it.

The Appetite

Eating without choosing. At the Appetite the hand goes to the mouth before the mind has agreed: a bite of tallow candle, a mouthful of earth from a flowerpot, the corner of a leather glove, a twist of one’s own hair. The sufferer will eat soap, wax, string, paper, chalk, rope, coal, and can digest a good deal of it. They cannot stop for conversation. They eat through sermons, through lovemaking, through their own children’s weddings, and they weep while they do it, because they can taste everything and everything is wonderful. Fatland courts have recognized “the Appetite” as a defence to theft since 312 A.G., provided the stolen article was eaten in full. Clerks with the Appetite keep their ledgers chained, because the ink is made from rendered fat. At this stage, many begin to want meat that is not animal. They smell the living. They notice, without wishing to, how a neighbour’s forearm would carve.

The Course

The body swells past all proportion and the feet begin to put down roots. These people are called the Laden, after the god, and in the Gut-lines it is a title.

The swelling is not ordinary fat. It is soft, cool, slightly granular to the touch, and it gives under the finger like freshly turned loam and holds the print for hours. The skin darkens to brown and red, mottled like a field seen from a hill. Hair thickens and coarsens into something fibrous. Small green shoots appear in the creases of the elbow and behind the knees; the Washers pluck them daily, and they grow back overnight. The Laden sweat a clear, sweet, faintly sticky fluid that draws flies and bees. They grow warm. A Laden person’s bed is warm for a day after they leave it, and nothing stored beneath it spoils.

The roots come last. They start as pale, hair-thin threads from the soles of the feet, and the Laden feel them as a pleasant tingling that becomes, over months, a desperate wish to stand still. If a Laden person stands on bare ground for an hour, the threads go down. If they stand for a day, the threads thicken into cords. Pulling free tears skin, and the cords bleed, and it hurts in a way the Laden describe as being torn out of a warm bed in Lack. Most Laden of the Gut-lines are moved on drays with iron floors, because iron is the one thing roots will not take in. Most Laden of the poor are simply allowed to plant.

The Brink

At the Brink the Laden person is more field than flesh. They are rooted somewhere and cannot be moved without killing them; their bulk spreads outward into the soil and the soil rises to meet it. The face sinks into the mound of the body. The limbs are hummocks. The eyes cloud green. Crops grow on them, densely, without being sown. A Brink-Laden can still speak, though slowly and from deep in the chest, and still eats, endlessly, and everything around them grows: the grass in a ring of thirty yards around a Brink-Laden is waist-high and toothed, and the wheat leans toward them when they speak. Visitors sometimes feel the ground pulse in time with the Brink-Laden’s heart. In the last weeks the person begins to forget their own name and to remember, instead, the names of the fields around them, and the names of those who have been Reaped into those fields.

The Seating

A Laden person stops being a person and becomes a place: a low hill, warm to the touch, where things grow very well. Some keep a mouth.

There is no single moment of Seating. The family notices, one morning, that Gran has stopped speaking and the hill has started breathing. The breath is slow, perhaps once an hour, and the whole mound lifts with it. The soil of a Seated hill is the richest on the Table. Its grass is the sweetest, its fruit the heaviest, its wheat the most toothed. Many of the best fields in the south are somebody’s great-grandmother. Fatlanders say this with pride and mean it.

Some hills keep a mouth. It sits somewhere in the turf like a wet red pond-edge, lipped and toothed, and it talks, and it eats whatever is put in it, and it is hungry. Some keep eyes, deep in the grass, that open in rain. And some, the College has recently confirmed, keep moving: very slowly, a few inches a year, toward the nearest other hill.

Land and Weather

The Fatlands are low, wet, endless green-and-red plain under a heavy yellow sky. From the Rim Road they look like a painted country: the green of pasture and the red of turned soil and the gold of toothed wheat, laid out in strips as far as the eye can follow, under a sky the colour of old butter that never quite clears. There are no mountains. There are hardly any trees outside the orchards. There are only the fields, the long wet roads, the slow brown rivers, and the hills, which are people.

It is always warm. Even in Lack the ground steams at dawn. The ground gives underfoot like a mattress over a sleeper, and if you stand still in an open field, you can feel it slowly rise and fall. Foreigners take a week to stop noticing. Fatlanders never notice at all, and are made seasick by stone.

Rain is called drip. It falls warm and heavy and leaves a yellowish film on standing water, which cooks skim off with flat spoons and use for frying; a good drip-pan after a storm is a housewife’s pride. The hot-season wind, the Belch, comes up out of the south in late Plenty smelling of rendering, of tallow-vats and singed hair, and lasts for days; tempers break, and the Feasting Laws are relaxed so that people may eat a sixth meal to steady their nerves. In late Plenty the fields sweat and the whole country glistens. Midges rise from the wheat in shimmering columns. Every surface is tacky. And at the turn of Carving comes Marbling, the first frost, when the fat in the soil whitens overnight in long branching veins, and the plains look from horizon to horizon like a cut of meat laid on a slab. Marbling morning is a holiday. Children run out barefoot to crunch it.

The rivers are slow and brown and thick and warm, and they are called, without irony, gravy: the Brawn, which runs south past Sated to the sea, is the Great Gravy, and its tributaries are the Little Gravies. Their water must be strained before drinking. What is strained out is eaten.

A Gazetteer of the Fatlands

Sated. The capital, on the Great Gravy, built in concentric rings of low, broad, buttressed halls around the Weighhouse. Every door is double-wide, every floor reinforced, every stair replaced by a ramp, and the smell of gravy rises from every drain, because the drains carry the city’s drip and dripping down to the rendering-houses on the river. The streets are paved with fat-stained stone and wide enough for a Gut-lines dray and its eight oxen. Sated never stops eating: street-cooks work all night beneath lamps that burn tallow of uncertain provenance, and at any hour the air is blue with frying. Its population is four hundred thousand by head and, as its proud citizens say, “a hundred and twenty million by the pound.”

The Weighhouse. The seat of the Board of Plenty, in the heart of Sated: a vast round hall under a dome of glazed bone tiles, with the Great Scales at its centre, iron and bronze, each pan large enough to hold a cart. Here the Weighing is held each Grace, and here the Board sits, on benches sunk into the floor because many members can no longer be lifted onto anything. The floor of the Weighhouse has been reinforced six times. Its cellars, which nobody below the Board visits, are said to be full of roots.

The Bleeding Orchards. Ten thousand acres of fruit trees east of Sated, in long rows on the slopes of what were once hills and may still be. At pruning time in early Grace the trees scream when cut: a high, wet, wavering sound, like a calf at the knife, from ten thousand throats at once, audible in Sated on a still day. Orchard-keepers go deaf young, by choice, with heated needles, and speak in a hand-language of their own. The fruit is the finest in the world. The sap is collected in buckets for blood-pudding.

Low Tilth. The richest farmland in the world, a wide shallow basin south of Sated where the soil is black and soft and sweats in Plenty like a basted joint. It yields three harvests a year. It has the highest Reaping of any district, and nobody there locks their door, because it has never helped. Low Tilth villages are small, quiet and well-fed, and every family has someone in the fields. It is the home of Pell Hogget and the Long Count, and of the Scarecrow.

The Dowager Hills. A range of low green mounds three miles outside Sated, along the old Weighing Road: nine generations of Gut-lines matriarchs, Seated, ninety-one hills in all. The grass on them is short and soft and bright, and the soil is warm right through Lack. Each hill has a name, a family, a gatekeeper’s hut, and a speaking-place: a hollow where the turf parts to show a mouth, or a pair of lids, or, on the oldest, only a warm damp crack that exhales. The Gut-lines families still consult their Dowagers on matters of marriage, inheritance and precedence, and bring them offerings. The offerings are meat. The Hills accept them, chewing for hours with a sound like a slow mill. Visitors walking the path between the mounds report that the hills breathe in sequence, a long slow wave of rising and falling turf, as though passing something along.

Consulting a Dowager

A family with a question for its Dowager brings her a joint (custom demands the best cut from the most recent wake) and the Hill-Speaker on duty lays it in the speaking-place. The Dowager eats. When she has eaten, she answers, sometimes in minutes and sometimes after a day. Her voice comes up through the turf and is felt in the feet as much as heard. Dowagers know things: the true parentage of heirs, the location of hidden debts, which fields will Reap this year. They are rarely wrong. They are also no longer entirely the women they were, and their advice now tends, more and more, toward the same few counsels: Plant him. Feed her to me. Come closer. Sit down. Lie down. Stay. A PC who sleeps a night on a Dowager Hill gains a true answer to one question (GM’s choice of how cryptic) and must make a Dread 3 check on waking, because the roots will have begun.

The Chute. The Rim Road export depot, at the Fatlands’ northern edge where the Great Gravy meets the Road: a mile of rendering-houses, salting-sheds, cooperages and stockyards built around a long stone ramp down which barrels roll, day and night, into the Company’s wagons. Meat goes out in barrels with the origin stamped over twice. The smell of the Chute reaches eleven miles on the Belch. The Renderers’ Union holds it absolutely. The Rim Road Company keeps an office there with a notary’s bench, and every barrel is tallied on a platter.

The Trencher. (new) The field where Ummer was eaten: a great shallow bowl of black soil a mile across, in the heart of the plain west of Sated. Nothing is planted there and everything grows anyway, in a dense tangle of toothed grain, veined roots and fleshy creepers that heal over any path cut through them in a night. At its centre is a rise of soil shaped, from the air, very like a sleeping figure lying on its side. The Board forbids entry. Pilgrims of the Second Helping go anyway and lie down in the creepers and are found, weeks later, smiling and partly absorbed.

The Gavage. (new) The Board’s house of correction for the Thin, outside Sated on the Brawn: a long, low, whitewashed building of a hundred cells, each with a chair of oak and iron, a set of leather straps, a funnel-stand, and a drain. Its kitchens never close. Its smell is of porridge, lard, and vomit. See the Thin, below.

The Dusk Acres. (new) The “far fields” of the Cullmasters: a belt of Board-owned land on the edges of Low Tilth and the eastern plains, rotated each Carving, where the Cullmasters’ dusk-shift labourers are sent. They are the most productive fields in the country, and the most carefully ploughed, and each plot carries a small numbered stone at its corner.

Gladbelly. (new) The commune of the Second Helping, a village of long open tables in a meadow beside the Little Gravy, where the cult eats together continuously and sings. The meadow is unusually lush. There is a slaughter-pavilion in the middle, hung with garlands, where the Offered go willingly. See the Second Helping, below.

Marrable Hall. (new) The seat of Dame Suet Marrable and the Unending Dinner: a great ramped house in the Dowager Hills whose dining hall has had no clear floor for eighty-one years. The table is three hundred feet long. The hall’s foundations have shifted a yard downhill.

Hogget’s Barn. (new) In the village of Kettle Furrow in Low Tilth, a plain timber barn whose inner walls are scored, floor to rafter, with tally-marks: the Long Count, kept in chalk, then knife, then paint, by Pell Hogget and the villages that copy him. Pilgrims come to touch the marks for their own dead. The Board has twice tried to burn it, and both times the village stood around it in a ring, eating, and the Bailiffs could not bring themselves to break up a meal.

History

Year (A.G.)Event
0The Meal on the Trencher. The Week of Rising: crops shoulder-high in seven days.
0–204The Sweet Reigns. The Fatlands feed the Table and grow rich and wide.
61First recorded Laden: Matron Ysolde Tullow, whose feet rooted in her own kitchen.
97First Seating. Ysolde becomes the first of the Dowager Hills.
131The Wake Ordinance. Burial forbidden; the dead to be served by kin.
204The Tooth Harvest. The Board rules toothed wheat “a new and superior strain.”
260The Weighing. Votes assigned by body weight.
300First Wolf-Warden appointed. The word “wolves” enters Board proclamations.
312The Appetite accepted as a defence to theft, if the article is eaten.
455The Thin Rising. Put down by force-feeding; fasting made treason.
457The Gavage built. The Cullmasters chartered as “an office of agricultural steadiness.”
560Dame Suet Marrable lays the Unending Dinner.
611Chairman Obb Tullow walks for the last time.
626Wren Hollowell born in Bramble Furrow, a Blank.
629Pell Hogget begins the Long Count.
631–641The Reaping doubles.
638First field-faces reported in Low Tilth: turnips, squashes, a cabbage that blinked.
640Tullow’s feet root through his cart. Tobias Wether crosses from the Fast and eats.

The Sweet Reigns

For two hundred years the Fatlands were the happiest country on the Table. The Week of Rising was followed by a century of harvests so abundant that grain was used for ballast and meat was fed to dogs. Sated grew from a market-village into the wealthiest city in the world. Fatland envoys went up the Rim Road in gilded wagons with presents of smoked haunch, and every other land, starving or merely ordinary, fell over itself to sign treaties. These were the years in which “You look heavy” became the highest compliment, and the years in which the Gut-lines, swelling, ruled from couches and then from beds, and everyone thought it was glory.

The Wake Ordinance of 131 A.G. merely made law of what had become custom. Nobody had been buried in the Fatlands for a generation. It seemed obscene to put good meat in the ground when the ground was already so full.

The Weighing and the Rising

By 260 A.G. the largest Gut-lines could no longer travel to the Board, and the Board came to them; the Weighing simply made their bulk a formal measure of power. The poor accepted it, because the poor were eating well. Two centuries later, they were not. Export had swallowed the surplus, the Reaping had grown, and a preacher named Hester Gaunt began teaching in the Orchards that the god was in the hunger, and that if the people stopped feeding it, it would starve back down into the soil. The Thin Rising of 455 A.G. was not an army. It was eleven thousand people in Low Tilth sitting down in the roads and refusing to eat. The Board sent the Bailiffs with funnels. Within a month most of the Thin were fat, and the rest were dead, and Hester Gaunt had been fed in the Weighhouse before the whole Board for nine days until she burst. Fasting has been treason since.

The Long Count

In 629, Pell Hogget of Kettle Furrow noticed that his village had been one smaller each autumn for as long as he could remember, and scratched it on his barn wall. He started asking neighbouring villages. Then they started sending him their numbers. The Long Count is now copied in two hundred villages, by people who share no organization but a habit, and it shows something the Board has spent three centuries calling wolves: the Reaping has doubled in ten years, and it is still accelerating.

Rule, Law and Politics

The Fatlands are governed by the Board of Plenty, seated in the Weighhouse at Sated. The Board has about two hundred members, drawn from the Gut-lines, the Renderers, the great granaries and a handful of elected district deacons. Each member’s vote counts in proportion to their weight, taken publicly once a year at the Weighing. A Gut-lines matriarch of fourteen hundred pounds outvotes nine farmers’ deacons together. The Chairman, Obb Tullow, at nineteen hundred pounds, holds more votes alone than the whole of Low Tilth. He has not walked in thirty years.

The Gut-lines are the nobility. They are the largest, the hungriest, and the furthest along the Regrowth, and their estates are run from beds, then from drays, then from the ground. Succession disputes turn on whether a rooted, mouthless hill can still be said to hold title. The courts have ruled that it can, which is why the Dowager Hills still own a third of the country and why their consultations carry the force of law.

Law in the Fatlands is mostly about eating. The Feasting Laws set five meals a day; leaving food on the plate is a fine of one lack per crumb-weight, assessed by the Bailiff’s scale; refusing a meal is sedition, punishable by the Gavage. Theft of food is barely a crime, since the thief will eat it and the court considers the matter closed. Theft of weight, by contrast, is grave: to starve a person, to keep a child thin, to purge, to bleed for the purpose of lightness, is treason against the Weighing. The worst crime of all is waste. A man who let a barrel of meat rot in 602 A.G. was rendered for tallow by order of the Board, and the tallow was used to light the courtroom for the next trial.

Punishment is by feeding (the Gavage), by fine, by the dusk-shift, or by the table. A convicted murderer in the Fatlands is executed in the Renderers’ yards, and the family of the victim has first cut. This is called making good.

Abroad, the Fatlands’ power is food. They feed half the Table by way of the Rim Road, and every other land depends on that meat while trying not to think about it. The Vigil eats Fatland salt-beef to keep its strength through sleepless decades. Oathen buys toothed flour by the shipload. Sallowreach, which needs little food, buys Fatland tallow for its Seamers. The Board knows exactly how much the world would starve without it, and charges accordingly.

Culture and Daily Life

Meals. Five meals a day are mandatory: Firstbite at dawn, Elevenses, Midday, Fourth Plate, and Supper, with whatever the purse allows in between. Every meal begins with the grace, which thanks the field by name (“Thank you, Long Acre. Thank you, Hessop’s Rise.”) and ends with the plate wiped clean with bread. Strangers add the common “Lack keep away.” Fatland cooking is lavish, rich and brown: pies and puddings, roasts and dripping, sausages fat as a forearm, gravy on everything. The poor eat potatoes and fat bacon and are not, by any outside measure, poor eaters.

Dress. Fatlanders dress in loose layered smocks, laced at the side so they can be let out as the wearer grows. Belts are a mark of ill-omen and worn only by the Thin. The rich wear silk in field-colours, red and gold and green, cut wide, and pin their folds with brooches of polished bone. Teeth from the toothed wheat are threaded into necklaces for children.

Marriage and the body. Weight is beauty, and courtship is conducted over food. A suitor feeds the beloved with his own hands at the betrothal supper, and the beloved’s family watches to see that the feeding is generous. Wedding vows are sworn over a shared plate. Couples speak of “growing together,” and Gut-lines marriages sometimes end with both partners rooted side by side in a single hill. What happens in a Fatland marriage bed is, in the Fatland view, simply another kind of appetite and is spoken of in the same breath as supper, with a knowing look. Outsiders are discomfited by how readily lovers there speak of wanting to eat each other, and by how literally some of them mean it.

Children. Fatland children are fed from the moment they are born and weighed every week. A child who fails to gain is a scandal for its parents and a matter for the Bailiff. Children glean behind the harvesters, turn spits, and are put to sleep with a strip of fat to suck. They are warned never to go into the fields alone at dusk in Carving, and they all do, once, on a dare.

Death rites. There are no graves. The dead are served at the wake, by the family, on the best plates. To be buried uneaten would be the deepest insult to a life; it is reserved for traitors and the Thin, whose lean bodies are thrown in the Brawn. A wake begins at noon on the day after death. A jointer is hired if the family can afford one; the deceased’s fat is rendered first, the heart goes to the eldest, the hands into a pie, the marrow to the most beloved. Neighbours bring bread and are fed in return. The bones are cracked, boiled for stock, and then returned to the family’s field, ground fine, so that the person goes back to the god and comes up again as crop. A good wake is talked about for years. “He ate well” is said of the dead, meaning he tasted good.

Remember, she was soft. Remember, she was sweet. Pass the plate along, along; there’s not a bit to waste.

Remember, she was heavy, love. Remember, she was kind. Lick the bowl and crack the bone, there’s marrow yet to find.

And when you’re in the furrow, love, and when you’re in the wheat, we’ll sit at board and say your name, and you’ll be what we eat.

— wake-song, sung across the plains while the copper boils

Festivals. The Weighing in Grace is a festival of three days, with pie-stalls the length of Sated and the Board brought to the scales on drays before a roaring crowd. Marbling morning is a children’s holiday. Harvest Home at the end of Carving is a week of feasting that the Long Count has made very quiet in recent years. And on Tablenight the whole country attempts a one-day fast in penance for the Meal. Pantries are locked, keys are given to the priest, and everyone sits in silence. Nobody has ever recorded a village that made it to sundown. By noon children are screaming; by mid-afternoon someone has broken the pantry door; by dusk there is a riot of eating, shameful and joyful, in every village on the plain, and the year begins again.

Crime and punishment. Fatland justice is fast and fed. Petty offenders are fined in meals owed. Brawlers are made to sit and eat together until they reconcile. Debtors are sent to the dusk-shift, from which they return, mostly, with the debt worked off. Mostly.

Proverbs. A thin man has a secret. Eat while it’s warm; it won’t be. The field remembers who fed it. Never trust a cook who isn’t heavy. Nobody’s full, but some are fuller. What the wheat took, the bread gives back.

Oaths on the dead. The binding oath of the Fatlands is sworn with a mouthful of a dead relative’s flesh held on the tongue: By my mother’s meat, which is in me. To break it is to have eaten your mother for nothing, and Fatlanders consider this the vilest thing a person can do. Wakes are often delayed so that the family can settle disputes by such oaths while the meat is fresh.

Wakes and the Outsider

A PC from another land will be invited to a wake sooner or later. It is the highest courtesy a Fatland family can offer a guest. Refusing to eat is not merely rude; it is sedition, and a Bailiff may be called. Eating counts as cannibalism for any Dread or Rites purpose the GM’s table cares about (Dread 2 the first time for a non-Fatlander; Dread 1 thereafter; Dread 0 for a native). It is also, without exception, the most delicious thing the character has ever tasted, and a non-Fatlander of Cut 1+ who eats at a wake gains 1 Hunger, because the meat is looking for somewhere to be hungry from.

Factions

The Board of Plenty

The government: two hundred members, vast, slow, and aware of the Reaping in more detail than it admits. The Board believes in continuity, export, and the Weighing. It knows the “wolves” are the fields; it has known for three hundred years; it has records, in the root-choked cellars of the Weighhouse, of every Reaping by district and year, and its private projections match Pell Hogget’s to the head. What the Board wants is to keep the Fatlands eating and the Table buying until the god arrives, and then, if possible, to be the god’s favoured guests. Its enemies are the Thin and the Long Count; its allies are the Renderers (uneasily) and the Rim Road Company (expensively). A PC joins by service: as a clerk, a Bailiff, a Weigher’s assistant, or a member’s Carrier.

RankTitleGrants
1LadleA Bailiff’s or clerk’s badge; right to enforce the Feasting Laws; free Supper at any inn.
2DeaconA district seat; one vote per hundred pounds; the ear of the Wolf-Warden.
3MemberA Board vote by weight; immunity from the dusk-shift; a Carrier retinue.
4Great MemberCommittee seat; access to the Weighhouse cellars and the real Reaping figures.
5ChairmanThe heaviest vote. Rule of the Fatlands, from a cart, then from the ground.

The Thin

Outlawed fasters who believe starving the body starves the god. They are gaunt, hunted, and the only people in the south who seem clear-headed. The Thin eat once every three days, in secret, a handful of ash-bread and water; they bind their bellies with cord, live in barns and ditches, and meet in the Orchards where the deafened keepers will not hear. Their faith is Purgation-adjacent, and the cross-border Purgation sends them money, but the Thin are stranger and gentler than their foreign cousins: they do not kill nobles. They simply refuse. They want the Fatlands to stop feeding the god for one whole season, and believe that if it did, the Reaping would end. Their allies are the Purgation and, secretly, a few Orchard-keepers; their enemies are every Bailiff on the plain. A PC joins by fasting in their company for nine days and being seen to suffer.

RankTitleGrants
1HollowA cord for the belly; a hiding place; the Thin’s hand-signs.
2LeanKnowledge of the safe barns; a share of the ash-bread.
3GauntLeads a cell; may rescue prisoners from the Gavage.
4BoneSpeaks for a district; carries messages to the Purgation.
5The Thin ManCorder Lank. Unopposed.

The Gavage. Captured Thin are not executed. They are fed. A prisoner is strapped into an oak chair, head locked back in a padded iron frame, jaw held open with a boxwood wedge. A funnel of polished horn is seated in the throat. The feeders are kindly, plump, singing women in white aprons, and they pour: warm lard-porridge first, then gravy thick with marrow, then a puree of pork and bread and dripping, slowly, a ladle every few breaths, while the prisoner chokes and heaves and the feeder strokes the throat downward with a buttered thumb to help it along, murmuring there, there, love, there’s a good belly. A Gavage session lasts three hours and comes five times a day. The prisoner’s body, after nine years of hunger, does not want to fight. It wants. That is the true torture of the Gavage: the Thin weep because it is wonderful, because the gravy is the best thing they have tasted in years, because their bellies stretch and gurgle and rejoice, and with every ladle they can feel the god in them waking up and growing fat and grateful. Most leave the Gavage in a season, heavy and silent and eating. Some come back to the Thin anyway, and weigh the cord around them, and begin again.

The Renderers' Union

The slaughter, salting, and shipping trades: butchers, renderers, coopers, drovers, salters, jointers and the dock-gangs of the Chute. They control what leaves the country and know what is in it. The Union’s members are broad, red-armed, practical people who smell of brine and tallow and talk frankly about anything. They believe in work and in the barrel. They want their wages, their monopoly, and the Board’s continued need of them; they also want, more and more, someone else to be blamed when the world finds out what has been in the barrels. Their allies are the Rim Road Company; their enemies, the Board when it tries to tax them. A PC joins by apprenticeship, or by doing a job in the Chute and keeping quiet.

RankTitleGrants
1HookWork in the yards; Union protection; a cleaver.
2JointerRight to carve at wakes for a fee; the trade’s secret cuts.
3YardmasterCommand of a rendering-house; a share of export profits.
4StamperControl of a barrel-mark; knows what is in each consignment.
5Mistress of the UnionBrisket Annalow. Can stop the Rim Road with a word.

The Cullmasters

A quiet office of the Board which holds that the Reaping can be steered. If the fields must take, the Cullmasters reason, better that they take vagrants, debtors and troublemakers than good farmers and children. They draw up the lists. They assign the dusk shift. They think of it as agriculture.

The dusk-shift is a ritual, though no Cullmaster would use the word. On Carving afternoons, a Cullmaster’s clerk reads the list in the village square: names, debts, and a plot-number in the Dusk Acres. The named are fed a large and excellent supper at the Board’s expense, a real feast with roast and pie and hot bread and as much as they can hold, because the Cullmasters have found that the fields take the well-fed more gently, and because, they say, it is only decent. Then the named are dressed in clean white field-smocks and walked out along the furrows in a line, each carrying a sickle with a ribboned handle, to their numbered stones. The Cullmaster walks behind them with a lantern. At each stone he stops, bows to the worker, and says the words: Work well. The field is grateful. You are paid in full. Then he unrolls a strip of red cloth across the end of the row, so that the worker will know which side of it to stay on, and walks back to the road, and stands with his clerk and his lantern to watch the light go. The workers who try to leave the row are turned back by Bailiffs. The ones who stay bent over their work, cutting and binding, see the wheat begin to lean. A good Cullmaster records each Reaping in his ledger with the plot-number, the time, and the weight of the following year’s yield. A great Cullmaster can tell you, to the pound, how much bread one debtor makes.

Not all of the dusk-shift are taken. Perhaps one in three walk back at full dark, shaking, their debts paid. That fraction, the Cullmasters insist, proves it is labour and not execution. The Long Count suggests the fraction is falling.

RankTitleGrants
1LanternbearerWalks the line; carries the light; a stipend.
2Listing ClerkDrafts the dusk-shift lists; may strike or add one name a season.
3CullmasterOwns a plot-ledger; command of Bailiffs on Carving evenings.
4Senior CullmasterChooses which districts are spared; reports to the Board’s inner committee.
5Cullmaster-GeneralVarn Sweetbread. Steers the Reaping, he believes.

The Second Helping

A joyous cult of the Bait doctrine. The god starved us so we would eat it, they say; it wanted to be inside us, and now it wants to be fed and to feed, and the holiest thing a person can do is join in. Eat, and be eaten, and be glad. The Second Helping meets at Gladbelly and in a hundred kitchens across the plain, and they are the happiest people in the south: fat, laughing, singing hymns about gravy, embracing strangers. They want the Seating, and they want it soon, and they intend to hurry it along by giving the god as much of themselves as it will take. Their allies are the Second Table, which finds them useful and gullible; their enemies are the Thin, who pity them, and the Board, which finds them embarrassing and quietly very convenient. A PC joins by sharing a meal at Gladbelly and accepting a second helping. Everyone is offered one.

The cult’s highest sacrament is the Offering. A member who has decided to go to the god announces it at table, and everyone cheers. There is a week of feasting in the Offered’s honour, in which they are fed by every hand in the commune. On the last evening they are bathed in warm dripping and garlanded with toothed wheat and carried in procession to the pavilion, singing. Their family walks beside them. Their family, too, is singing, and it is only afterward, on the long benches, with the plates going round, that the singing becomes something else: a widower holding a fork he cannot lift, a daughter who keeps saying but she was happy, she was happy, she said she was happy, a small boy asking where his mother has gone while a sweet brown smell drifts out of the kitchens. The Second Helping does not talk about the ones left behind. They are expected to rejoice, and to eat, and to offer themselves in their turn. Many do. That is how the cult grows: by grief that has nowhere else to go.

RankTitleGrants
1GuestA seat at the long tables; the hymns; never to eat alone again.
2ServerFeeds newcomers; may speak at table.
3PlateholderLeads a household kitchen; tends the Offered in their last week.
4GarlandHas given part of themselves (a finger, an ear) and is honoured.
5The ProphetBrother Glut, who is being served one piece at a time.
Cross-Border Powers in the South

The Second Table is strong in the Fatlands, because the Gut-lines are its natural members: who better to eat a god twice than a family already eating everything? Its southern chapter meets in Marrable Hall under cover of the Unending Dinner. The Cutwrights’ College keeps a southern registry in Sated and knows, from three centuries of weighing records, exactly which families will Seat next. The Purgation funds the Thin. The Reckoners find the Fatlands hard going: a high-Cut Gut-line, rooted on its estate, is almost impossible to kill, and the hills do not die when stabbed. The Rim Road Company owns a third of the Chute’s wagons and does not inspect the barrels.

The Fatlands Now

The Reaping has doubled in ten years, and the fields are turning up things with faces: a turnip with a nose and two shut lids, a squash with the profile of a missing child, an ear of wheat that, when split, held a single human molar with a silver filling. The Board’s answer is the Cullmasters, and the dusk-shift lists grow longer every Carving. The Thin are growing, recruiting among the families of the culled. A girl has appeared who feels no hunger at all, and the Board has put a price on her that does not specify alive. And for the first time, an exile from the Fast has sat down at a Fatlands table and eaten. What is happening to him has no name yet.

Underneath all of it is the arithmetic the Board will not publish. The Reaping doubles; the hills multiply; the Dowagers creep toward one another. Ummer is gathering itself up out of ten thousand graves and ten thousand bellies, and it is hungry, and it has the whole of the Fatlands for a body. Many Fatlanders have started, without saying why, to dream of walking in procession.

Adventure Hooks

  • The Notched Barrels. Quartermaster Ivo Stockpot sends a sealed list to a PC he trusts: the export barrels he has notched. A Vigil buyer has fallen ill in a way that sounds very like the Appetite. The PCs must trace a consignment from the Chute to the Rim Road, against the Renderers, the Company, and the Board, and decide who on the Table should know what they have been eating.
  • The Dusk List. A PC, or someone they love, is named on a Cullmaster’s list. Varn Sweetbread is courteous and immovable. The PCs have until Carving dusk to bribe a Listing Clerk, find a substitute (Fatlanders will suggest one), break the Gavage open for a Thin rescue as distraction, or walk the row themselves and survive.
  • Wren for Weight. Wren Hollowell is hidden in a Thin barn in the Orchards. The Board will pay her weight in bone coin; the Second Table will pay more for her organs; the Thin will die for her. The Fasting Girl wants none of it. She wants to see the sea.
  • The Hill That Walked. Mercy Sowerby, the Hill-Speaker, reports that two Dowager Hills have moved close enough to touch, and that their mouths are talking to each other in a language no one living speaks. The Gut-lines want it hushed. The College wants measurements. The hills want visitors.
  • The Scarecrow Turns. In Low Tilth, the Scarecrow has turned around, and it is facing Pell Hogget’s barn. The villagers want it burned. Nobody who has tried to light it has come back from the far field.

Rumors of the Fatlands

d10Rumor
1The Chairman’s roots have reached the Weighhouse cellars and are drinking from the Gravy. (True.)
2There are wolves after all; a pack was seen near Kettle Furrow. (False; it was a Cullmaster’s line in white.)
3Dame Marrable’s Dinner has a second table in the cellar where only nobles sit, and the meat there is different. (True: it is the Second Table.)
4Eat a Blank’s heart and you’ll be full forever. (False, but it is why Wren is hunted.)
5The Fast’s god is walking the Rim Road, and if you follow it you’ll find a meal that fills. (Half-true.)
6The Board fasts in secret and only pretends to eat. (False. They eat more than anyone.)
7The Thin Man drinks something from the Orchards that kills the hunger. (False. See Corder Lank.)
8Granny Cracknel can tell who’s next for the Reaping by the teeth in the flour. (True.)
9Low Tilth was once twice the size, and half of it is under the wheat. (True.)
10The Brother Glut who preaches now is the third man to bear that name. (False; it has always been the same man, less each year.)

The People of the Fatlands

Chairman Obb Tullow, the Heaviest Vote. Head of the Board at nineteen hundred pounds, he is moved by dray and eight oxen through streets cleared by Bailiffs. Up close he is a landscape: rolls of cool, brown, loam-soft flesh draped over the dray’s iron bed like a slumped haystack, crusted with the green shoots his Washers never quite get off, and at the summit a small, pink, clever face that looks out of the folds like a man peering from a cellar. His voice is reedy and precise. He is still the shrewdest mind on the Board. His feet rooted through the cart’s iron floor last spring, through a seam the smiths had missed, and the Board has agreed not to notice; the dray has not moved since, and the Board now meets around it. He wants to die Chairman. He fears the moment his mouth closes and the hill keeps voting. His secret is that the roots go all the way down to the Weighhouse cellars, and he can feel the Reaping through them, every one, as a warm full mouthful.

Obb Tullow — Chairman of the Board of Plenty
AttributesHand 1 · Gut 6 · Lung 1 · Eye 3 · Tongue 4 · Caul 3
Cut & RegrowthCut 5 (Gut-line) · Regrowth 10 (the Brink) · Hunger 8
SkillsFeast 5, Endure 4, Clause 3, Persuade 3, Intimidate 3, Reckoning 3
BodyFlesh 18 · Guard 12 · Armor 1 (loam-flesh) · Fray 5
Attacksrolling crush +2 (4); cannot pursue
GiftsField-Body (feels every footstep in the Weighhouse and on the Weighing Road); the Board’s grain bends toward him when he speaks; regains 1d6 Flesh per meal
Wantsto eat whatever is placed within reach; never to be moved; to be told the Reaping figures, aloud, slowly
Dread3 (to watch him eat, or to see what grows under the dray)
SecretTullow has arranged for the Cullmasters to list the families of every Deacon who votes against him.

Dame Suet Marrable. Gut-lines matriarch, mistress of Marrable Hall, and hostess of the Unending Dinner, in continuous service for eighty-one years. She sits at the head of the three-hundred-foot table on a reinforced throne that is slowly sinking into the floorboards, swathed in gold silk, her face powdered white and her many chins hung with pearls like dew on a hedge. She smells of rosewater over roast pork. Her voice is warm and husky and she calls everyone duck. Guests have been born at her table and several have been served at it, when they died there; the custom is that no one leaves, and some have not. She wants the Dinner to outlast her and fears that it will not, because her feet have begun to grow down through the floor. She is the Second Table’s southern chair, and the cellar beneath her dining hall holds a smaller table where the guests are older and the meat is something rarer.

Dame Suet Marrable — Hostess of the Unending Dinner
AttributesHand 2 · Gut 5 · Lung 1 · Eye 4 · Tongue 5 · Caul 3
Cut & RegrowthCut 4 (Gut-line) · Regrowth 8 (the Course) · Hunger 7
SkillsPersuade 4, Feast 5, Clause 3, Endure 3, Search 2, Blades 1
BodyFlesh 16 · Guard 12 · Armor 1 · Fray 3
Attackscarving knife +3 (2)
GiftsTaste the Name (one bite of a guest’s blood tells her their family, Cut and one secret); her hall’s food compels (Caul + Resolve, Hard 14, to rise from her table)
Wantsthat no guest leave hungry; that no guest leave
Dread2 (to see a guest served)
SecretShe has Tobias Wether’s name on a place card, and a seat waiting for him in the cellar.

Pell Hogget, the Counter. A farmer from Kettle Furrow in Low Tilth: short, broad, sunburnt, with a wheat-coloured beard and a stub of chalk always behind one ear. He speaks slowly and carefully and gives numbers instead of opinions. He noticed his village was one smaller each autumn and wrote it down, and now two hundred villages send him their tallies and his barn wall is a ledger of the dead. He eats less than he should and the Bailiff has begun to look at him. He wishes he had never learned to count. He fears that the numbers have a shape: his projection crosses his own village’s population in nineteen years, and the whole country’s soon after. His secret is that his wife was culled four years ago, and he has never put her mark on the wall.

Corder Lank, the Thin Man. Leader of the Thin. He has eaten nothing but water and ash for six years and can be counted bone by bone: a long, brown, tendon-strung figure in a rope belt, his skin tight as a drumhead over ribs and hips and knuckles, his eyes huge and calm and very clear. He smells of woodsmoke and nothing else. He speaks quietly and always first asks whether you are hungry. He is the only man in the south who does not feel the hunger, and he will not say how. The truth is that the hunger did not leave him: it went out of him, piece by piece, into those who fast beside him. Every Thin cell carries a share of Corder Lank’s gnawing on top of its own. He worked this out three years ago. He has not told them. He cannot stop leading, because it is the only thing that keeps him clear.

Corder Lank — the Thin Man
AttributesHand 2 · Gut 1 · Lung 3 · Eye 3 · Tongue 4 · Caul 5
Cut & RegrowthCut 2 · Regrowth 3 (the Taste, dormant) · Hunger 0
SkillsResolve 5, Endure 4, Persuade 3, Stealth 3, Athletics 2, Rites 2, Blades 1
BodyFlesh 13 · Guard 15 · Armor 0 · Fray 6
Attacksknife +3 (2)
GiftsPassing the Plate: anyone who fasts a day in his company loses 1 Hunger and he loses none; they gain it back, doubled, the day they leave him
Wantsto be needed; never to be fed
Dread1
SecretHis hunger lives in his followers. If he dies, it goes back to the god all at once, and the Thin will feel it go.

Mistress Brisket Annalow. Boss of the Renderers’ Union: a vast, red-armed woman in a leather apron stiff with salt, her grey hair cropped short, a cleaver on a chain at her hip and a pencil behind her ear. She talks like a drover and laughs like a kettle. She can stop every barrel on the Rim Road with one word, and she knows precisely which of them should never have been filled, because she has kept a second ledger for twenty-two years. She wants the Union paid and her people safe. She fears the day the Table stops buying. She would sell the Board out in an afternoon to keep the Chute open.

Brisket Annalow Threat 5 · Flesh 15 · Guard 12 · Attack +6 (cleaver 3) · Armor 1 · Dread 0

Hob Gristle, the Honest Butcher. A big, mild, sorrowful man with forearms like hams and a bald head beaded with sweat. He can tell by taste what a cut used to be, down to the name: a mouthful of sausage tells him the pig, the field it ate from, and the name of anyone Reaped into that field. It has ruined him for the trade. He still works, because jointing at wakes is the only honest money left, and he apologizes to every joint, quietly, by name. He wants one barrel from the Chute that tastes of nothing but beef. He fears the day he tastes someone he loves. He has already tasted his brother, in a pie in Sated, and has told no one.

Cullmaster Varn Sweetbread. The Board’s quiet hand: a neat, plump, pink man in grey broadcloth, with soft white fingers, rimless spectacles and a ledger chained to his belt. He smells faintly of lavender, which he uses to cover the field. His voice is gentle and his manners perfect. He decides which vagrants, debtors and troublemakers are assigned the dusk shift, and he thinks of it as agriculture, in the most literal sense: he weighs the next year’s yields and has proved, to his own satisfaction, that a culled vagrant makes better bread than a Reaped farmer. He walks every line himself and bows at every stone. He is not cruel. That is the worst thing about him.

Varn Sweetbread — Cullmaster-General
AttributesHand 2 · Gut 3 · Lung 2 · Eye 4 · Tongue 3 · Caul 3
Cut & RegrowthCut 3 · Regrowth 5 (the Appetite) · Hunger 4
SkillsReckoning 4, Clause 3, Intimidate 3, Resolve 3, Rites 2, Endure 2, Blades 1
BodyFlesh 13 · Guard 13 · Armor 0 · Fray 2
Attacksribboned sickle +3 (3)
GiftsField-Reading: he knows, on any Carving evening, which plot will Reap first
Wantsto see the line through to the end; to taste the bread of each plot he culled
Dread2 (to watch his dusk-shift)
SecretHis own name is on next year’s list, in the Chairman’s hand.

Tansy Lard, the Gleaner. A girl of ten who gleans behind the harvesters in Low Tilth: skinny for a Fatlander, with tangled straw hair and a smock too short in the arms, and dirt permanently under her nails. She dug up a root with her mother’s birthmark on it, a brown splash shaped like a running hare, and has replanted it behind the house and waters it every day. It has grown. It has leaves like hands. Last week, at dusk, it said her name. Her father has noticed she has stopped eating at table and goes out after dark with the bowl. She wants her mother back. She is the reason the PCs may first learn what a Fatland root can become.

Brother Glut. Prophet of the Second Helping: enormous, radiant, and happy, a mountain of pink flesh in a garland of wheat, his face shining with sweat and tears of joy, his voice a deep golden bell that fills a meadow without trying. He preaches that being eaten is the highest form of being loved, and he has volunteered parts of himself to prove it: his left hand, both ears, three toes, a long strip from the flank. The wounds are bound with clean linen and he shows them off like medals. He embraces every stranger. He believes every word. What he does not see is the widows at the back of each meeting, holding their plates.

Brother Glut — Prophet of the Second Helping
AttributesHand 2 · Gut 5 · Lung 1 · Eye 2 · Tongue 5 · Caul 4
Cut & RegrowthCut 3 · Regrowth 8 (the Course) · Hunger 5
SkillsPersuade 5, Rites 4, Feast 4, Endure 4, Godsign 3
BodyFlesh 17 · Guard 11 · Armor 1 · Fray 0
Attackscrushing embrace +2 (1, held)
GiftsThe Shared Plate: anyone who eats his flesh loses 1d6 Hunger and must pass Caul + Resolve (Hard 14) or come back for more
Wantsto give; to see others give
Dread2 (to see him carve himself, smiling)
SecretHe has not felt the hunger since his hand was eaten. He thinks this is grace. It is the god, moving out.

Old Mother Rind. A Laden woman who rooted forty years ago and is now a small orchard hill outside the village of Kettle Furrow, with nine pear trees growing from her back and a working mouth half-hidden in the clover at her foot. Her lips are brown and cracked like bark and her teeth are wheat-teeth, many rows. Her voice is a dry old woman’s, amused and sharp. Her village asks her advice on marriages; she is always right, and always hungry, and her fee is meat. Lately she has asked for particular people.

Dr. Emmerich Paunch. The Board’s physician: a stooped, heavy, myopic man with ink-stained cuffs and a voice like a dry quill. He opened a Gut-lines stomach, under licence, to measure its capacity, and lowered a plumb line into it. He ran out of line at two hundred feet. He has since obtained longer line. He has not been able to bring himself to use it, because when he drew the first one up, the lead weight had been chewed. He wants to publish. He fears the Board, and what he heard echoing up the line. He will pay adventurers very well to hold the rope.

Sal Trotter, the Drover. A lean, weathered woman in a dung-crusted oilskin, with a crook, a whip she never uses, and a pipe she never lights. She walks herds to market at the Chute that the buyers call cattle. They walk on two legs when no one is watching the road. She has stopped naming them, because they started answering. She speaks little, mostly to the herd, in a low, even croon. She wants to finish one drive without looking back. She fears the day one of them asks her where they are going. It will be soon; the lead steer has begun to hum her songs.

Sal Trotter’s Herd (each) Threat 2 · Flesh 16 · Guard 10 · Attack +4 (trample 3) · Armor 1 · Dread 2 (to see them stand)

Wren Hollowell, the Fasting Girl. A Blank of fifteen from Bramble Furrow who has never once felt hungry. She is small and narrow and pale, with a long plain face and grey eyes that rest on things without wanting them, and in a land of the vast she looks like a drawing of a girl rather than a girl. She eats when reminded, without interest. The Thin kneel to her, which she hates. The Board has offered her weight in bone coin to whoever brings her in, and has not specified alive; the Second Table has a surgeon waiting. She wants to see the sea, and to be left alone. She is beginning to notice that fields go quiet when she walks through them, as though they cannot smell her at all.

Wren Hollowell Threat 2 · Flesh 10 · Guard 14 · Attack +2 (knife 2) · Armor 0 · Dread 0 · cannot be Reaped; no Cut, no Hunger

Garrick Tripe, the Weigher. Keeper of the official scales at the annual Weighing: a jovial, oily man in a brass-buttoned coat, with a waxed moustache and a dozen rings. For the right fee your pockets fill with lead, and for a better one your rival’s empty. He has personally elected three governments. He wants to retire rich. He fears that the Chairman knows exactly how much of his vote is lead; Tullow does, and is waiting for the right moment.

Lady Aspic Dellamore. A noble chef whose speciality is preservation: tall for a Gut-line, sleek and plump, in a white silk apron, with lacquered nails and a cold, musical laugh. Her rivals are displayed in her gallery, set in clear golden jelly, garnished with herbs and quail’s eggs, and blinking. The jelly keeps them; the Gut-line blood keeps them hungry. They watch visitors eat at her table. She wants to be the greatest cook on the Table. She fears blandness. She is working on a new piece for the gallery, and has been measuring Dame Marrable.

Jem Crackle, the Cook’s Knife. A former spit-boy and now the most reliable assassin in Sated: wiry, quick, red-knuckled, with burn scars to the elbow and the cheerful, sweaty face of a kitchen lad. He smells of onions and hot iron. He kills only in kitchens, and what he kills is on the table by evening, jointed, dressed and served so beautifully that the families often do not complain. He is proud of his work and owes nothing to anyone. He fears only being bored. He takes contracts from the Board, the Union and the Second Table impartially.

Jem Crackle — the Cook’s Knife
