The First Night

It came on the third night of Grace, 341 A.G., which had been a warm and pleasant evening. There was no sign. Ludmere went to bed. In the morning, roughly a third of it did not get up: they lay in their beds breathing slow and even, smiling, and no amount of shaking would rouse them. Their families screamed in the streets. The physicians were sent for and could not wake them. By the next night the city understood only that a sickness had come; and most of it, exhausted with weeping and fear, went to bed. In the morning, half of what remained did not wake.

Those who survived the third night were the ones too frightened to lie down: the anxious, the guilty, the insomniac, the mad, the nursing mothers, the drunks, the watchmen, the children too hungry to sleep. They sat up through the dark in kitchens together, slapping each other, shouting, banging pans, holding hands and squeezing until the knuckles cracked. Those people are the ancestors of the Vigil. The city descends, by a kind of hideous selection, from its worst sleepers. Vigilants say it with pride.

The Waking Laws and the Burning of the Beds

In the spring of 342 the survivors met in the old Ludmere Square and passed the Waking Laws by acclamation. Lying down was forbidden. Closing the eyes for longer than a breath was forbidden. Every bed, couch, mattress, pillow and cushion on the plateau was carried into the squares and burned, along with the goose-down warehouses, the oracles’ dream-books, and the dreamers themselves when they protested. The pyres burned for a month; they were the first Bonfires. The city took its new name from a word the old priests had used for the night before a feast: the vigil. It was meant to sound temporary.

The Count

In 401 a diver named Iselde Marrow, on her eleventh descent, walked further into the long room than anyone had and stood for a long while near the eye. When she was hauled back, half-dead with pain, she said she had heard the number. It had been told to her, she said, very gently, as if by a mother explaining to a child how many more days until a holiday. She was brought before three officials of the Watch, in a sealed room, and made to say it once. Then the officials agreed that the number was too dangerous to leave in a living head, and they had her laid down in a bed. Her bed was the next one in the row. Two of the three officials were dead within the decade, by accident; the third was the first Matron of the Dormitory, and the number has passed from Matron to Matron since, whispered once at the bedside of the dying.

GM Advice — What Is the Number?

The number is a state secret, and the book does not fix it. Choose one of these, or write your own. (1) The number is 60,001. The Dormitory was built to hold exactly one fewer, by a Matron who thought she could stop it with carpentry. (2) The number is the population of Ludmere on the Nine Nights, every man, woman and child who ate of Iss. The god is calling its table back. (3) The number has already been passed. Iselde Marrow lied, or was lied to. The eye began to open years ago, very slowly, and what the Hourkeeper is measuring is the lid going up. (4) There is no number. The Watch invented it in 401 to give the city something to fear that was not the truth, which is that the eye will open when it is ready. Whatever you choose, the Matron should believe it absolutely.

Rule, Law and Politics

The Vigil is governed by the Watch of Watches, a council of some three hundred Eye-line nobles who sit, or rather climb, in three shifts around the clock on the Nodding Stair. It has not adjourned in two hundred years. Its members are lidless by law, attended by eye-wetters, and watched by one another, since in the Vigil the oldest political truth is that anyone may blink. At its head is the Warden-Prime, always an Eye-line, always lidless, watched in turn by attendants who wet the royal eyes with a brush every half minute.

Beneath the Watch sit the Offices: the Apothecary-General (rouse), the Lamplighter-General (oil and light), the Hourkeeper (time and bells), the Matron (the Dormitory), the Registrar of the Seeming (the public record), and the Captaincy of the Wakers (everything else).

The Law of the Lid

The law is simple. Lying down is a crime. Closing your eyes for longer than a breath is a crime. Letting someone near you nod off is negligence, punishable as manslaughter if they go down. Selling sleep is a crime. Singing The Lamb and the Lid is a crime. Possession of down, feathers, wool batting or any soft stuffing in a quantity greater than will fill a shoe is a crime. Speaking of the room in a soothing manner is incitement.

The police, the Wakers, carry rattles and long needles, and they are entitled to needle any citizen who appears drowsy, without warrant and without apology. A citizen who objects to being needled is presumed to be drowsy.

Punishment is wakefulness. Minor offenders are sentenced to hours at the Rattlehouse, kept on their feet by Wakers with needles. Serious offenders are sentenced to the Lantern: an iron cage hung from a pole in a public square, open on every side, lit by its own lamp, in which the condemned is kept awake by any passing citizen with a pin, for as long as the sentence runs. Long sentences in the Lantern produce Seeming so violent that the condemned believe they are being eaten by the crowd, and sometimes the crowd believes it too.

Until 590 the capital sentence was Bedding. The condemned were led to the Dormitory in a white gown, given warm milk and poppy, laid in a bed and allowed to sleep, while a crowd outside sang the forbidden lullaby, the one day in the year it was permitted. It was considered the most merciful execution on the Table, and envied. It was suspended when the Matron reported that beds were scarce. Since then, the worst criminals have been held in the Rattlehouse awaiting a sentence that cannot be carried out, and the Rattlehouse is very full.

The Three Parties

The deepest political question is the Dormitory, and the Watch is split three ways over it.

The Builders want more beds. They are the oldest and largest party, the party of the Architect and the Matron’s office, and their position is that the number can be postponed by construction, because the Counted must be housed somewhere and every bed is a delay. Their critics observe that a bed does not change the number, and that building more beds is only building a bigger waiting room.

The Removalists want the Counted moved out of the country: carted down the Pilgrim Road, laid along the Rim, sold to Sallowreach or the Fatlands, buried, sunk, anything to get them off the Lid. Their theory is that the count is local. The Sleepers’ Mile, they point out, has been beyond the border for three centuries and the eye has not opened. Their opponents point out that nobody knows whether the Sleepers’ Mile is counted or not.

And one party, very quietly, wants the number reduced. They do not have a name in the public record. Among themselves they call themselves the Lessening, and their position is arithmetic: if the eye opens when the Counted reach a certain number, then the Counted must not reach it, and since the Counted cannot be woken, some of them must stop being Counted. The Lessening does not use the word murder. It uses the words reduction, thinning and relief. It has drawn up lists.

Culture and Daily Life

No Beds

There is not a bed, couch or cushion in the city. Floors slope, a little, so that a person who lies on them slides. Chairs have one leg, and must be balanced on; a person who dozes on a one-legged chair falls off it. Walls are studded with iron knobs at shoulder height, so that no one can lean. Doorways have no frames to rest against. Tables are chest-high. The Vigil eats, works, talks and loves standing up, and its people have the thick calves, the bad backs and the swollen ankles to show for it.

Nudging

Everyone has a nudger. A nudger is the person whose job is to keep you awake: a spouse, a sibling, a friend, a hired child. Nudgers watch for the drooping lid, the slackened jaw, the long pause; they pinch, slap, shout, prick and shake. In a family, everyone nudges everyone, in a ring, so that no one is ever unwatched. A person without a nudger is called unwatched, and it is the loneliest word in the language.

Marriage is the promise to keep each other awake, and the vow is two words: Pinch me. Weddings are loud, bright, short, and held at the Bonfires. The couple pinch each other on the inside of the wrist until they bleed, and the guests throw bells. Love between spouses is tender and fierce and frightened, because every intimacy is a danger; what comes after love, in a body, is drowsiness, and the Vigil’s lovers keep a rattle by them and a lamp at full wick, and their tenderness is shot through with watchfulness. The little death is the big one here, the rouse-house joke goes, and nobody laughs.

Rouse

Rouse is a bitter black stimulant, ground and roasted from the dried caps of staremoss, a grey lichen that grows only on the cliff-faces of the Lid, mixed with Bitterhouse salts whose composition is a state secret. It is sold as pressed cakes, as powder, and as a thick black syrup, and it is taken hourly, chewed, sipped or packed against the gum. It tastes of burnt sugar, iron and bile. It makes the heart race, the hands shake and the pupils widen. Teeth go first: they blacken and loosen and drop out, and a Vigilant over forty with a full set is either rich, lidless or lying. Then the heart. The ordinary death of an ordinary Vigilant is a rouse-heart: a burst of thudding, a grey face, a hand to the chest, and the long-awaited lying down on the floor.

The dose has risen every decade since 390. A modest citizen spends two lacks a day on rouse. On the Slope it is cut to stretch it, and the cuts are worse than the drug.

Pain as Courtesy

A slap is a favour. Guests are offered a pin on arrival, as other lands offer bread and salt, and to refuse it is an insult. Clothes are made of burr-cloth, a coarse wool woven with dried thistle-heads; the rich wear galled silk, laced with fine wire that pricks at every movement. Shoes are cobbled with a pebble in the heel. Collars are set with pins. A Vigilant’s skin is a map of small courtesies: the scabs on the wrists, the bruises on the upper arm, the neat rows of needle-scars along the forearm. To bear them is respectability. To have unmarked skin is suspicious.

Food

A full belly is a bed. Meals in the Vigil are small, frequent, cold and sour: pickled roots, hard bread, salt meat out of Fatlands barrels, vinegar, sorrel, smoked cliff-goat. Warm milk is illegal. Sugar is rationed. Soup is served lukewarm, by law. Rich households eat from vessels with sharp rims. The grace is the common one, Lack keep away, said with the eyes open, and followed in the Vigil by a slap on the table.

The Seeming

After enough waking, everyone hallucinates. A Vigilant hears voices in the hiss of the lamps, sees insects walking across the plaster, watches faces rise up in the patterns of the cobbles, sees a dead mother at the end of a lane. These private visions are a nuisance and are ignored. But sometimes a whole street sees the same thing. A woman made of moths walking down Gutter Lane. A rain of teeth over the Pinchmarket. A door in the side of the Nodding Stair that was not there before. When that happens, the Vigil has made it a civic sense. Witnesses report it to the Registrar of the Seeming, the Seemers record it, and when enough unconnected people have seen the same thing, it is entered in the public record as news, read aloud at the Bonfires, and printed in the bell-sheets. A Seeming entered in the record is, for legal purposes, true. Contracts have been voided because of it. Houses have been condemned because the street agreed they were on fire.

The power to enter a Seeming, or refuse it, is the power to decide what happened. The Watch knows this very well.

From the Public Record of the Seeming, as read at the Ludmere Bonfire, fourth watch, the second day of Carving, 641.

ENTERED: In the lanes of the Slope between Thimble and Lanternside, thirty-one persons unconnected and of good character, between the ninth and tenth bells, did see a tall figure in a grey coat, stooping, which passed down the lane laying out upon the cobbles a long table, with cloth and plates and cups, and with chairs drawn back. The table was nine hundred paces long. At every place was a bowl of something steaming. The figure did not speak. At the tenth bell it was gone and the cobbles were clean. Several witnesses report the smell of new bread. Similar matter entered this month in ten other districts. ENTERED AS TRUE.

NOT ENTERED: In Thimble Lane at the eleventh bell, nine persons report that the figure returned, and that one of the chairs had been sat in. Insufficient witnesses. The Registrar reminds the public that a Seeming not entered did not occur.

Children

Infants born in the Vigil do not sleep. They come into the world wide-eyed and quiet, and for their first years they lie awake in their mothers’ arms staring at the lamps, never crying for rest, because they do not yet need it. Vigilants call them starers and consider them a mercy of the god. The weight comes later, at about four years old: the Coming-Heavy, when a child first yawns, first rubs its eyes, first asks, in a small cross voice, why it cannot lie down. That is when the Vigil loses its children. A child cannot be told what the room is. A child cannot be made to understand why the warm, the soft, the dim, the quiet are deadly. There is a wing of the Dormitory called the Small Rows, where the beds are short, and the mothers who visit them do not speak to each other.

Children of the Slope who survive the Coming-Heavy are named for the bell they were born at, and many of them become nudgers by six: Pip Eleven-Bell, Rook Quarter-Bell. It is cheap work and they are good at it, sharp-eyed and quick-fingered. They do not last long on rouse.

Death

People still die in the Vigil, of rouse-heart, fever, accident and violence. A corpse is the only thing in the city allowed to lie down, and the body is laid out flat on a board in the street for a day so that the neighbours may come and look at it, and touch its closed eyes, and envy it. The mourners are allowed to sit, for one hour, on the kerb. Then the body is carried to Lampwrights’ Row and burned in the furnaces, and its light goes out into the lamps. The rich pay to have a particular lamp lit from their ashes. The poor go to the general flame.

Festivals and Days

The Night of Lying Down, on the anniversary of the First Night, is the city’s great mourning: every family that has a sleeper in the Dormitory goes to stand at the foot of the bed for an hour, and the Dormitory’s doors are open from bell to bell. The Shouting Day remembers the Grey Ninth. The Pinching Fair, at midsummer, is a riot of bells, needle-dances and wake-games. And on Tablenight, the longest night of Lack, the city puts out every lamp for one minute, to prove it still can. People stand in the dark in the streets holding hands and counting aloud together, all of them, so that no one can drift off unnoticed, sixty seconds, the only darkness they will ever see. Every year a few hands go slack in the dark. Every year, when the lamps come back, someone is still counting into silence.

Crime

Theft and violence are common and treated as ordinary. The great crimes are the crimes of rest. Selling sleep; harbouring a sleeper; failing to report one; lying down; singing the song; and the newest, which the law has not yet decided what to call: the blink-murder, the killing done by someone who was not there.

Proverbs and Oaths

  • Pinch me. (I love you; I trust you; I am afraid.)
  • A full belly is a bed.
  • Never trust a rested face.
  • The eye is patient. Be rude.
  • Count your nudger’s blinks.
  • Sleep is a door that only opens inward.
  • He’s on the Row. (He is dead.)
  • She went to the room. (She fell asleep; she is gone.)

The Vigil swears on its sleepers. By my mother’s bed is a common oath, and the bed’s number is spoken after it. The heaviest oath in the city is sworn at the foot of Bed One with a hand on the rail: by the first of us, who lay down for all of us. A Vigilant who breaks an oath sworn on a sleeper’s bed is held to have broken faith with the Counted, and no nudger will watch them again.

A note found pinned to the coat of Annick Rell, laundress, of the Slope, discovered lying in the open yard behind Gallow Street, the eighth day of Plenty, 640, and carried to bed 58,921. Entered in the Lain Book.

Teodor. I am sorry about the coat. I am sorry it is the good one. I have been awake for thirty-one years and I am so tired that I cannot remember your face when you are out of the room, I have to go and look. I cannot taste anything. I hear my mother in the lamps. The baby has been in the Small Rows for six years and I visit and she is still four and I am forty and I will be fifty and she will still be four. They say the room is warm. They say it does not hurt. I am not leaving you, I am going to her. Do not let them say I slipped. I did not slip. I chose it. Please come and stand at the foot of the bed sometimes, and talk, because they say we can hear. Do not lie down after me. Promise. Pinch the children for me. A.

The Lain-Down

Every year, hundreds of Vigilants lie down on purpose. The law calls it voluntary rest, prosecutes the nudger for negligence, and fines the family. The city calls it going to the room and does not talk about it. Those left behind carry it for the rest of their lives: they go to the Dormitory and stand at the foot of the bed, and the person they loved is there, warm, breathing, unchanged, smiling, unreachable, and will be there unchanged long after they themselves have grown old and gone onto the Row. There is no grave to leave, no body to bury, no end to the grief, only a bed with a number and a face that is still, horribly, at peace. GMs should play the Lain-Down as tragedy and as pressure, never as a solution: a contact who has started talking about how warm it must be; a nudger who has stopped pinching quite so hard; a widow who visits the same bed every day and has begun to bring a stool. The god’s pull is gentle, reasonable and kind. That is the horror of it.

Factions

The Watch of Watches

The lidless government: sleepless, paranoid, and correct to be. Its members believe that the Vigil survives only because someone is always looking, and that the someone must be a person who cannot look away. They want to hold the city together until the number can be outwitted, and they are prepared to do anything that does not require them to admit how close it is. A PC joins as an aide, eye-wetter or clerk of the Stair; only the lidless may hold a vote. Enemies: the Bedded, the Tuckers, anyone who says the number aloud. Allies: the Wakers, the Rim Road Company, the Second Table, which several Watchers secretly belong to.

RankTitleGrants
1Stair-ClerkAccess to the Nodding Stair; a sworn nudger at state expense.
2Eye-WetterAttendance on a Watcher; hears everything said on the Stair.
3Watcher of the Third ShiftA vote (lidless only); may commandeer Wakers for a watch.
4Watcher of the Lid’s EyeA seat on the inner committees; sight of the true rouse and oil figures.
5Warden-PrimeThe city. Only one, ever.

The Wakers

The police. Their job is to hurt people for their own good, and after three centuries they are very skilled. Every Waker is trained at the Rattlehouse in the Atlas of the Quick, a manual of the body’s points of pain, and in the use of the rattle and the long needle: a nine-inch steel spike, ground fine, driven into the places where pain is sharpest and harm least. They believe that pain is love made practical. They want to keep the count from rising, one drowsy citizen at a time. A PC joins by apprenticeship at the Rattlehouse and a year’s probation in the Slope. Enemies: the Tuckers, the Bedded, the Lessening (which they do not know exists). Allies: the Watch, the Lamplighters, every frightened household.

RankTitleGrants
1RattleA rattle, a pin-roll and a patrol beat. Legal right to slap.
2NeedleThe long needle; may needle without warrant.
3Sergeant of the WardCommand of a station; may sentence to the Rattlehouse for a watch.
4Inquisitor of the QuickInterrogation rights; keys to the Rattlehouse’s lower floors.
5Captain of the WakersCommand of every Waker; answers only to the Watch.

From the Atlas of the Quick, schoolroom edition, Rattlehouse press, Lesson the Fourth.

The needle is not a weapon. Repeat this until you believe it, and then repeat it until the citizen believes it. You are not there to punish the sleeper but to fetch him. Go in under the nail of the great toe, where the quick is shallow and the harm is small; then the web of the thumb; then the soft of the armpit; then the hollow behind the ear. If these do not answer, the citizen is gone and you may stop. Do not stop before. Many a sleeper has been lost by a Waker who was squeamish at the armpit. The scream is the citizen thanking you. Learn to hear it so.

The Lamplighters' Guild

The keepers of the light. They trim the ten thousand public lamps, stoke the Bonfires, polish the roof-mirrors, and burn the dead on Lampwrights’ Row. Oil is the Vigil’s largest import, by Rim Road from Brinehollow whale-yards and Fatlands rendering-houses, and the Guild knows exactly how many days of it remain. They believe that darkness is death, and they are right. They want oil, at any price, from any source. The source has lately become a matter for the inner Guild alone, and the tallow vats behind the furnaces on the Row are bigger than they were. A PC joins as a wick-boy or mirror-climber. Enemies: anyone who hoards oil. Allies: the Wakers, the Renderers’ Union of the Fatlands, Lukas Marre, oddly, whose cell they keep brightest of all.

RankTitleGrants
1WickA pole, a lamp-round and free light at home.
2ClimberAccess to the roof-mirrors; knowledge of every rooftop route.
3Stoker of a BonfireA square of one’s own; the right to refuse light to a street.
4Burner of the RowCharge of the furnaces where the dead are burned, and of what is rendered there.
5Lamplighter-GeneralThe oil ledger, and the date on its last page.

The Tuckers

A criminal mercy. For a price, the Tuckers will guard you while you sleep for sixty seconds, then haul you back: they lay you on a straw pallet in a cellar, count to sixty, and drag you up by a hook-and-harness that they will not let customers examine. The method works more often than not. Their failures are delivered to the Dormitory steps before the next bell, washed and wrapped and labelled with a number from the Tuckers’ own register. They believe sleep is a human right; they also believe it is a month’s wages. A PC joins as a counter, the Tucker who keeps time over the sleeper. Enemies: the Wakers, the Watch. Allies: the Bedded, rouse dealers, a surprising number of Watchers who have taken their minute.

RankTitleGrants
1DoormanKeeps the queue; a cut of the waiting fee.
2CounterCounts the sixty over sleepers; knows the method.
3HaulerWorks the hook; may sell a minute without asking.
4Cellar-KeepRuns a cellar of one’s own and its Waker bribes.
5King of the TuckersOld Nod’s chair, and his register of failures.

The Dream-Divers

State explorers who go to sleep on purpose, under a tether, and are dragged back by force. They believe the room can be understood and the eye negotiated with, and they want to map it to the wall. Most manage three dives before they fail to come back. Each dive leaves a diver less tethered to the waking world: they forget names, lose the taste of food, and start to speak of the room as home. A PC joins by volunteering, which the Hall accepts from anyone, because few volunteer twice. Enemies: the Bedded, who call them grave-robbers. Allies: the Watch, the Hourkeeper, the Dormitory.

RankTitleGrants
1HaulierA place on the winch rope; a share of the diver’s wage.
2Novice of One DiveHarness, tongue-ring and state pension to your family if you stay.
3Diver of ThreeA name on the Hall wall; first sight of the room-maps.
4Deep DiverLeads a dive-team; may dive without the Watch’s leave.
5Master of the TetherThe Hall itself, and the right to say who goes under.

The Bedded

Heretics who preach that sleep is a homecoming, that the eye is kind, and that the city is three hundred years late. They meet in Slope cellars and in the shadow of the Dormitory, in rooms with no lamps, and they hum. Their faith is the oldest consolation in the Vigil: that the people lost to the room are not lost, but at rest, and waiting. They want the Waking Laws repealed and the city allowed to go home. The most devout of them help others to lie down, and call it ministry; the law calls it murder. A PC joins by attending a dark-meeting and not reporting it. Enemies: the Wakers, the Watch, the Lessening. Allies: the Tuckers, the Lain-Down’s grieving families, the Second Table’s quieter members.

RankTitleGrants
1ListenerAdmission to dark-meetings; the name of a safe cellar.
2HummerKnows the whole of The Lamb and the Lid.
3ShepherdKeeps a flock; may sit with those who wish to lie down.
4PillowHas slept in a blink and come back speaking well of it; preaches.
5Sister of the LidVesper Null’s circle; may speak for the room.

The Lessening

The faction that wants the number reduced. They are Eye-line Watchers, Dormitory clerks, a handful of Wakers and two Matron’s deputies, and their reasoning is arithmetic. The Counted cannot be woken; the number cannot be reached; therefore some of the Counted must be removed from the count, by pillow, by needle, by a drop of Bitterhouse salts in the drip, quietly, in the oldest rows first, where there are no visitors. They speak only of relief. They have drawn up lists, ordered by bed number, and a schedule that would reduce the Counted by eleven thousand in two years. They have not begun the schedule. They have begun the trials, and the trials have shown them something they cannot explain (see Matron Cecily Dorm), which they have decided to ignore. A PC is approached, never applies. Enemies: the Bedded, the families of the Counted, Inspector Grimmer, unknowingly. Allies: the Second Table, the Removalists, the parts of the Watch that do not wish to know.

RankTitleGrants
1Reckoner of BedsCopies the registers; knows which rows are unvisited.
2Orderly of ReliefWorks the night rows; carries the salts.
3Sitting MemberA vote on the lists.
4Keeper of the ScheduleDecides which bed is next.
5First of the LesseningSabine Larch, and the arithmetic.
Cross-Border Powers in the Vigil

The Rim Road Company runs the Last Beds and the oil convoys, and holds the Watch’s debts. The Cutwrights’ College keeps a house on the Height whose ledgers show which Eye-line families have produced no Counted in three centuries, and which Slope families have produced the most. The Purgation has a cell in the Bitterhouse that believes Iss can be vomited back up by a rouse strong enough to keep the whole city awake for a year. The Second Table has three Watchers and a Lamplighter-General’s deputy, and a very simple plan for the morning the eye opens: knives, felt-wrapped, and a lullaby. The Reckoners have never sent a raid to the Vigil. The Vigil’s nobles do not sleep, and that makes them hard to kill in their beds.

The Vigil Now

Everything is running out at once. Rouse is failing: the dose that held a generation ago now barely holds an hour, and the Apothecary-General knows the year when the dose that keeps a person awake will be the dose that stops their heart. The Dormitory has fewer than two thousand empty beds. The Lamplighter-General has ninety days of oil. The hours themselves seem to be lengthening; the Hourkeeper’s pendulum swings a hair slower every week, and the city’s watches feel longer than they did, and nobody can prove that they are not imagining it, because everybody is always imagining something.

The Warden-Prime has sent an envoy to Sallowreach with a proposal too terrible to put in writing: the dead do not sleep. The Lessening has drawn up its lists. The Seeming has shown eleven districts a tall figure laying a table in the street. Rouse cut with Brinehollow brine is sending the Slope’s addicts walking west in their sleepless trances, toward a sea four hundred miles away. Forty-one people have killed someone they loved in a sleep of two breaths, and the inspector on the case has started to notice what the victims had in common. And in Bed One, the first sleeper, who has not stirred in three hundred years, has begun to move her lips.

Adventure Hooks

  • The Fourth Pillow. The Matron hires the party, off the record, to sit the night rows of the Dormitory’s east wing, where three Counted have been found smothered in a month. The Matron suspects the Lessening. The Lessening suspects the Matron. The party, sitting in the breathing dark for a whole watch with the air rising and falling around them, must stay awake to catch a killer, and each time a sleeper dies, someone in the city blinks and does not come back.
  • The Brine Walkers. Rook Quarter-Bell’s customers are walking west in a shuffling column, eyes open, down the Pilgrim Road past the Sleepers’ Mile. A Waker sergeant with a brother among them hires the party to bring them back before they reach the Rim, where the Company’s porters have orders to stop them by any means. Somewhere on the road, the column stops, turns as one, and points.
  • The Deadwatch. The Watch sends the party north as escort to Envoy Castellan Dray, with a chest of platters, a dozen nudgers and orders to ensure the Regent of Sallowreach says yes. On the road the nudgers begin to blink. In Lastgate, Dray asks the party privately whether they would volunteer to be the first.
  • Forty-One. Inspector Grimmer needs outsiders. Every blink-murder victim, he has found, was a secret member of the Lessening. Somebody, or something, is defending the Counted. Grimmer wants to know what, and he wants the party to blink deliberately, under guard, to find out what it is like to be used.
  • What Aveline Says. The Matron’s notebook of Bed One’s lip-words has been stolen. The thief is selling pages in the Pinchmarket. The pages contain names, and the people named on them are going to the room, one a day, in order.

Rumours in the Pinchmarket

d10Rumour
1The number is sixty thousand and one. The Matron counts to it every morning, and every morning stops at sixty thousand. (Possibly true.)
2Old Nod takes his own minute every Plate, in a cellar no one has found. (False. He has never slept.)
3If you blink in the Pillow, you can see the eye from the other side. (Unknown. Nobody who tried has been asked.)
4The Warden-Prime’s daughter has eyelids and sleeps a minute at a time behind locked doors. (True, in part.)
5The lamps on the Row are burning people. Smell them. (True. The Guild calls it economy.)
6The Sleepers’ Mile has been counted all along, and the Watch knows it. (Unknown. Very possibly true.)
7Sister Vesper sleeps every night and wakes every morning. (True. What wakes is the question.)
8Dr. Crane has a rouse that will keep you awake for ever. (False. He has one that will keep you awake until it kills you.)
9The tall man laying tables is the eye, come to call. (False, as far as anyone in the Vigil knows.)
10If you hum the first three notes of the Lamb song, every Counted in the Dormitory smiles. (True. The orderlies have tested it, once.)

The People of the Vigil

Warden-Prime Ilvane Stroud, the Unblinking

Ruler of the Vigil, fifty-eight years old, born lidless, and she has not shut her eyes once since birth. Her eyes are enormous, pale grey, red-rimmed and webbed with veins, and they never stop moving. Two attendants stand at her shoulders with sable brushes and warm rosewater, and every half minute one of them strokes the wet across her eyes, and she does not flinch; she has never been able to. She has seen everything that has happened in front of her since the hour she was born, and she can forget none of it. She remembers her mother’s face over the cradle, every execution she has signed, every lie told to her on the Stair, and the exact weight of each. She speaks softly and precisely, and she never asks a question twice. She wants the Vigil to survive her, by any means at all, including the dead. She fears her daughter. PCs meet her on the Lid’s Eye landing, where she will remember them, perfectly, forever.

She has also done the sum for the Deadwatch: if the Vigil is moved to Sallowreach and killed and Kept, the city’s sixty thousand Counted will be left behind, unwatched, on the Lid. She has decided that is acceptable.

Lady Oriel Stroud

The Warden’s daughter, twenty-three, born with eyelids, which in the highest Eye-line is a deformity and an embarrassment of state. She has been kept hidden in a suite of bright rooms at the top of the Stair since birth, attended by deaf nudgers. She is small, soft-voiced, dark-haired, with ordinary hazel eyes that she keeps fixed open in company until they stream, because her mother cannot bear to see her blink. Alone in her rooms, she closes her eyes for whole seconds at a time, and nothing has ever felt so good. She wants to be allowed to be ordinary, and she wants her mother to look at her once without that face. She fears she will be married off to a lidless cousin and never close her eyes again. Her secret: when she closes them, she does not see darkness. She sees the long room, from the far end, through a great grey lid, and every sleeper in it turning their head to look at her.

Maud Sexton, the Hourkeeper

Mistress of the city’s clocks, sixty, stooped, with a jeweller’s loupe screwed into one eye socket and a pocket full of brass escapements that she fidgets with like rosary beads. She sets the time for every bell in the Vigil from the great pendulum in the Pendulum Hall. Over eleven years of measurements she has proved, by pendulum, sand, candle and the pulse of her own wrist, that each hour is a little longer than the last. Not by much: a breath per watch, now two. Something is stretching the night the Vigil will not admit it is having. Her report was suppressed. She has written it again, smaller, in the margins of the bell-schedules. She wants someone with authority to stand in the Pendulum Hall for an hour and feel it. Her secret: she has run the curve forward. On a night not long from now, the hour will stop ending.

Captain Brannoch Pyre of the Wakers

Captain of the city’s police, fifty-two, a big slope-shouldered man with a shaved head, needle-scarred forearms and a voice worn to gravel from three decades of shouting people awake. He has kept a hundred thousand citizens out of the Dormitory with rattle and needle, and he has not been thanked once. He believes absolutely in what he does. He also knows, better than any man alive, what it does to the people he does it to. His own nudger, his wife Merrit, died last year, and he has not replaced her. He walks his rounds unwatched, which is illegal, and none of his Wakers will report him.

He has also blinked three times this month and come back with blood under his nails that is not his.

Old Nod, King of the Tuckers

He sells one minute of guarded sleep for a month’s wage, and people queue around the block. He is seventy, small, quick and courteous, with a soft white beard, half-moon spectacles and the black stumps of a lifetime of rouse, and he receives customers in a warm cellar off the Slope under a sign that says only Rest. He has never tried his own product. He says a man should not get high on his own supply. He keeps a register, in his own hand, of every customer the hook failed to bring back: one in eleven, these days, up from one in thirty. He wants a better hook. He fears the Bedded, who say his failures are the lucky ones. His secret: he was a Dream-Diver once, three dives, and he knows what sixty seconds in the room feels like from the inside. It feels like a lifetime. That is what he is really selling.

Tucker Hauler Threat 3 · Flesh 13 · Guard 14 · Attack +6 (hook-and-harness 3, Hooking) · Armor 1 · Dread 0

Senna Vole, Dream-Diver

Forty descents, where three is the usual career. She is thirty-four and looks fifty: grey-haired, gaunt, her wrists and throat ridged with harness-scars, a silver ring through her tongue where the Hall’s hook goes. She speaks slowly and seldom, as if words came from a long way off. She has mapped the long room to within thirty paces of the eye: the soft floor, the warm air, the sleepers standing in their silent ranks, and the place near the wall where the floor begins to slope downward, toward the lid. On her last dive, something behind the lid said her name. She wants to go back. She tells the Hall she wants to finish the map.

Dr. Aldous Crane, Apothecary-General

Inventor of the current strain of rouse, sixty-one, thin as a heron, with the steady hands of a man who has never in his life taken his own product and the yellow fingertips of a man who handles it all day. He speaks to people as though reading them a dosage. He knows the dose curve and where it ends: there is a point at which the amount of rouse needed to stay awake is the amount that stops the heart, and it is eleven years off, for an average adult; three or four for the Slope, where the cut is worse; less than one for children. He wants a new compound, and has tested nine hundred in the Proving Rooms on prisoners lent by the Rattlehouse. His secret: the Watch has ordered one more compound, the nine hundred and first, finished and warehoused, for the day the beds are full. It is a rouse that does not wake you. It stops you, gently, standing up, and you do not go to the room. He calls it the Last Cake.

Matron Cecily Dorm

Keeper of the Dormitory, fifty, broad and soft-spoken, in a starched grey gown and felt slippers, with a heavy ring of bed-keys at her belt that she holds still with one hand as she walks so it will not jingle. She is the only living person who knows the number, and she walks the rows every day, counting, under her breath, from one. She has been seen removing a pillow and standing over a bed for a long time. She loves the Counted. She knows their faces as a mother knows her children’s. She hates them, sometimes, with a hatred she confesses to no one.

Garron Ashlock, Lamplighter-General

He keeps ten thousand lamps burning. He is forty-eight, red-faced, burn-scarred to the elbow, with no eyebrows and a cheerful bellow that he has cultivated to hide the fact that he cannot sleep, of course, and cannot rest either, ever, because he can count. He has ninety days of oil, a Brinehollow supplier who has doubled the price and a Fatlands one who has stopped answering, and a standing order from the Watch to tell no one. He wants a miracle and will settle for tallow. His secret: he has already found it. The furnaces on the Row do not burn the dead to ash any more. They render them. A quarter of the city’s lamps now burn on the people who used to read by them, and the Guild has begun to look, with a professional eye, at the Dormitory.

Pip Eleven-Bell

A street nudger of nine, born at the eleventh bell on the Slope, paid by the hour to pinch strangers in the Pinchmarket. Pip is fast, sharp, thin as a pin, all elbows and grubby knuckles, with a voice like a gull and a laugh like a rattle, and the best pinch-fingers in the market. Pip has been unpaid for two weeks by a client who has gone to the room and has been taking rouse from the cheapest dealers to keep working. Children do not last on rouse, and Pip has begun to blink. Pip wants a proper client, a hot meal and a nudger of their own. Pip fears nothing out loud. Pip’s secret: in the blinks, there is a kind lady in the room, in a baker’s apron, who holds out her hand and says it is all right to stay. Pip has started to hold on longer each time.

Lukas Marre, the Yawning Man

His yawns are catching beyond all reason: one gape of his jaw and a room goes down, a street sways, and once, at nineteen, before he knew, a whole market square. He is thirty-one now and has lived twelve years in a cell in the Glass House, masked in a leather muzzle that holds his jaw half shut, alone, in the coldest corner of the city. He is gentle, bookish and painfully polite, and he apologises through the pane to everyone who visits, and to the guards, and to the Matron, whom he writes to every Plate asking after the people from the square. He wants to be forgiven. His secret: the muzzle does not stop it any more. Lately he only has to feel the yawn rising in himself, and the people on the far side of the glass sway.

Sister Vesper Null, Prophet of the Bedded

She preaches that the eye is kind, the room is home, and the Counted are the only citizens of the Vigil at peace. She is about forty, with smooth unlined skin, clear bright eyes and a calm low voice, and she looks more rested than anyone in the city, and nobody can explain it. Her sermons in the Slope cellars are given in the dark, in a murmur, and her listeners sway. She is not cruel. She holds the hands of the grieving and tells them their dead are waiting, and they weep with relief.

Corwin Half-Bell, the Man Who Woke

The only sleeper who ever came back without a tether, after half an hour under, twelve years ago, when a cart-horse kicked him in the ribs where he lay in the street. He is forty, gaunt and grey, and he has not blinked since: his lids have gone stiff and fixed half open from disuse. He flinches whenever a door opens. He will not describe the room. He works as a rope-walker at the Rattlehouse, where the noise comforts him. He wants never to be asked again. His secret, which he will tell only to someone who has been in the room themselves: he heard knocking. Far behind him, at the other end of the long room, at a door none of the sleepers face, someone was knocking, slow and patient and polite, the way a guest knocks. And the eye, he swears, was not sleeping. It was holding still, the way a mouse holds still. It was hiding.

Thaddeus Knell, Chief Bell-Ringer

The city’s bells sound every quarter hour to keep it awake, and they deafened him years ago. He is sixty-four, bull-necked, with forearms like hawsers and ears that ooze, and he rings from the great tower over Ludmere Square by the clock and by the shaking in his teeth. He speaks too loud and reads lips badly. He is the most rested-looking man on the Height, because he hears no lullaby, no rain, no hush; the silence inside him is total and it does not soothe him at all. He wants an apprentice who will not go deaf. His secret: lately the bells do not shake his teeth on the quarter. They shake them a little after, a little later each day, and he has begun ringing by his teeth instead of the Hourkeeper’s clock.

Mirela Sconce, the Seemer

She reads the Seeming for the public record. Forty, sharp-chinned, ink-stained, with a habit of narrating what she sees under her breath, she spends her watches walking the districts with a slate, taking statements, cross-matching witnesses. This month eleven districts, separately, hallucinated the same thing: a tall figure laying a table in the street. She has interviewed two hundred witnesses. Their descriptions match down to the stoop under the doorways and the warmth on the cobbles afterward. She wants to know what it is. She fears the Registrar, who has started striking her entries. Her secret: she saw it too, on Thimble Lane, and it looked up at her, and there was a card on the nearest plate, and her name was on it.

Jack Tenterhook, Wake-Valet

Keeper-awake to the rich, an artist of the precisely tolerable pain. He is forty-five, elegant, soft-handed, with a velvet roll of silver pins and a voice like warm oil. He arrives at a client’s house at the first bell and leaves at the last, and between them he keeps his client awake with an exquisite programme of pinches, pricks, ice and pressure, never too much, never too little. His clients swear by him and recommend him to their friends. He was a torturer before, for the Rattlehouse’s lower floors, and says the only difference is the tipping.

SkillsStitching 5, Blades 3, Persuade 3, Intimidate 3, Deceive 3, Search 2, Endure 1
BodyFlesh 11 · Guard 16 · Armor 0 · Fray 2
Attackssilver pins +7 (2, plus the target’s next roll at −2); scalpel +7 (2)
GiftsThe Exquisite (when he needles a person, they lose 1d6 Weariness and owe him a favour they will feel). The Ledger of Nerves (he can make a captive talk without leaving a mark; Clause-proof).
WantsTo watch (he cannot resist observing a person in pain to the end).
Dread2 (to watch him practise)
SecretHe keeps clients awake. He also keeps them sleepy. He has six on the Height whom he has been very carefully not quite waking for a year, just enough to keep them blinking, on commission from the Lessening, who needed members of the Watch to be suggestible. Two of those six have blink-murdered.

Inspector Hale Grimmer

He investigates blink-murders, killings done by ordinary people during a two-second sleep, with no memory after. He has forty-one cases. The method is the same in each: the victim laid flat on the floor, a folded cloth beneath the head, hands crossed on the chest, eyes closed under the killer’s thumbs, and the killer’s palms laid gently over mouth and nose until the breathing stops. Every killer comes back with no memory and the victim’s teeth in their palm. Grimmer is fifty, ragged, chain-chewing rouse, with a mind that goes on working long after his body has stopped wanting to. He wants to know who is doing it. He fears that he will be next, in one direction or the other. His secret is what he found last week: all forty-one victims were members of the Lessening, down to Tobin Coyle, the Slope rope-twister, who copied Dormitory registers for them at night for beer money. Something is defending the Counted.

Odile Farthing

Her son, Marten, fell asleep at four, eleven years ago, in her arms, on a grey afternoon, while she was counting out loud to him. She visits bed 40,112 daily, and stands at its foot for an hour, and talks. She is thirty-eight, rouse-thin and quiet, with the scabbed wrists of a woman who has had no nudger but herself. The Counted do not age, but her boy has grown. He is the size of a man now, long and broad under the sheet, with a man’s hands and a man’s jaw and a beard coming in, and he is smiling. She wants him back. She fears what will come back. Her secret: when she leans close, he smells of bread, and his lips move along with hers when she counts.

Benedikt Lour, the Architect

He designed the modern city: the sloped floors, the one-legged chairs, the studded walls, the endless Stair. He is seventy, frail, bent, with the elegant scrawl of a man whose hands shake for everything but a pen, and he is proud of every discomfort he has ever invented. He is now drawing a Second Dormitory. He has been told to plan for the whole population. He has drafted it on the Pillow, the only open ground left, and the drawings show four hundred thousand beds, in rows, radiating outward from the hollow like the rays of an eye. He wants to finish before he dies. He fears that the Watch will not wait. His secret: the Second Dormitory has no doors that lock from the inside, and its ventilation is designed to carry warm air.

Rook Quarter-Bell

A rouse dealer on the Slope, twenty-two, lean, quick, wolfish, his teeth already gone, gums packed black with his own product. He cuts what he sells with bottled Brinehollow brine, bought by the cask from Dry Jonah’s agents, because it is cheap and it works. His customers stay awake longer than anyone else’s. They have also started bailing salt water every dawn and dusk, and walking west. There are two hundred of them now, in a slow eyes-open column. Rook wants to stop selling it and cannot, because nothing else holds. His secret: he has been taking it himself. He tastes salt every morning, and he has started standing at windows facing west.

Envoy Castellan Dray

The Warden’s ambassador to Sallowreach, fifty-five, a tall immaculate Eye-line courtier with a lidless stare and a chest of documents he never lets out of sight, travelling with twelve paid nudgers and a cask of Bitterhouse rouse. His commission is to buy the secret of Keeping, so that the Vigil’s citizens can be killed and kept upright: a city of the dead, who never need to sleep. He has been in Lastgate for two months, negotiating with the Regent. He wants to save his city. He fears that the price will be paid in its people. His secret: he has learned that the Kept cannot leave Sallowreach, and that the Vigil would have to move there, all of it, to die; and he has not yet told the Warden, because he thinks she will say yes.

Aveline Morne, the Sleeper in Bed One

A baker’s daughter, nineteen years old forever, who lay down on the First Night in 341 and was the first not to rise. She has lain unmoving for three hundred years under a white sheet in a bed with a brass rail, a plump fair girl with flour still in the creases of her knuckles, cheeks pink, lips slightly parted, breathing with the rows. Last month her lips began to shape words. The Matron has started writing them down. Most of them are names, one a day, and each person named has gone to the room the next day. One, last week, was a sentence: There is someone at the door who has not been fed. Set another place.

New Characters

Deputy-Watcher Sabine Larch, First of the Lessening

An Eye-line Watcher of the second shift, forty-four, lidless, soft-voiced, with a mathematician’s courtesy and the kind of face people forget while it is in front of them. She sits on the Matron’s oversight committee and has read every register in the Dormitory. Her lists are in her own hand.

Sabine Larch — Deputy-Watcher, First of the Lessening

Registrar Constance Hobb

Keeper of the Public Record of the Seeming, sixty, white-gloved, iron-haired. She decides which Seemings are entered and which are struck. A Seeming not entered, she says, did not occur. She has struck forty Seemings of the tall figure this year, and every report of blink-murders, and she has entered, on Watch instruction, three Seemings that nobody saw: a fire that justified condemning a Bedded cellar, a riot that justified the doubled needle-patrols, and the death of Corwin Half-Bell, who is still alive. When citizens come to her to insist on what they saw, she shows them the record, kindly, until they doubt it. She sleeps, she believes, not at all. Her secret: her own clerk tells her she has blinked eleven times today, and she has entered none of them.

Sister Agathe Pinch, Mistress of the Needle

Head instructor at the Rattlehouse and author of the current edition of the Atlas of the Quick, sixty-eight, tiny, bright-eyed and grandmotherly, with a cap of white lace and a lap-tray of needles laid out like embroidery tools. She has trained every Waker alive. She believes that pain is a teacher and that the city’s Wakers must learn it first on their own bodies, and every recruit spends their first week strapped in a standing-stall under her needles, so they will know. She is loved by her students the way a scar is loved. Her secret: on the Rattlehouse’s lowest floor she keeps a man who has been awake under the needle for nineteen years. She uses him to teach. He has stopped screaming. He hums.

Teodor Rell, Keeper of the Lain Book

A laundress’s widower, forty, from Gallow Street on the Slope, who found his wife’s note pinned to her good coat and has not been able to stop reading it. He took a clerk’s post at the Dormitory so that he could see her every day, and the Matron gave him the Lain Book: the register of those who went to the room by choice, with their notes copied out, two hundred to four hundred a year. He reads every note. He answers some of them aloud, at the foot of the bed. He is gentle, tired beyond tiredness, and very dangerous to himself. He has kept his promise not to lie down after her. His secret: he has begun writing a note of his own, a line a day, so that it will be ready.

Lord Evander Quell of the Second Table

An Eye-line Watcher of the first shift, fifty, handsome, lidless, beautifully mannered, and the Second Table’s senior hand in the Vigil. He believes the eye’s opening is the best news in six centuries: the god of sleep, whole again, in one place, awake and blinking and catchable. He has a set of felt-wrapped knives in a case on his wall, a choir of twelve trained in The Lamb and the Lid, and the Matron’s spare keys. He wants the number reached. Not exceeded, not prevented: reached, cleanly, on a date he can plan for. His secret: he has been feeding Sabine Larch’s lists to Jack Tenterhook’s clients, and he knows exactly what the blink-murders are, and he finds them encouraging.

Factor Joss Mallory of the Last Beds

The Rim Road Company’s innkeeper at the foot of the Pilgrim Road, fifty, big-bellied, foreign, comfortable, with the only soft voice and the only soft bed within thirty miles of the Vigil. Every Company caravan stops at his inn so its drivers can sleep before the climb, and every Vigilant coming down on business stops at his sleeping-hall doorway and looks at the beds. He keeps a book of the ones his porters could not stop. He sells passes across the border, maps of the Sleepers’ Mile, rouse, nudgers and gossip. He is the first friendly face most PCs see before the Lid, and the last one some see before the room. His secret: the Watch pays him a bounty for every Vigilant his porters drag back from the beds. The Lessening pays him a larger one for every Vigilant they don’t.

Waker Patrol Threat 2 · Flesh 11 · Guard 14 · Attack +5 (long needle 2, target loses 2 Weariness; rattle-club 3) · Armor 1 · Dread 0

Slope Blinker (an innocent mid-blink) Threat 1 · Flesh 9 · Guard 11 · Attack +4 (bare hands 1, Smother: a grappled target lying down loses 2 Flesh a round) · Armor 0 · Dread 2
