Meeting the PCs: she asks them to audit a Crumb-Runner’s tally, and they find the Company’s shortfall.

Abstain Rooke, called Abby

Eleven, bird-boned, curious, with a gap in her front teeth and a habit of asking why. Raised on the rules, she can recite them faster than anyone in her hamlet, and she has started leaving a crust on the windowsill at night, saved from her own three-quarter measure. Each morning it has been replaced with something better: a corner of white bread, a ripe plum, a sugared almond, a little honey-cake wrapped in a leaf. She has eaten none of it. She hides it under a loose floor-stone. The pile is getting large, and it does not rot, and it smells wonderful through the stone at night. She is not afraid. She thinks of it as a pen-friend. Her mother does not know; her mother is on Stint Avery’s list. Meeting the PCs: Abby asks them, very seriously, if it counts as accepting if you are only keeping it for someone else.

Brother Hallow Crust, the Seated

He has sat at a table on the valley road for forty years, eating air with a silver fork. He was a stout man; now he is a draped coat with a head on it, the cheeks hollowed to the teeth, the eyes sunk into blue pits, the hair gone to a few white strands. He is perfectly happy and perfectly sane. He describes each course in detail, in a voice like dry leaves: the mutton with caper sauce, the eel pie, the syllabub with nutmeg grated over. He asks after your family. He remembers your answers. He cannot remember his own wife’s name, but he remembers every dish he has been served since 601. People who listen too long pull out a chair. Secret: he was a Tablebreaker, and sat down deliberately, to see if he could get up. He has been meaning to, all forty years. Meeting the PCs: on the Long Table road; he calls them by name.

Dr. Mercy Thrane

A physician of starvation, forty-seven, gaunt and grey-eyed, with spectacles mended with wire and a satchel of scales, calipers, and notebooks. She measures the Unfed: arm circumference, the pinch of the skin, the colour of the gums, the slow pulse. She has written the only proper book on what hunger does to a body over a lifetime. She was the first to document the trade in Unfed bodies. She has traced her missing patients to surgeries in four countries, where blank blood and blank organs fetch a noble’s ransom: Unfed kidneys sewn into Laden matriarchs, Unfed eyes into lidless Vigil heirs, Unfed hearts for Sallowreach Unvacated who want to feel one beat that is not Ossel’s. She has a ledger of names and buyers. The trail leads to the Second Table. She fears she will not live to publish it. Meeting the PCs: she hires them to bring a body home.

The Blank-Organ Trade

Godsign does not live in Unfed flesh. A kidney, liver, eye, length of gut, or pint of blood taken from one of the Unfed is, so far as any surgeon can tell, wholly clean, and when it is sewn into a Godeater it is the one part of that body the god does not grow into. For a few months, or a few years, the High Cut buyer has one organ that is only theirs. Laden matriarchs buy Unfed stomachs to feel, for a season, what it is to be full. Lidless Eye-lines buy Unfed eyes that can close. The price for a whole pair of Unfed kidneys in Sated is about 6,000 lacks; a heart in Lastgate, twice that. The organs are taken from the living where possible, because the Unfed die very quickly of the surgery and the buyers want the organ warm. Poachers keep their captives alive, and fed, for exactly that reason. Then the godsign of the buyer slowly grows into the new organ, as ivy grows into a wall, and in a few years they need another.

Kale Dragoman, the Poacher

A Fatlander of thirty-five, broad, ruddy, and handsome in the Fatlands way, with heavy jowls, beautiful teeth, and a laugh that rolls. He smells of woodsmoke and roast fat, always, because he cooks. He hunts the Unfed for the Blank trade and takes them alive with net and cosh, and he feeds them well on the road: stews, roast fowl, soft white bread, honey, warm milk. He coaxes, he spoon-feeds, he holds their heads. Half his captives refuse and starve before they reach the buyers. The others eat, and weep, and arrive at the surgeries plump and healthy and full of self-loathing. That is the part his captives find hardest to forgive. He thinks he is kind. He is, by Fatlands lights. Meeting the PCs: across a campfire on the Rim, offering them supper. Three times.

Kale Dragoman — the Poacher
AttributesHand 3 · Gut 4 · Lung 3 · Eye 3 · Tongue 4 · Caul 2
Cut & RegrowthCut 2 (common Fatlands blood) · Regrowth 4 (the Appetite) · Hunger 5
SkillsWayfaring 4, Feast 4, Brawl 3, Shooting 3, Persuade 3, Stitching 2, Endure 2
BodyFlesh 14 · Guard 16 · Armor 2 (boiled leather) · Fray 3
Attacksweighted cosh +6 (3; damage may be taken as stun); throwing net +6 (target is held, Lung + Athletics Hard 14 to escape); crossbow +6 (4)
GiftsHe may Partake as any Fatlander of his Cut. The Kind Spoon (once per day, offers food with such warmth that an Unfed who hears him must spend 1 Want or make an Invitation check at Hard 14).
WantsHe eats constantly, and grows uneasy if he cannot see food. He wants someone to thank him.
Dread1 (to see a captive eat)
SecretHe was born in the Fast, of an Unfed mother who sold him to a Fatlands drover as an infant for a sack of oats. He does not know this. His kidneys are worth a fortune.

Envoy Prudence Lowell

Fifty, thin as a lath, in a high-collared black coat buttoned to the throat, with a voice like a cold chisel. She is the Fast’s one ambassador, posted to a hired room above a chandler’s on the Rim Road, and her entire brief is to remind six nations that they are damned and her people are not. She attends every treaty-sitting and every Company congress, refuses every refreshment three times, and then reads aloud, in perfect Table-speech, the latest numbers of their Regrowth. She is very good at it. She has no friends. She has eaten alone, standing, facing a wall, in fourteen capitals. Secret: a Vigil envoy once offered her a fourth time, sincerely, and she very nearly accepted; she has dreamed of his face every night since. Meeting the PCs: she needs Unfed escorts, and she needs, though she would never say so, someone to talk to.

Scour, the Returned

A Reckoner of thirty, lean and fox-faced, sleeves always buttoned to the knuckle. He spent a year undercover in the Fatlands as a renderer’s labourer to scout a Gut-line house, and had to eat to keep his cover. He ate their meat for a year. He came home with godsign. Under his sleeves the skin of his forearms has gone soft, warm, and faintly loamy, like turned earth; there are fine pale threads in it, like root-hairs. He is hungry in a way no Unfed has ever been hungry: a hunger that has nothing to do with the belly. He hides it under his sleeves and volunteers for every raid, because on a raid he can carry his own food and refuse it, and because he wants to die doing something clean. Meeting the PCs: on a raid, when a PC sees him, alone, eating dirt from a Fatlands field.

Scour — the Returned
AttributesHand 4 · Gut 4 · Lung 3 · Eye 2 · Tongue 2 · Caul 3
Cut & RegrowthCut 1 (Ummer, acquired) · Regrowth 3 (the Taste, advancing) · Hunger 7
SkillsBlades 4, Brawl 3, Stealth 3, Endure 3, Deceive 3, Resolve 2
BodyFlesh 15 · Guard 17 · Armor 1 · Fray 6
Attacksblack-iron knife +8 (2); bite +5 (1, and he must make a Want check not to swallow)
GiftsPartakes as a Fatlander of Cut 1; his Tooth bites back on a 1 or 2, not just a 1 (the Empty Room, see Playing the Unfed).
WantsEating without choosing; soil, tallow, leather. Lately, at the bedside, the sleeping.
Dread2 (to see his forearms)
SecretThe god in him has begun to talk, in the voice of the Gut-line matriarch he killed on his first raid.

Verger Sober Osmond

Seventy-nine, stooped, with soft white hair, a sweet vague smile, and a long black cassock gone green at the seams. He keeps the Empty Chair, the last temple of Orrum, alone. Every night he lays one place at the head of the long table, against all law, with the old temple plate: pewter platter, horn cup, a linen napkin folded into the shape of a bird. He lays nothing on it. Every morning the plate is clean, wiped, still faintly warm. He believes this is why the god has stayed gentle: someone has kept faith with it. He is not wrong. He fears dying, because no one will lay the place. Secret: for the past month the morning plate has not been clean. It has had a single crumb on it, as though someone had eaten and, being a well-mannered guest, left a little. Meeting the PCs: he asks one of them to stay and learn the duty.

Yield Hartsell, the Farmer

Seventy, wiry and bowlegged, brown as a nut, with the cracked thumbs and quiet humour of a woman who has spent fifty years doing something useless because someone should. She has planted the dead soil of her family’s ten acres every spring since she was twenty. This year one seed came up. She has built a fence around it and told no one, because she does not know who watered it. She sits up with it at night, with a lantern and a hayfork. Each morning the soil around the blade is wet, and there are no footprints, but the frost around the field is melted in a wide ring, as though something large had knelt there. She is more frightened than she has ever been, and happier. Meeting the PCs: she asks them to sit up with the wheat, and to see what comes, and not to hurt it.

Little Fain

An orphan of six, small and sturdy, with curly hair and dimpled hands: dimpled, in the Fast. Fain went missing for a week and came back plump, clean, rosy, and happy, with a ribbon in their hair and the smell of warm milk on their breath. Someone had said “Come in,” and Fain had. Fain will not say who cooked, only that they cried when it was time to go, and that there was a big kitchen and a fire and lots of chairs but most of them were empty. The Abstinent do not know what to do. Fain cannot be Seated; Fain got up. The other children follow Fain about. The adults will not touch Fain. Secret: Fain was not let go. Fain was sent, and Fain is supposed to bring someone back. Meeting the PCs: Fain takes a PC’s hand in the street and says, “You can come too.”

Marshal Keep Aldane

A heavy-boned man of fifty with a broken nose and an old crossbow wound in the thigh, commanding sixty Unfed spearmen at Brindle Cross. He holds the border against poachers coming in, and, lately, against pilgrims: starving Fatlanders who have heard that somewhere in the Fast there is a table where you finally feel full. He was trained to kill poachers. He was not trained for three hundred hungry people kneeling in the mud of the toll-road, begging him to let them in so they can sit down and die happy. He has turned back nine hundred. He has started to wonder why he is doing it, and what right an Unfed has to refuse anyone a meal. Meeting the PCs: he needs men; or he arrests them as poachers.

Brindle Cross Spearman Threat 2 · Flesh 12 · Guard 14 · Attack +5 (spear 4) · Armor 1 · Dread 0

Osanna Blythe, the Pilgrim

A Fatlands woman of forty, enormous by Unfed standards and gaunt by her own, her skin hanging in folds from a body that has been ravenous every second of her life. Her eyes are bright, her voice is warm and rolling, and she laughs often, a great hungry laugh. She is leading three hundred like her into the Fast to find the Host and sit down. She knows what happens to the Seated. She thinks it sounds wonderful: to be full, finally, for decades, smiling, among friends. She has an Unfed name sewn on her coat, given her by a Tablebreaker who could not bring himself to stop her. Her pilgrims are dying on the road, and the Unfed do not feed them, because that would be hospitality. Meeting the PCs: she asks them for directions. She is very polite about it. She asks three times.

Meek Garrity, the Historian

A small, round-shouldered man of sixty-six, ink to the elbows, with thick spectacles, a voice barely above a whisper, and the long bloodless fingers of a lifelong copyist. He has spent forty years in the oldest records of the Pantry, and he has found the seating plan for Hallowboard: a slate, scratched in the old hand, listing the order in which the households of the heartland were to stand around the table on the night. It is dated. There was no refusal. The Unfed arrived on the tenth day, with knives. The table had already been cleared. Something had eaten first. Secret: the slate shows eight sides, and seven are allotted to households; the eighth has a word scratched beside it, and the word has been scraped away, and Garrity has spent a year with a lens trying to read the shadow of the chisel. Meeting the PCs: he needs the slate moved before the Abstinent burn it.

Welcome Ardent, the Steward

He walks a mile ahead of Orrum, laying the tables. He is tall and very thin and wears an old-fashioned steward’s coat of dark green, the cuffs immaculate, with a white apron over it and a ring of keys at his belt. His face is gentle, lined, and grey with an exhaustion so deep it has become a kind of serenity. His hands are warm, always, and smell of bread. He was the first of the Unfed ever to accept, on the eleventh morning, six hundred and forty years ago, and the only guest who was offered a position. He lays the cloths, sets out the plates, angles the chairs, and writes the place cards in whatever hand will be loved. He is polite, exhausted, and would like very much to be relieved. He has been laying an extra place lately, and he will not say for whom; when asked, he only says, We’re expecting one more.

Welcome Ardent — the Steward of the Host
AttributesHand 3 · Gut 6 · Lung 2 · Eye 4 · Tongue 5 · Caul 6
Cut & Refusalnone (in service; not of any blood) · Want 0 · Pangs 0, forever
SkillsPersuade 5, Rites 5, Craft 5, Instinct 4, Lore 4, Resolve 1
BodyFlesh 19 · Guard 12 · Armor 0 · Fray 10, steady, unbreaking
Attacksnone; he has never struck anyone and cannot
GiftsLay a Place (in one minute, he lays a table for any person he can see; it calls them by name, and they must make an Invitation check). The Fourth Offer (he alone may make a fourth offer, and it is sincere; an Unfed who refuses him a fourth time gains 3 Want and his deep gratitude). The Steward’s Keys (any door, gate, lock, or bricked hearth opens for him).
WantsTo be relieved. Someone must accept the position freely.
Dread3 (to see him at work); 4 (to read a place card in his hand)
SecretHe knows who the extra place is for. He has been told, by his master, that when that guest arrives, the Steward will be released, and everyone else will be served.
Orrum, the Host

Orrum has no stat block. It does not fight, cannot be harmed by any weapon known on the Table, and has never been seen clearly by anyone who returned whole. To see it at a distance (a tall shape stooping in a lit doorway) is a Dread 4 check. To see its face is Dread 5. It is warm, and always kind. If PCs approach it, it will offer them food three times, sincerely, in voices they love. It will never make the fourth offer. If they refuse three times and remain in its presence, it will weep, and the ground for a hundred yards will grow warm enough to raise blisters, and they must leave or be Seated by the heat. If they ask it a question, it will answer with a gesture: a long hand laid on the back of an empty chair.

New Faces

Scarce Odell, the Kin-Reader

A former under-clerk of the Cutwrights’ College in Sated, forty, dry and fastidious, with a squint from decades of tiny genealogical script. He is Unfed by birth, and was placed in the College as a boy by the Reckoners, to read. Now he is home, and he supplies the Reckoners with complete kin-trees so they can murder whole lines: not just the main house but married-out daughters, bastard sons, cousins at sea, infants placed with wet-nurses in other towns. He makes his lists like a careful tailor, measuring twice. He sleeps well. Secret: his trees include Unfed foundlings who carry High Cut blood without knowing, and he has started adding them, quietly. Meeting the PCs: he asks them to verify a name.

Withy Gaunt, Matron of the Lean House

A spare, kind-faced woman of fifty-eight with chapped hands and a soft voice, who keeps the Lean House where the omitted go to die. She does not feed them; that would be against the rule and, she believes, cruel, since it would only extend the waiting. She washes them. She changes the straw. She holds their hands and listens to them talk about food, as they all do at the end, in loving detail, for hours. She writes down every name in the Book of the Omitted, with the date they came and the date they stopped, and what they said last. Most last words are recipes. Secret: she has started reading the Book’s recipes aloud at night to the dying, and Orrum has started standing outside the door, listening. Meeting the PCs: a PC’s friend is in the Lean House.

Abide Kettering, the Sexton

A wiry, cheerful man of forty-five with a pickaxe on his shoulder and a cart he drives to the Lean House and back. He buries the omitted and the starved in the fields, face down, without markers, as is proper. Or he did. For six years he has been selling them, still warm, to Kale Dragoman’s men at a crossroads three miles west, and burying sacks of stones. The bodies of the dead are worth less than the living, but blank kidneys keep a few hours, and blank blood a day. He tells himself the dead do not need them. He has started to look at the Lean House’s residents with an eye to timing. Meeting the PCs: they see his cart at the crossroads, lamp lit, at the wrong hour.

Kettering’s Cart-Hands Threat 1 · Flesh 10 · Guard 12 · Attack +4 (shovel 3) · Armor 0 · Dread 0

Factor Joss Mardle of the Rim Road Company

A smooth-shaven, prosperous Oathen-trained factor of fifty, in a good grey coat, who never says anything unqualified. He holds the Fast’s grain contract at Brindle Cross. He shorted the autumn deliveries on Company orders, diverting the grain north to buy oil for the Vigil’s lamps, at three times the price. The contract allows it, in a clause about “force of circumstance” he drafted himself. He knows exactly how many Unfed will starve. He has done the sum and filed it. Secret: the Company has instructed him to exercise its “first refusal” on the Unfed dead this winter, and he is ashamed enough to have delayed. Meeting the PCs: he offers them a contract.

Hollow Ann Pruett, the Card-Keeper

A spry, birdlike old woman of seventy-five with a bag over her shoulder, who walks the Fast collecting place cards from broken tables: over three hundred, kept in an oiled box, sorted by name. She has cards for people now Seated, people now dead, people who were never born in the Fast. She has cards with Rim names. She has three cards with the names of PCs, collected years ago. And she has one card that has no name on it at all, only a small, careful drawing of an empty chair, pushed in, square to the table. She found it at a table with eight chairs. She will not let anyone hold it. Meeting the PCs: she gives one of them their own card, and asks them to keep it, since it is theirs.

Minor Folk and Foes

Reckoner Knife Threat 3 · Flesh 13 · Guard 16 · Attack +7 (black-iron knife 2; first strike on a sleeper is a Grace) · Armor 1 · Dread 1

Tablebreaker Axe Threat 2 · Flesh 14 · Guard 14 · Attack +6 (axe 4) · Armor 1 · Dread 0

Seated of the Long Table Threat 0 · Flesh 3 · Guard 8 · Attack none · Armor 0 · Dread 2 (Dread 3 when they all turn and look); each call by name forces an Invitation check at Routine 10

Fatlands Poacher Threat 2 · Flesh 13 · Guard 13 · Attack +5 (cosh 3, or net) · Armor 2 · Dread 0

Fatlands Pilgrim Threat 1 · Flesh 12 · Guard 10 · Attack +2 (fist 1) · Armor 0 · Dread 1 (to hear them beg)

Playing the Unfed

Hunger is honest.
— Unfed proverb

You are the only person on the Table with nothing in your blood but blood. You have never tasted a god. You have also never, not once in your life, been full. You are proud, cold, thin, disciplined, and very, very hungry, and the warmest, kindest thing in the world is following you, laying tables.

Attribute bonus: +1 to any one attribute of your choice. (Most Unfed take Caul or Gut.)

Cut: 0. You cannot Partake. You have no Tooth, no Hunger track, no Regrowth, no Gifts, no Wants, and no Sop. Instead you have Want and Pangs.

Want: The Refusal Mechanic

The Godeaters have the god in them. You have the space where a god would be, and you have learned to use it. Want is a pool from 0 to 10 that measures how much you have refused, and how sharp the refusing has made you. The Unfed say the other peoples have many Wants and they have only one, and it is the size of everything. Start play with Want 3.

Earning Want.

  • Refuse an offer of real value (food, drink, shelter, rest, a gift, a kindness) in a scene where accepting would clearly help you: +1 Want. Once per scene. It must cost you something; the GM may ask for a Caul + Resolve roll (Routine 10) if the offer is sincere and you are Hollow or worse.
  • Refuse Orrum. Pass an Invitation check against a laid table, a “Come in,” a place card, or a Steward’s offer: +2 Want (+3 on a Grace).
  • End a day hungry. A day on half a ration or less: +1 Want. A day with nothing at all: +2 Want (and a Pang, below).
  • Say the Decline at a deathbed (a companion’s, or a Seated guest’s): +1 Want, and you gain 1 Fray.

Spending Want.

  • The Second No (1 Want): reroll one die of a Grace Roll you just made. Keep the new result, even if it is worse.
  • The Gnaw (2 Want): add a d6, the Empty Tooth, to any roll. This is the Unfed’s answer to Partaking. It adds no Hunger. If the Empty Tooth shows a 1, you gain 1 Pang: your body paid.
  • Nothing to Hold (2 Want): add +4 to resist any godsign effect aimed at you: a Closer’s touch, a Calling, a Sayer’s word, a blink-dream, a Fatlands meat-lure, a Cradlewrack door. Your blood is empty; there is nothing in you for the god to hold on to.
  • Clean Through (5 Want): ignore a godsign effect aimed at you entirely, once, as though it had never been made. Witnesses who carry godsign make a Dread 2 check: something in their blood flinched.
  • Steady (1 Want): add +2 to any Dread check about hunger, food, tables, or the Seated.

At Want 10: Hollow. You are perfectly empty, and Orrum notices. That night, a table is laid for you within sight of wherever you sleep, with your name on the card. You must make an Invitation check each hour until dawn. Want cannot rise above 10. Spend it down.

Invitation Checks

When Orrum offers (a laid table, a voice at a door, a smell of bread on the wind, a place card, a chair pulled out), roll Caul + Resolve against the offer’s strength.

OfferDifficulty
Smell of baking on the windRoutine 10
A laid table, seen from a roadHard 14
A voice saying “Come in”Grim 18
A place card with your name in a loved handGrim 18
A chair pulled out, within reach; TablenightDire 22

Add your Pangs to the Difficulty: the hungrier you are, the better it smells. On a success, you refuse; gain Want. On a failure, take one step toward the table and roll again next round at +2 Difficulty; companions may hold you (an opposed Gut + Brawl) or speak the Decline for you (their Tongue + Persuade as a bonus die, once). On a Lack, you sit. On double 1s, you thank the chair.

The Seating. A PC who sits is Seated, and is lost: they become a guest, smiling, eating air, and will waste for decades at the table. The player may play out the First Course for a scene: the food is real to them, the best they have ever eaten, and they will say so. They can be dragged away only to die. They can never be rescued. Lent Ashby got up; the GM may decide that one other person in history might. It will not be cheap, and Welcome Ardent will want something.

Pangs: Starvation

Every character in the Fast tracks Pangs, from 0 to 10.

  • A ration is a day’s adequate food (about 1 lack’s worth). A Pantry measure is half a ration.
  • A day on a full ration: −1 Pang. A day of real plenty (two rations, rest, warmth): −2 Pangs, but an Unfed must succeed at a Gut + Endure roll (Hard 14) or lose 1d6 Flesh to cramps, sweats, and the heart’s stutter, refeeding sickness.
  • A day on a Pantry measure: no change. Unfed live here.
  • A day on less than a Pantry measure: +1 Pang.
  • A day with nothing: +2 Pangs. (Non-Unfed: +2, and +1 more after the third consecutive day.)
PangsStateEffects
0–2PeckishNone for Unfed. Others: −1 Caul + Resolve vs food.
3–4Hollow−1 to Gut and Lung rolls. Smells of baking everywhere.
5–6Gaunt−2 Gut and Lung; −2 Flesh max; you dream of meals.
7–8Wasting−3 all Hand, Gut, Lung rolls; −4 Flesh max; +1 Fray daily.
9BrinkEach dawn, Gut + Endure (Grim 18) or suffer Ruin.
10StarvedYou die, unless something feeds you in the night.

The Unfed feel it differently. At Hollow the cold gets in, and the fingers go white and dead; at Gaunt the hair comes away in the comb and the gums bleed when you bite; at Wasting the heart thuds slow and heavy, the ankles swell, sores open on the hips where you lie, and the mind goes sharp and strange and full of food: you recite recipes you have never been taught. At Brink you stop feeling hungry. That is the worst sign, and every Unfed knows it.

When the Unfed Eat a God

An Unfed who eats the god-meat of another land (Fatlands crop or meat, Brinehollow brine, anything grown in a Godeater soil long enough to carry its god) has done what Tobias Wether and Scour did, and it cannot be undone.

  • They gain that land’s godsign. They become Cut 1 of that land’s line, at Regrowth 1 (the Taste), and gain the Tooth, a Hunger track, and that land’s Gifts, Wants, and Sop as their Regrowth rises.
  • They lose the Refusal. Want drops to 0 and can never again be earned. Orrum never again lays a place for them. That sounds like freedom. It is felt as being struck off a list.
  • The Empty Room (something worse). An Unfed body has no ancestral habit of the god, no six centuries of bloodline to dilute and slow it. The god moves into them as into an empty, well-kept house, and makes itself comfortable. Their Tooth bites back on a 1 or a 2. Each time their Hunger empties, their Regrowth rises by 2, not 1. And the meat in them is looking for a god to belong to: within a season they will hear its voice, in the voice of someone it was eaten with.
  • A second land’s meat. If a Returned eats the god-meat of a second land, roll on the Mangling table at once: two gods are fighting over the house.

The Unfed call them the Returned, never to their faces. Most hide it. Some go to the Lean House. Some go back over the Rim and eat, and eat, and are not seen again.

What You Carry

Every Unfed PC starts with a ration-cloth, a water flask, a wax tin, a small household axe, three days’ Pantry measures, a coat that is not warm enough, and a name chosen for refusal. They have no money worth counting: 2d6 lacks.

Background Concepts

  • Measure-Bearer. You carried the list to the hamlets, and you know whose names were missing. You have never forgiven yourself for not looking at it first.
  • Tablebreaker’s Rope-Holder. You have pulled your Breaker back from a chair a dozen times. Last week you didn’t pull fast enough.
  • Poacher’s Escapee. You were taken over the Rim, fed for a month, and broke loose before the surgeon came. You came home plump and ashamed, and nobody will stand next to you on Tablenight.

Names

  • Given names: Forbear, Abstain, Decline, Stint, Tarry, Nay, Spare, Lent, Wont, Want, Meagre, Scant, Yield, Keep, Abate, Withhold, Forswear, Fallow, Bare, Pinch, Sparing, Lean, Scarcity, Reft, Abide, Hesitate, Cease.
  • Old (shameful) given names: Welcome, Ardent, Mercy, Hallow, Blythe, Bounty, Cheer, Plenty, Supper, Kindle.
  • Surnames: Ashby, Hollis, Moss, Avery, Rooke, Bellamy, Garrity, Hartsell, Wend, Corliss, Marsh, Tolland, Osmond, Aldane, Odell, Kettering, Hume, Corve, Kell, Pruett, Fennick, Lammas, Brindle, Hatch.

Horrors of the Fast

For the GM

The Fast is the quietest chapter of the book. Nothing attacks. Everything offers. Run it slowly: golden afternoons, empty roads, the smell. Let the players be hungry. Track Pangs openly. Describe food constantly, lovingly, and never let them eat it. The horror of the Fast is that the god is good, the food is real, and the only thing between your players and perfect contentment is a rule their grandparents made up while starving to death. Let them doubt it.

d20Scene
1A farmhouse kitchen with the table laid for a family of six. Five plates are clean. The sixth has the PC’s name, and the food on it is still steaming.
2The Long Table at dusk. Three hundred Seated lift their forks together, chew together, swallow together. The sound is like a herd grazing.
3A mother in Wanting carries her child’s ration to the Lean House, where her husband lies omitted. She stands at the door, and does not go in, and eats it.
4A Seated girl of perhaps twenty has been at table so long her hair has grown into the cloth. She asks a PC to brush it.
5A Reckoner band comes home through Brindle Cross. One of them has a christening spoon in his pocket and does not know how it got there.
6A warm front crosses the camp at night. In the morning everyone’s lips are glazed, sweet, and sticky. Nobody remembers eating.
7An Unfed grave in an open field, with a little table beside it. The earth of the grave has been disturbed from inside. The chair is pulled out.
8Kale Dragoman’s camp: four Unfed captives, fat and clean, sitting by the fire with bowls of stew in their laps, weeping, unable to stop eating.
9A Starved Saint’s novice offers a PC a twist of cloth with honey-cake crumbs in it, and asks them to taste it and tell her if it is poison.
10A Seated man dragged from the Long Table by his son dies in the road in two minutes, all at once, his body collapsing like a dropped tent. He thanks the host.
11A child’s voice from a cottage door calls a PC by their childhood nickname, and says supper’s ready, and says Mam’s made your favourite.
12An empty Rim inn, every table laid, every chair pulled out except one at each table: pushed in, square, its back to the lamp.
13A pilgrim column on the road, dying. A Fatlands woman asks a PC to hold her up so she can smell it one more time.
14A Reckoner Knife in a Wanting alley, alone, sobbing into a baby’s knitted blanket, saying the Decline over and over.
15Abide Kettering’s cart at the western crossroads. A sack moves.
16The bricked hearth in a PC’s lodging is warm to the touch. Through the mortar comes the soft sound of a spoon in a pot.
17A table on a frozen pond. Under the ice, a family of the Seated, perfectly preserved, smiling up, forks raised.
18The Pantry, at midnight, with every door locked. Inside, the ledgers are laid out on a long cloth like place settings, open at the names of the omitted.
19Hallowboard on a still evening. On the eighth, unworn side, a single chair stands in the untrodden chalk, pushed in. There are no footprints near it.
20Orrum, at a distance, across a gold field: a tall shape in an open doorway, stooping, lamplight behind it, holding out one long arm. It is crying. It is holding the door for someone it is not looking at. (Dread 4.)
Chapter 10

Threads Between the Lands

Every land is certain that the cure is next door.
— Rim Road saying

The lands of the Table are not separate stories. They share a road, a coin, a grace and a doom, and the crises in each are beginning to touch. This chapter takes the open storylines that cross borders and lays them out as campaign threads: who is involved in each land, how the thread escalates if nobody interferes, what player characters can do about it, and how it might end. Most of the endings are bad. That is not a failure of imagination; it is the setting. A thread resolved well is a thread that ends one way rather than a worse way.

Each thread is written in stages. Advance a thread one stage whenever the characters spend a season elsewhere, or whenever the GM wishes the world to feel the weight of the clock. Threads touch: the Sayer’s Sentence feeds the Deadwatch, the Blank Trade feeds the Second Table, and almost everything feeds Eight Chairs.

Running Threads

Pick two or three threads to run in the background of a campaign and let the others exist only as rumors. Keep a simple track for each, Stage 1 to Stage 4, on a card the players never see. When a thread reaches Stage 4 it resolves, with or without the characters, and the world changes. Characters who intervene can hold a thread at its current stage for a season, push it back one stage at great cost, or steer which ending it reaches. They cannot make it not have happened.

The Deadwatch

Summary. The Vigil cannot sleep and is running out of everything: beds, rouse, oil and time. Its Warden-Prime has sent Envoy Castellan Dray to Lastgate to buy the secret of Keeping from Regent Ansel Grue: if the Vigil’s citizens could be killed and kept upright, a city of the dead would never need to sleep. The flaw is geography. The Kept cannot leave Sallowreach. If the plan goes ahead, the Vigil will have to move there.

The Players.

  • The Vigil: Envoy Castellan Dray; Warden-Prime Ilvane Stroud; Dr. Aldous Crane, whose dose curve gives the Vigil eleven years; Benedikt Lour, already drawing plans for the whole population.
  • Sallowreach: Regent Ansel Grue, who is tempted by a hundred thousand new taxable dead; Lady Corrow Vane, who would have to Close nobody and keep everyone; the Heirs, who see a new population of the never-dying arriving to sit on top of them forever; Tam Ruddock, who already knows how to move people across the Drop.
  • The Rim: the Company, which would carry the migration and price it; Fogmouth, where the line is painted.
StageWhat Happens
1Dray negotiates in Lastgate. Small trials: Vigil volunteers are brought north, killed in Sallowreach, and kept. They do not sleep. It works.
2The Watch votes in secret to relocate. Caravans of Vigil citizens, mostly the poor of the Slope, begin moving west along the Rim under Company contract.
3The first mass Killing at Fogmouth: thousands of Vigil folk die north of the Drop and stand back up. The Heirs riot. The Mortuary Court demands a toll per head.
4Lastgate’s lower levels fill with sleepless dead foreigners. The Vigil’s lamps begin to go out, one district at a time, as the city empties into the fen.

What PCs Can Do. Escort or sabotage the trial caravans. Expose to the Vigil’s poor what Keeping actually feels like (Kept bodies rot and feel it for centuries). Uncover the Court’s hidden reason for agreeing: the Court believes new dead without Hand-line blood may slow the Hushes. Steal Dray’s commission, which the Warden-Prime would rather die than see read aloud.

Endings.

  • The Dead City: the Vigil moves north and becomes a district of Lastgate, a hundred thousand rotting, wakeful foreigners. The Dormitory is abandoned with its Counted inside, unguarded, and the lamps go out over sixty thousand beds.
  • The Broken Deal: the Heirs drag Dray to a Hush; the Vigil, betrayed, closes the Rim at Lampwick Halt; Sallowreach loses its rouse and oil, and Lastgate’s candle-makers turn to the only fuel left.
  • The Worst Arithmetic: a Vigil sleeper is brought north, unconscious, and killed in Sallowreach. They do not wake and do not die. They lie there, Kept and Counted at once, and the Dormitory’s number goes up by one.

The Host on the Road

Summary. For six centuries Orrum kept to the Fast. Now its tables have been found laid at crossroads in three other lands, and the seemers of the Vigil, the scavengers of Brinehollow and the pilgrims of the Fatlands have all, separately, seen the same tall figure laying a table. That figure is Welcome Ardent, the Host’s steward, walking a mile ahead of his god, and he is working his way around the Rim.

The Players.

  • The Fast: Welcome Ardent, polite and exhausted; Spare Tolland of the Hostwatch, mapping the warm ground; Decline Marsh and the Tablebreakers; Envoy Prudence Lowell.
  • The Vigil: Mirela Sconce, who recorded eleven districts hallucinating a table being laid in the street.
  • The Fatlands: Osanna Blythe and her three hundred pilgrims, hungry every second of their lives, looking for a table where they will finally feel full.
  • Brinehollow: salvagers on the Uncovered who have found tables laid on the dry seabed with the plates still wet.
  • The Rim: the wardens at Saltlick Cross; every innkeeper who has seen a tall shape stoop to look in at the window.
StageWhat Happens
1Tables appear at Rim crossroads, one a season. Tablebreakers cross the Hem to smash them. Place cards bear the names of people who live nearby.
2Welcome Ardent is seen in person at a Rim inn. He asks, politely, whether anyone would take over his duties. The first non-Unfed sit down: a Fatlands family, a Vigil nudger, a Kept man a yard north of the Drop at Fogmouth, who now cannot leave the table or the fen.
3Orrum itself is seen on the Rim at night, stooping to look in at windows. Whole villages along the Fatlands border are found Seated. Osanna Blythe’s pilgrims find their table.
4Tables are laid in every capital on the same night, with a place card for every head of state. In each, one chair is left without a card.

What PCs Can Do. Track Ardent and talk to him (he is the only one of Orrum’s guests who can still get up, and he will answer questions honestly if he is not invited to sit). Smash tables, at the risk of finding their own names. Protect or stop the pilgrims. Discover that the cardless chair at each table faces away from the others.

Endings.

  • The Long Table Grows: the Seated spread along the Rim, a second endless table around the whole continent, happy, wasting, praising the food. Trade stops because the road is full of diners.
  • The Relief: a player character accepts Ardent’s position. Ardent finally sits down and eats, and dies in moments, weeping with gratitude. The character now walks a mile ahead of the god forever, and knows exactly whom the tables are for.
  • The Unanswered Door: the tables stop, all at once. Orrum stands still at Hallowboard facing the eighth side. The Hostwatch reports that it has never looked so frightened.

Brine in the Rouse

Summary. Captain Jonah Skerry, called Dry Jonah, bottles what Brinehollowers cough up at bailing and sells it inland as tonic. It sells best in the Vigil, where the Slope dealer Rook Quarter-Bell cuts it into rouse because it is cheap and it works. The sleepless are now feeling the Calling, four hundred miles from any coast. Customers stay awake. They have also started walking west.

The Players.

  • Brinehollow: Dry Jonah; Tolly Brack, who knows by the color of bailing water who will be Called next; the Netwatch, who are going to see Called strangers arrive from the east.
  • The Vigil: Rook Quarter-Bell; Dr. Aldous Crane, desperate for anything that stretches the dose; the Wakers; Inspector Hale Grimmer, whose blink-murders begin to cluster on the western edge of the city.
  • The Rim: Lampwick Halt and Lowmark Spur, the two ends of the walk.
StageWhat Happens
1The Slope’s addicts stand at west windows. Dr. Crane notices that brine-cut rouse holds an hour longer and does not report it.
2Vigil citizens begin walking west across the plateau in their sleep-that-is-not-sleep, eyes open, straight lines. The Wakers net them at the city edge.
3Crane formulates brine into the official rouse. The whole Vigil now carries a little of the sea. Lines of walkers cross the Rim heading for a coast they have never seen.
4The first Vigil walkers reach the Uncovered and keep going, out toward the Trench. Some come back Tenanted: calm, courteous, rested. They are the first people in the Vigil in three centuries who sleep and wake again.

What PCs Can Do. Trace the supply chain from bailing buckets in Lowmark to dealers on the Slope. Kill or bargain with Dry Jonah. Shepherd walkers home or follow them to see where they go. Present the Watch with the choice: brine buys the Vigil years of wakefulness at the cost of the sea pulling on every citizen.

Endings.

  • The Walking City: the Vigil adopts brine-rouse openly and loses a tenth of its people a year to the west. The Watch calls it emigration.
  • The Tenanted Wardens: Tenanted Vigil-folk, rested and calm, are found to be immune to the Dormitory’s dream. The Watch begins appointing them to office, as Brinehollow did with its judges. Nobody asks whose eyes are looking out.
  • The Meeting of Waters: the Trench, the draining sea and the long dim room in the Vigil’s dream turn out to be closer than anyone thought. Senna Vole, on her forty-first dive, hears water.

The First to Eat

Summary. Tobias Wether, a runaway raised on six centuries of refusal, crossed into the Fatlands and ate. The Reckoner called Scour spent a year undercover in the Fatlands, had to eat to keep his cover, and came home with godsign. Two Unfed bodies now carry a god that was never theirs, and the meat inside them seems to be looking for something.

The Players.

  • The Fast: Scour, hiding his godsign under his sleeves and volunteering for every raid; Reckoner-Captain Scant Hollis; the Abstinent, for whom this is the worst possible news; Meek Garrity, whose research says the Unfed never refused at all.
  • The Fatlands: Tobias Wether; Corder Lank of the Thin, who is very interested in a man who came from emptiness into hunger; Brother Glut of the Second Helping, who sees a convert.
  • Cross-border: Odo Venn of the College, who wants to taste them; the Second Table, who want to know whether an Unfed stomach makes room for a god.
StageWhat Happens
1Tobias shows his first godsign. It is not purely Ummer’s: he dreams of a long dim room and closes doors behind him. Scour’s signs are similar.
2The College learns of them. Unfed blood with godsign is, by the ledgers, impossible. Odo Venn tastes Tobias and goes pale and does not report the flavor.
3Scour’s comrades find out. The Abstinent strike his name from the Pantry. He flees to the Rim, where the Second Table is waiting.
4Tobias and Scour, kept apart, begin to show identical signs at the same hour. Neither carries any one god. Both are getting hungrier for the same thing, and when they meet, they set a table.

What PCs Can Do. Protect them, hide them, study them or kill them. Bring Tobias back into the Fast and see what happens to the Lack around him. Learn, from Venn’s private notes, that what grows in an Unfed body is not the god the body ate.

Endings.

  • The Empty Vessel: the Second Table buys Scour and serves him, as a test. The diners all sleep badly afterward, and dream of a room where someone is laying a table.
  • The Lack Breaks: Tobias returns to the Fast and plants. The dead soil sprouts where he walks. The Abstinent call it a miracle and then realize what it means: the heartland can be fed if its people eat. Wont Bellamy wins the next vote.
  • Two Places Laid: Tobias and Scour vanish from their guarded rooms on the same night. Two Orrum tables are found the next morning at the Rim, with their names on the cards, and the chairs pushed in.

The Blank Trade

Summary. Wren Hollowell in the Fatlands, Cassian Wry in Oathen and the entire population of the Fast are worth more in parts than whole. Blank blood, marrow and organs are believed to slow the Regrowth. Dr. Mercy Thrane of the Fast is following the buyers, and the trail leads to the Second Table.

The Players.

  • The Fast: Dr. Mercy Thrane; Marshal Keep Aldane, holding the border against poachers; every Unfed child sent to fetch water at dusk.
  • The Fatlands: Kale Dragoman, poacher; Wren Hollowell, with a bounty on her weight that does not specify alive; the Board of Plenty.
  • Oathen: Cassian Wry, the crown’s Blank spy, kept in luxury and never let out of sight; the Bench of Clauses, which has received an offer.
  • Cross-border: Master Quillon Barr and Lady Seraphine Dalgety of the Second Table; the Rim Road Company, whose wagons carry sealed brine-barrels it does not open.
StageWhat Happens
1Unfed disappearances double along the eastern border. Thrane finds a surgery in Sated with an Unfed man’s name scratched inside a cupboard.
2Wren Hollowell is taken. A Fatlands Gut-line matriarch is seen at the Weighing ten stone lighter and, for the first time in thirty years, not eating.
3Oathen’s Bench agrees, in a forty-page conditional, to lease Cassian Wry’s kidney to a foreign buyer. The surgery is scheduled at Treaty Stair.
4Thrane traces the trail to Master Barr’s surgery, and finds Abide, nine years a donor, fat and smiling, and the eighth course on a menu pinned to the wall, still blank.

What PCs Can Do. Raid a surgery. Escort Wren out of the Fatlands, which will put every bounty-hunter in the south on their trail. Free Cassian Wry, who has been kept all his life and does not know how to live unwatched. Follow the money to the Rim Road Company’s sealed barrels and make the Company choose between its neutrality and its conscience. If a player character is a Blank, this thread is about them.

Endings.

  • The Market Holds: the trade goes on, and prices rise. The Fast begins to sell its own people to buy grain, and calls it Pantry policy.
  • The Exposed Table: the trail is published. In every capital, a few High Cuts are revealed to be carrying Unfed organs, and the Reckoners have a new list.
  • Room Made: Barr’s patients begin, one by one, to feel empty inside, in exactly the places where a Blank organ was sewn in. They become very hungry. They do not know for what.

The Missing Hand

Summary. In a guarded barn in Cradlewrack, Dov Marrin and the Assemblers have fitted four hundred Parts from four hundred families into one figure eleven feet long. It breathes. It is missing a left hand and a voice. Hester Lowe bore a left hand and is hiding it. Juniper Dell was born saying half a sentence. Every Part, the Assemblers say, belongs to one body born piecemeal; and the figure has begun to turn its head toward the Sill.

The Players.

  • Cradlewrack: Dov Marrin; Hester Lowe, who will kill for the hand; Juniper Dell, called Firstword; Ambrose the Eldest Infant, who claims to remember being Vey’s left eye; Old Hinge at the Sill; Dr. Lazar Voss of the Vigil, who has drawn the figure and counted more than two of several things.
  • Sallowreach: Marrow Jack, the part-thief, who has been buying Cradlewrack Parts on the Rim; Sister Tisane Halloway’s jar of grey hinged joints, which fit together.
  • The Rim: Petra Quick, who smuggled a Part across the border without knowing it.
StageWhat Happens
1The Assemblers hire outsiders to find the hand. Hester moves house every night. The hand has begun to point.
2Juniper Dell meets someone, somewhere, who says the other half of her sentence. Nobody hears it but them.
3The hand is taken, or given. The figure’s left arm is complete. It sits up. The pangs fall to seven days.
4Juniper is brought to the barn. She speaks her half and the figure speaks the other half. The Sill door swings fully open for the first time since the Gorging.

What PCs Can Do. Protect Hester and the hand. Find the person with the other half of the sentence before the Assemblers do. Burn the barn (the figure will not burn easily; it will begin again out of the ashes). Learn from Dr. Voss’s drawing that the figure is not Vey alone: some of its Parts came from outside Cradlewrack, and some belong to no god anyone has named.

Endings.

  • The Firstborn: the figure stands, walks to the Sill and goes through. Whatever was describing the view to Old Hinge comes back through the other way.
  • The Hand Withheld: Hester refuses to the last and is killed; the hand crawls away into the hills and is never found. The figure lies incomplete and breathing, and Cradlewrack’s pangs continue to shorten anyway. It was never the figure the land was in labor with.
  • The Sentence: the full sentence is spoken aloud once. Everyone who hears it understands exactly what is being born out of the ground, and when. Nobody who hears it can be persuaded to say it again.

The Sayer's Sentence

Summary. Every land with a failing cure has thought of the same thing: go to Oathen, and have Lady Imre Dath, the Sayer, say that it is fixed. What a Sayer says, is. Nobody knows what Tolm would make true if she did. The Bench of Clauses is debating, in forty-page conditionals, whether to take out her golden bit; and she has begun to write her own sentences.

The Players.

  • Oathen: Lady Imre Dath; Sorrin Vael, Chief Clausewright, who would draft the sentence; Ket the Ninth, who must nod; Garl Tome, who made the gold bit; Yusra Thole, Rainwarden, whose silence about the late rain is being noticed.
  • Every land: envoys from the Vigil (Let the Vigil sleep and wake), Brinehollow (Let the sea return), Sallowreach (Let the dead finish), the Fatlands (Let the hungry be full), Cradlewrack (Let nothing more be born wrong).
  • Cross-border: the Rim Road Company, which needs the Kept Rain kept; the Second Table, which wants a single sentence of its own: Let the second meal hold.
StageWhat Happens
1Envoys arrive in Tacit and bid. The Bench begins drafting. Lady Imre is caught with chalk and a wall full of her own sentences.
2An envoy, impatient, bribes a guard. Someone gets into the Gilded Cells with a question. The Sayer answers. A valley in Oathen changes overnight.
3The Bench agrees on a text, four hundred conditions long, to be spoken at the next unmuzzling. Every faction on the Table tries to alter one clause.
4The bit comes out. She speaks.

What PCs Can Do. Carry an envoy’s bid, or forge one. Guard the Cells or break into them. Edit the sentence, one clause at a time, through bribes, threats and Clausewrights. Read Lady Imre’s own wall, where she has written, over and over, a sentence she has never been allowed to say. Learn that she has never once been asked what she wants.

Endings.

  • It Is Fixed: she says the Bench’s sentence. Every Regrowth stops dead where it stands. So does every other change, of any kind. See the Secrets chapter.
  • Her Own Sentence: she says what she has been writing. It is short. It is about her. The god in her gets what it wants.
  • The Slip: the sentence is spoken and does not take. A god’s word has slipped again, worse than the rain. Every oath in Oathen loosens by a hair, and every Forsworn body in the Breakdowns begins, slowly, to heal, and every sworn contract on the Rim begins to fail.

Eight Chairs

Summary. Cray Lobbett found a stone table on the seabed of the Uncovered, older than the Gorging, with eight chairs, seven pushed in. Hallowboard, at the center of the world, has eight sides. Grandfather Peat, a bog body hauled from the Sump, is the last witness to the Night of Seven Tables and says the god was smiling. Meek Garrity has found the seating plan for Hallowboard. Someone is going to put these together. This is the thread that leads to the Secrets chapter, and it should be the spine of any long campaign.

The Players.

  • Brinehollow: Cray Lobbett, who cannot stop going back; Hask Tarn, the only pilot who knows the ground; Ilse Marl, whose transcriptions of the Tenanted’s singing make a chart.
  • Sallowreach: Grandfather Peat; Old Bettany Shroud, whose forty thousand shelved dead all whisper the same word.
  • The Fast: Meek Garrity and his plan; Welcome Ardent; Verger Sober Osmond at the Empty Chair.
  • Cross-border: Archprovost Hesper Lune of the College, who has been reconstructing the chiseled figure; Envoy Prudence Lowell, who will do anything to keep Garrity quiet; the Second Table, who want the eighth line of their menu filled.
StageWhat Happens
1Garrity’s plan leaks. The Abstinent call it forgery. Lobbett tries to sell the table’s location again and finds a buyer who pays in Company platters.
2Someone brings a translator to Grandfather Peat. He describes the Night in full. He describes the bank behind the god, and what was on it.
3Rubbings from the seabed table are compared with Hallowboard and with Lune’s reconstruction. They match. The eighth chair on the seabed is the only one pulled out, and it faces the same way as the eighth side of Hallowboard.
4The word Bettany Shroud’s dead whisper is the older word for guest. It is said aloud, in full, by someone who has put it together. Everything that has been hiding hears it.

What PCs Can Do. Everything, and that is the danger. Dive to the table. Interrogate Peat. Steal Garrity’s papers. Visit Hallowboard and count the sides. Each discovery should cost Fray. The right questions in the right order lead, inevitably, to the Secrets chapter’s answers, and the answers are not survivable in any comfortable sense.

Endings.

  • Counted: the chairs are counted aloud. It does not matter by whom. The eighth chair, on the seabed, at Hallowboard, at every inn on the Rim, turns from the wall to face the table.
  • The Silence Kept: the characters destroy the evidence and kill or silence those who know. The world goes on not knowing for a few more years. The characters do not get to.
  • The Place Card: at the end of a long investigation, a character finds a table laid for them, with a card in the Host’s handwriting, and a second card, in another hand, at the chair beside them.

The Second Table

Summary. In every capital, a few of the highest Cuts are sharpening knives for a meal they intend to eat twice. When the gods finish regrowing, they will eat them again, a few diners instead of a mob, and inherit another six centuries of grace. Wont Bellamy, a heretic on the Fast’s own council, wants the Unfed to join them, starting with the one god that is still whole.

The Players.

  • Every land: the Carvers: Lord Absalom Thrale (Grand Carver, Sallowreach); Lady Seraphine Dalgety (the Vigil); Master Quillon Barr (surgeon); and in every capital two or three Trenchermen of the highest Cut, some of them named in land chapters and never suspected.
  • The Fast: Wont Bellamy, who argues the Refusal was only a postponement.
  • Cross-border: Lysander Coyle of the Company, selling them the price of the world; Silas Fenwright, whose stolen ledgers would tell them which gods are ripe.
StageWhat Happens
1Practice dinners. Characters of standing are invited to one. The dish is not named until afterward.
2The Table commissions its knives: eight, of grey bone, from a Sallowreach bone-carver who is found Closed afterward.
3Wont Bellamy carries a motion before the Abstinent: the Unfed should do now what the others did then. Orrum is seen, for the first time, standing still while the Hostwatch approaches, as if waiting.
4The Second Table gathers at Hallowboard on Tablenight, all of them, around the eight-sided table, with knives, and the Host lies down.

What PCs Can Do. Infiltrate a dinner and finish the plate. Expose a Carver. Steal a knife. Warn the Fast, which may not believe them. Discover that the Head of the Table presides from an empty chair, and that nobody at the dinners has ever seen anyone sit in it.

Endings.

  • The Second Meal: they eat the Host. See the Secrets chapter for what this does. It is the worst thing anyone has ever done.
  • The Table Turned: the characters expose the cult; the Reckoners and the Purgation do the rest. Every High Cut in the world is now suspect, and the Lancings begin on a scale not seen since Brookhythe.
  • Served: at the final dinner, the Carvers discover that they are not the diners. The empty chair is occupied.

The Undying Flame

Summary. A new thread. The Vigil has ninety days of oil. Lamplighter-General Garron Ashlock has a supplier who doubled his price and a standing order to tell no one. In Sallowreach, fires smolder for decades and nothing can finish, and Wick Tallow renders the unclaimed dead into candles that feel themselves burn and give a very steady light. A Sallowreach flame does not go out. The Vigil has noticed.

The Players.

  • The Vigil: Garron Ashlock; Benedikt Lour; the Lamplighters’ Guild.
  • Sallowreach: Wick Tallow, the Chandler; Regent Ansel Grue, who would sell the unclaimed dead by the cartload; the Loft-Wardens, whose forty thousand shelved dead are also, technically, unclaimed.
  • The Fatlands: Mistress Brisket Annalow of the Renderers’ Union, who supplied the Vigil’s tallow and is being undercut; Quartermaster Ivo Stockpot, who has noticed what goes into the Vigil’s barrels.
  • The Rim: the Company, which must decide whether candles of people are freight or Hush-toll.
StageWhat Happens
1Ashlock buys a crate of Tallow’s candles in secret. They burn for a month without shortening. He weeps with relief.
2A contract is sworn in Oathen. Wagon trains of Kept-candles go east along the Rim. The Lofts begin to empty. Bettany Shroud reports her shelved dead are being taken in the night.
3The Vigil’s street-lamps are lit with people. Citizens can hear them at night, a faint high keening from every bracket. The Seeming begins to show faces in the flames.
4A candle is carried out of Sallowreach and should, by the Rule, finish at the Drop. It does not. It keeps burning. Something has changed about what can end, and where.

What PCs Can Do. Guard or hijack a candle train. Speak to a candle (they can hear and, with care, be made to answer). Help Ashlock find another way, or help him justify this one. Bring the Loft-Wardens’ witnesses into it: the Set-Aside are aware, and they have opinions about being burned.

Endings.

  • Light Eternal: the Vigil lives in a permanent glow of its neighbors’ dead, and Sallowreach is paid in rouse and mirrors. Nobody in either city sleeps well.
  • The Lofts Rise: the Set-Aside, learning what is planned, refuse. Forty thousand dead begin to whisper the same word louder. The Loft-Wardens open the doors.
  • The Finished Light: the candles all go out at once, everywhere, on the night the first Hush opens in the Vigil, four hundred miles from Sallowreach. The Hushes are not bound to the fen anymore.

The Slipping Seal

Summary. A new thread. Oathen’s Kept Rain came three days late, which means a god’s promise slipped. Every Rim Road Company contract, every platter, every bond of every Bonded Hand is sworn in Oathen and rests on the word of one notary, Jessamy Quill. If Tolm’s word can slip, so can hers. The Company is quietly auditing everything and looking for something better to swear by.

The Players.

  • Oathen: Jessamy Quill; Yusra Thole, Rainwarden, silent for a month; Ottoline Vant, whose miscut word broke a man; Ona Fell, the Surety, one default from death.
  • The Rim: First Spoke Odalys Penhallow; Auditor-General Lysander Coyle; Reeve Calder Stokes, the Company auditor in Brinehollow who tasted salt this morning.
  • Everywhere: every government that has ever sworn a treaty in Oathen, which is every government.
StageWhat Happens
1A Bonded Hand steals from the Company and does not break. The wardens hang him anyway, quietly. The Company begins re-swearing contracts.
2Jessamy Quill becomes ill. Her body begins to show marks that match no oath she has broken. The Company doubles her guard and hires a second notary in secret.
3A treaty fails: two lands discover that a border sworn in Oathen two centuries ago no longer binds either side. War is spoken of, carefully.
4Quill breaks, or dies. Half the trade of the Table comes unbound in an afternoon. Every platter is worth its weight in bone and nothing more.

What PCs Can Do. Protect Quill. Investigate why the Kept Rain was late (Yusra Thole knows and cannot lie, so she will not speak). Find the Company’s secret second notary and decide whether to expose them. Carry the Company’s frantic re-swearing across the Rim. Discover that Odalys Penhallow is preparing for the Company to survive the lands, and what she means to feed the wagons.

Endings.

  • Unbound: the Rim dissolves into seven tolls and seven armies. Every land must now get what it needs from neighbors it finds obscene without a neutral road in between, and it gets it by force.
  • The New Witness: the Company finds something else to swear by. It is listening, and it is not Tolm, and it is very glad to be asked.
  • The Last Wagons: Penhallow’s sealed wagons set out, carrying the Spokes and the archive, around and around the Rim, and the Company becomes a procession with no destination, lit at night, stopping at no inn.

The Stolen Ledgers

Summary. A new thread. Silas Fenwright, a renegade Lineman of the Cutwrights’ College, walked out of Quire with three quires copied from the Master Concordance: the full lines of the highest houses of three lands, and the College’s graph of every Regrowth bending upward at the same moment after 600 A.G. Everyone wants them. Whoever holds the ledgers knows where each god is regrowing fastest, and who is next.

The Players.

  • The College: Archprovost Hesper Lune; Odo Venn; Provost Carrion Sedge in the north, who has already learned what it is to hold a dangerous ledger.
  • Cross-border: the Purgation, who want a massacre list; the Second Table, who want a menu; the Reckoners, especially Deny Fallon, who wants a target roll.
  • Every land: noble houses who would pay anything to have their own line removed, and their rivals’, added.
StageWhat Happens
1Fenwright offers a single page for sale at the Groaning Board. The buyer is murdered before dawn.
2A Lancing in the Fatlands follows the ledger’s exact order of houses. A Reckoner raid in the Vigil follows the same page.
3The College’s graph is copied and nailed to toll-houses on the Rim. The Bait doctrine takes it as proof. Riots in three capitals.
4The third quire, the one Fenwright has not shown anyone, is opened. It is a list of every Blank born on the Table in two centuries, with their present whereabouts.

What PCs Can Do. Catch Fenwright, buy from him, or protect him. Return the quires to Quire, or not. Read them, which is a Grim Eye + Lore roll and a Dread 3 check; a character who succeeds learns their own line, and what it ends in. Track the Blank list before the Second Table does.

Endings.

  • The Lists Are Read: massacre and counter-massacre along family lines in every land. The Regrowth slows a little where the High Cuts are gone. The College records the numbers.
  • The Ledgers Burn: the characters destroy the quires; the Master Concordance at Quire burns soon after, in a fire that no one admits setting. Nobody now knows where the gods are, which helps no one.
  • Your Own Line: the ledger shows that a player character is closer to a Seating than they knew, by far. Every faction that holds a copy knows it too.
Part Two
The Rules
How to make a person of the Table, how dice decide their fate, how the god in the blood is spent, how the mind breaks, and how violence is done.
Chapter 11

Making a Guest

Ask a child of the Table who she is, and she will tell you three things, in this order: where her people ate, what part they were given, and what she does to earn her bread. Only then, if you are still listening, will she tell you her name.
— Provost Carrion Sedge, Introductory Lectures in Cutwrighting

From the intake ledger of the Thimble Cross waystation, Rim Road Company, month of Carving, 641 A.G.

Name: Halloway Brisk. Origin: Fatlands (Low Tilth, says she; accent says Sated). Cut: Gut-line, common. Middling. Bites her nails to the quick and then keeps going. Trade: Renderer, Union card, lapsed. Carrying: three cleavers, a rendering hook, eleven lacks, a jar she will not open. Purpose of travel: “Going north.” Asked why: “Because something in the south has my name on it.”

Name: Tolly Fane. Origin: the Vigil. Eyes like two holes burned in paper. Cut: Eye-line, low. Has lids, uses them sparingly. Trade: Courier, sworn. Carrying: a sealed satchel, a pin-cushion of needles, rouse enough for nine days. Purpose of travel: Did not answer. Had fallen asleep standing up. Woke before we could catch her. Says she did not.

Name: None given. Origin: the Fast, by the look of him. Thin as a fence. Cut: None. Refused bread three times and took it on the fourth, very politely. Trade: Says “breaker.” Has an axe. Carrying: the axe. A place card, folded small, which he showed to nobody but which I saw when he paid. It had his name on it, in a good hand. Purpose of travel: “To find the table it came from.”

Every player except the Carver makes one character, called a Guest. A Guest is a person of the Table: born in one of its seven lands, descended from a bloodline that ate some part of a god or refused to, trained in a trade, owing debts and loyalties, and carrying, in all but the rarest cases, a god that is slowly growing back inside them.

Character creation takes about an hour the first time. It works best done together, at the table, so that the Guests can be bound to each other before play begins. A group of strangers who meet at an inn is the oldest beginning there is, and on the Table it is also the most honest: the Rim Road is where everyone ends up.

The Steps

  • Concept. Decide, roughly, who you want to play.
  • Land. Choose where you were born. This sets your signature attribute, your god, your Gifts and your Wants.
  • Cut. Choose your bloodline’s station: Blank, Scrapling, Common, Prime or High. This sets how much god is in you, where you start on the Regrowth, and what you own.
  • Attributes. Distribute points among Hand, Gut, Lung, Eye, Tongue and Caul.
  • Calling. Choose your trade. It gives you skills, a Calling talent, Standing, and starting gear.
  • Skills. Distribute skill points.
  • Knacks. Choose two Knacks: small, specific advantages.
  • Derived traits. Calculate Flesh, Guard, Hunger, Regrowth and Fray, and note your Gifts, Wants and Sop.
  • The Four Questions. Answer the Last Meal, the Oath on the Dead, Who Waits at Home, and What You Will Not Do.
  • Gear and money. Spend your lacks at the Rim Market.

Step One: Concept

Start with a sentence. A Seamer from Lastgate who has stitched her own mother back together thirty times and is beginning to resent it. A Fatlands drover who walks herds of things that are not cattle and has stopped naming them. A Clausewright’s apprentice who said one careless word as a child and has spent twenty years keeping it. The best concepts carry a wound and a want, and a reason to be on the road.

Discuss concepts as a group. Guests should have a reason to travel together, or at least a reason not to kill each other. Good shared premises include: a Rim Road Company caravan crew; a Cutwrights’ College survey team; a band of pilgrims or refugees; a Purgation cell; the household staff of a dying noble; a Tablebreaker company; strangers stranded at the same inn when the snow comes down and turns out to be fat.

Step Two: Land

Choose the land of your birth. Each land is described at length in Part One; its chapter ends with a section called Playing a Lander, which you will need now. The land gives:

  • +1 to a signature attribute (applied after you distribute points, and the only way to start at 5).
  • Your god. If your Cut is 1 or higher, the god your ancestors ate is in your blood, and the land’s rules for the Regrowth apply to you wherever you go.
  • Gifts: powers you gain as the god grows back.
  • Wants: the compulsions that come with them.
  • The Sop: the act that quiets your god, at a price.
  • The Tooth: how your god shows itself when you call on it.
LandGod EatenSignatureThe Rule of the Land
SallowreachOssel, the Closing HandHandNothing dies. Everything rots.
The FatlandsUmmer, the LadenGutEverything is meat. Nobody is full.
BrinehollowDromm, the FathomLungThe sea is inside the people.
The VigilIss, the LiddedEyeWhoever sleeps never wakes.
CradlewrackVey, the OpeningCaulNothing is born right; too much is born.
OathenTolm, the WitnessTongueWords bind flesh.
The FastOrrum, the Host (refused)Any oneNever accept.

Exiles and the Rim-Born

A character born on the Rim Road, in a waystation or a caravan, still has a land: the land of the bloodline they descend from. The god goes where the blood goes. A Brinehollower born in a Sallowreach inn still bails at dawn. If your parents were of two lands, choose one; the other god is too weak in you to count, though the Carver may give you a single Taste of it as a quirk.

Step Three: Cut

What part of the god your ancestors were given decides your station, your wealth, and how much of a god you are carrying. Choose one.

CutStationStarting RegrowthTeethStarting Wealth
0 — BlankBorn without godsign. Hunted.0 (cannot rise)None10 lacks
1 — ScraplingThe poor; descended from the bone-lickers.0One15 lacks
2 — CommonTradesfolk, yeomen, clerks.1One40 lacks
3 — PrimeGentry, guildmasters, minor Cuts.2Two120 lacks
4 — HighNobility. The god is close.4 (the Appetite)Two400 lacks and a retainer

Cut 5 exists, but only among the oldest houses, and their members are usually too far gone to walk the Rim Road. It is not available to Guests.

Blanks (Cut 0)

A Blank is a child born with no godsign at all in a land where everyone else has some. Blanks cannot Partake and their Regrowth can never rise, unless they eat godflesh (see the Fast chapter for what happens then). They gain +2 to any roll made to resist a god’s influence (a Hush, a Calling, an oath’s Breaking, a Seated presence), and they never gain Hunger. They are also the most valuable people on the Table. Every land wants them: as saints, as specimens, as surgical stock. A Blank Guest begins play with a Bounty: somebody, somewhere, has posted a price for them. Agree with the Carver who.

The Unfed

A Guest born in the Fast is Unfed, not Blank. They carry no god because their ancestors refused, not because of a fluke of birth. Their Cut is 0; they gain +1 to any attribute instead of a signature, and use the Refusal and Want rules in the Fast chapter. They are not hunted quite as hard as Blanks, but only because there are so many more of them.

High Cuts

Playing a noble means starting closer to the end. A High Cut Guest begins at Regrowth 4, in the Appetite, with the land’s Taste and Appetite Gifts already in hand and its first Want already active. They are rich, connected, feared and despised: Scraplings spit at them, Reckoners have their names on lists, and the Second Table sends them invitations. A High Cut Guest also gains +1 Standing in their Calling and a retainer: a loyal servant (Threat 1, Flesh 9) who will die for them, and probably will.

Step Four: Attributes

Every attribute starts at 1. Distribute 9 points among them. No attribute may be raised above 4 at this stage. Then add your land’s +1. An adult of the Table averages 2 in everything; a 3 is notable, a 4 is remarkable, a 5 is the best in a city.

The Six Attributes
  • HAND: dexterity, violence, delicacy, craft. Picking a lock, gutting a pig, stitching a lip, cutting a throat.
  • GUT: strength, toughness, endurance, appetite. Carrying a corpse, holding down poison, taking a beating, eating what must be eaten.
  • LUNG: speed, agility, stamina, stealth, breath. Running, climbing, hiding, swimming, outlasting.
  • EYE: perception, reason, memory, learning. Noticing the extra joint, reading the ledger, remembering the face.
  • TONGUE: persuasion, deceit, command, oaths. Talking, lying, bargaining, swearing, and knowing when to say nothing.
  • CAUL: will, instinct, faith, the uncanny. Resisting your god, enduring horror, praying, feeling the thing in the next room before you see it. Named for the membrane some are born in.

Step Five: Calling

Your Calling is how you earn your bread. Each Calling gives:

  • Calling Skills: +1 to each of three listed skills (this may raise a skill to 4 at creation).
  • A Calling Talent: a unique ability.
  • Standing 1 in the Calling’s institution, guild or loose fellowship. Standing measures how much the Calling’s people trust you and what they will give you. It rises from 1 to 5; each Calling has its own ladder of titles.
  • Starting gear, in addition to what you buy.

The seventeen Callings below are found in every land, though they take local shapes. A Sallowreach Seamer sews the dead together; a Brinehollow Seamer opens drowned chests at high tide. The Carver may allow a Calling to take a faction’s form described in the land chapters (a Waker as a Nightwarden, a Netwatch lieutenant as a Nightwarden, a Thin faster as a Purger, a Dream-Diver as a Delver).

Seamer

Surgeons, embalmers, bone-setters, suture-witches and stitchers of the dead. In Sallowreach they are the Guild that holds the country together; elsewhere they are the only people who will open a body and look at what is growing in it.

  • Calling Skills: Stitching, Endure, Reckoning.
  • Talent — Tight Seams: when you treat a wound, the patient recovers +2 Flesh. Once per session you may perform a Reseat on a character at 0 Flesh: roll Hand + Stitching vs Grim (18); on a success they do not suffer a new Injury from this Ruin.
  • Gear: a roll of needles and awls, gut and wire thread, a bone saw, a jar of vinegar, a flask of something for the pain.
StandingTitleGrants
1ThreaderGuild lodging, cheap thread, permission to practise
2StitcherAccess to the guild’s corpse-stock for practice; 10% off services
3SeamerYour own clients; a Seamer’s mark that opens hospital doors
4Master SeamerApprentices (2); a seat at guild councils; surgeries in any city
5Guild ElderThe guild acts on your word; Thessaly Mort knows your name

Factor

Clerks, buyers, caravan-masters and agents of the Rim Road Company and the merchant houses. They price everything, including you.

  • Calling Skills: Haggle, Reckoning, Clause.
  • Talent — The Company Rate: you buy at 20% less and sell at 20% more than listed prices on the Rim Road. Once per session you may produce a document (a letter of credit, a toll waiver, a manifest) that gets you or a cargo past a single checkpoint without a roll.
  • Gear: a ledger, ink, a Company seal, a set of bone-coin scales, a lockbox, 20 extra lacks.
StandingTitleGrants
1Tally-ClerkLodging at Company waystations at half rate
2FactorA line of credit of 100 lacks; a mule
3Senior FactorYour own caravan contract; credit 500 lacks; 4 Wardens on hire
4Road-MasterAuthority over a stretch of the Rim and its tolls
5DirectorA voice in the Company’s Oathen-sworn councils

Warden

Road guards, sellswords, caravan muscle, bounty-collectors. The Rim Road Company employs ten thousand of them; the Admiralty and the Mortuary Court and the Board of Plenty employ more.

  • Calling Skills: Blades, Endure, Intimidate.
  • Talent — Shield the Cargo: when an adjacent ally is hit, you may take the blow instead (before damage is rolled). You gain +2 Armor against it.
  • Gear: a sword or axe, a crossbow and 12 bolts, boiled leather armor, a Company tabard or local equivalent.
StandingTitleGrants
1Hired BladeSteady pay (2 lacks a day on contract)
2Sworn WardenOathen-sworn contract; a mount
3SergeantCommand of 6 Wardens
4CaptainCommand of a waystation’s garrison
5Marshal of the RimCommand of a stretch of road and everything on it

Cutwright

Genealogists of the Cutwrights’ College. They trace every bloodline back to the portion its ancestors ate. Their ledgers decide marriages, inheritances and executions.

  • Calling Skills: Lore, Reckoning, Search.
  • Talent — Read the Line: by examining a person for a few minutes (eyes, hands, teeth, the smell of their sweat), you can roll Eye + Lore vs Hard (14) to learn their land, their Cut, and their approximate Regrowth stage. With a Helping you also learn one Gift or Want they have.
  • Gear: a portable ledger of the major lines, calipers, a magnifying glass, a sample case of dried blood.
StandingTitleGrants
1CopyistAccess to the College’s public ledgers
2SurveyorTravel papers; the right to demand an examination
3LecturerAccess to restricted ledgers; College lodging anywhere
4Reader of LinesYour rulings are accepted in courts of four lands
5ProvostYou know where every god is regrowing fastest

Clausewright

Lawyers, contract-drafters and oath-makers, trained in Oathen and hired everywhere. Abroad they draft treaties; at home they draft the sentences by which the condemned are made to break themselves.

  • Calling Skills: Clause, Persuade, Lore.
  • Talent — Exits: you speak in careful conditionals. Once per scene, when you would be bound by your own words (an oath in Oathen, a contract, a promise sworn on the dead), you may declare the clause you buried in it: roll Tongue + Clause vs Hard (14) to escape the binding without penalty.
  • Gear: a quill-knife, a writing case, sealing wax, a copy of the Book of Conditions, a soft leather bit (in case).
StandingTitleGrants
1ScrivenerBench lodging in Tacit
2DrafterYou may witness contracts for fees
3ClausewrightThe Bench recognises your drafting; foreign courts fear it
4Senior of the BenchTreaty work; diplomatic immunity in three lands
5Chief ClausewrightYou draft the sentence a Sayer speaks

Surety

People who carry other people’s oaths for a fee, taking the risk of the Breaking in their own bodies. In Oathen they are a profession; elsewhere, they are guarantors, hostages, co-signers, and the ones sent when somebody’s word has to be backed by flesh.

  • Calling Skills: Endure, Clause, Resolve.
  • Talent — Borne Weight: you may take on another character’s oath, debt or curse (with their consent and a ritual of a few minutes); the consequences of breaking it fall on you instead. You gain +3 Flesh permanently from the toughening that comes with the trade, and you ignore the first Injury each session.
  • Gear: a ledger of the oaths you carry (start with 1d6 small ones from paying clients, and 30 extra lacks), bandages, splints.
StandingTitleGrants
1BondsmanSmall contracts
2SuretyContracts worth hundreds
3Senior SuretyNoble clients; your scars are your credit
4PledgemasterThe Rim Road Company’s oaths
5Ledger-BearerTreaties between nations ride on your body

Nightwarden

The uncanny police of the Table: the Netwatch on the Brinehollow shore, the Wakers with their needles, the Echo-Wardens of the silent gorges, the Hostwatch trackers of the Fast, the Loft-Wardens of the Set-Aside. Their work is to watch for the god and drag people back from it.

  • Calling Skills: Instinct, Search, Intimidate.
  • Talent — Seen It Before: you gain +2 on Dread checks against horrors of your home land, and once per session, when someone near you fails a Dread check, you may grab, slap, needle or shout them back: they reduce the Fray gained by your Caul rating.
  • Gear: the local tools of the trade (boathook and net, needle and rattle, lantern and horn), a lantern, a whistle, a warrant.
StandingTitleGrants
1WatcherPay, a beat, a warrant to detain
2Warden of the NightAuthority to enter homes
3LieutenantCommand of a patrol of 8
4CaptainA district
5CommanderThe land’s whole watch answers to you

Renderer

Butchers, slaughterers, salters, cooks and shippers of meat. In the Fatlands the Renderers’ Union decides what leaves the country; on the Rim Road every inn needs a cook who does not ask questions.

  • Calling Skills: Blades, Feast, Labor.
  • Talent — Know the Cut: by taste, smell or a single cut, you can tell what a piece of meat used to be: species, age, and roughly how it died. On a Hard (14) Eye + Feast roll you can tell whether it was a person, and on a Helping, which one. You also gain +1 damage with cleavers and knives.
  • Gear: a set of cleavers and knives, a rendering hook, salt, a leather apron that will never be clean again.
StandingTitleGrants
1Spit-HandKitchen work anywhere
2CutterUnion card; access to slaughterhouses
3Master RendererYour own shop or kitchen
4Barrel-WardenYou stamp the export barrels
5Union BossEvery barrel on the Rim Road stops at your word

Midwife
