Trained by the Attendance of Cradlewrack or by the village wise-women of the other lands. They bring things into the world and decide whether they stay. Abroad, they are also the best surgeons of the belly on the Table.

  • Calling Skills: Stitching, Instinct, Rites.
  • Talent — The Two Questions: you can tell at a glance whether a living thing is what it appears to be (Caul + Instinct vs Routine 10 for the obvious, Hard 14 for a Tenanted, Grim 18 for a Seated). You also gain +2 on rolls to treat or deliver anything, of any kind, from any body.
  • Gear: an apron, birthing tools, a knife called the Second Opinion, cord-ties, a ledger of names.
StandingTitleGrants
1HandmaidLodging with any midwife’s house
2MidwifeYou attend births alone
3Senior MidwifeYour Second Opinion is law in your district
4Matron of the AttendanceCommand of a lying-in house
5Midwife-ParamountYou are the government

Crumb-Runner

Smugglers, carters and night-haulers, who move food and contraband across borders the law says are closed. Despised by the people they feed.

  • Calling Skills: Stealth, Wayfaring, Deceive.
  • Talent — Hidden Hold: any cart, pack or boat you load has a hidden compartment that will not be found except on a Grace. You know one safe route between any two adjacent lands, and on the Rim Road you travel a third faster than others.
  • Gear: a handcart or mule, oilcloth, rope, a dark lantern, a forged travel pass.
StandingTitleGrants
1RunnerContacts in two lands
2HaulerA safehouse; regular cargo
3Route-HolderA route of your own and three runners
4Night-FactorA network across three lands
5Boss of the Dark RoadThe Company pays you to leave its cargo alone

Taker

Bounty hunters, poachers and kidnappers: the people who catch Blanks for the surgeons, Called for the Netwatch, runaways for the Board, and Unfed for the trade. A loathsome calling, and a profitable one. Guests who take it are usually trying to stop.

  • Calling Skills: Wayfaring, Brawl, Search.
  • Talent — Taken Alive: you gain +2 on rolls to grapple, bind, track or subdue. Damage you deal can be declared non-lethal at no penalty. You can tell a Blank or an Unfed on sight.
  • Gear: manacles, a weighted net, a cosh, a cage-cart (or rights to one), sedative syrup.
StandingTitleGrants
1Hand-for-HireSmall bounties
2TakerNotice of bounties in two lands
3Licensed TakerA legal warrant in one land
4HuntmasterA crew of 5; noble clients
5PurveyorThe Second Table buys from you directly

Celebrant

Priests, rite-keepers, mourners and cult preachers: the Finishers of Sallowreach, the Bedded of the Vigil, the Deepening of Brinehollow, the Barren Order, the Quiet, the Starved Saints, and the hedge-priests of the Three Doctrines. Whatever they preach, they are the ones people come to when someone they love starts to change.

  • Calling Skills: Rites, Persuade, Resolve.
  • Talent — The Words Over the Body: once per scene you may lead a rite: everyone present who joins you removes 2 Fray. Once per session, you may preach to a crowd (Tongue + Rites vs Hard 14) to move it to an act of faith or fury.
  • Gear: vestments, a holy book of your doctrine, candles, incense or vinegar, a relic of doubtful origin.
StandingTitleGrants
1AcolyteShelter in your faith’s houses
2CelebrantYou may lead rites
3ElderA congregation of 30
4High CelebrantA temple, a district, a flock of hundreds
5ProphetThey will walk into the sea if you ask

Gleaner

Scavengers, salvagers, rag-pickers, grave-robbers and part-thieves: the salvage crews of the Uncovered, the gleaners behind the Fatlands harvesters, the diggers of the Sump. They know the worth of what others have left behind.

  • Calling Skills: Search, Filch, Craft.
  • Talent — Something Worth Having: once per session, in any place where people have lived or died, you find something useful: a tool, a coin purse, a key, a relic, a body part of value. Roll Eye + Search vs Hard (14); each Helping adds 10 lacks of value. You also halve the time it takes to search.
  • Gear: a pry-bar, a sack, a shovel, a lantern, gloves, a fence’s name.
StandingTitleGrants
1PickerYou know where the pickings are
2GleanerA fence who pays fair
3Salvage-BossA crew of 4; a claim
4Wreck-LordClaims across a district
5Master of LeavingsEvery fence on the Rim knows your mark

Delver

Explorers of god-places: the Dream-Divers of the Vigil, the Hushwalkers and surveyors of Sallowreach, the pilots of the Uncovered, the watchers at the Dilation, the trackers who follow the Host. They go where the god is closest and come back changed, if they come back.

  • Calling Skills: Athletics, Instinct, Godsign.
  • Talent — Gone Under: you may spend an hour preparing to enter a god-place (a Hush, the long room, the Trench, a crowning). While inside, you gain +2 to all rolls and reduce Fray gained by 1 (minimum 1). When you come out, gain 1 Hunger (or 1 Want, if Unfed).
  • Gear: a tether-line and harness, chalk, a compass that may not work, smelling salts, a death-mask or veil.
StandingTitleGrants
1NoviceA patron who pays per descent
2DelverMaps of the near reaches
3VeteranYour own expeditions
4PathfinderState commissions
5The One Who Came BackYour maps are the only maps

Purger

Members of the Purgation: the cross-border movement that believes the gods can be thrown back up. Purgers range from gentle fasters and bleeders to the cells that burn high-Cut houses with the families locked inside.

  • Calling Skills: Feast, Rites, Stealth.
  • Talent — Bring It Up: you know the emetics, bleedings and fasts. Once per day, you may spend an hour purging yourself or a willing (or held) subject: roll Gut + Feast vs Hard (14); success removes 1d6 Hunger, a Helping removes 1 more, a Grace lowers Regrowth by 1 (only once per stage). The subject suffers 3 damage and is Weakened (−2 to all rolls) for the rest of the day.
  • Gear: a Purgation kit (emetics, lancets, leeches, a basin), a hair shirt, a hidden pamphlet, a list of names.
StandingTitleGrants
1PenitentShelter in Purgation safehouses
2PurgerAccess to the cell’s resources
3Cell-ElderCommand of a cell of 6
4Voice of the PurgeA district’s cells
5The Clean HandYou decide which bloodlines burn

Reckoner

Zealots out of the Fast who carry the Refusal across the border on a blade, killing the highest Cuts of the Godeaters in their beds. Nearly all are Unfed; a few are converts from Scrapling families who hate their lords. Taking this Calling makes you a wanted murderer in six lands.

  • Calling Skills: Blades, Stealth, Resolve.
  • Talent — In Their Beds: you deal +4 damage against an unaware target, and +2 damage against any target of Cut 3 or higher. You can sense godsign on a person (Caul + Instinct vs Routine 10) and estimate its Cut.
  • Gear: a long knife, a garrotte, dark clothes, a ration bag, a list of names with some crossed out.
StandingTitleGrants
1Brother/Sister of the KnifeA cell’s protection
2ReckonerYour own targets
3Raid-LeaderCommand of a raid of 6
4Reckoner-CaptainAuthority to declare a bloodline ended
5The Hand of HallowboardThe Abstinent listen to you

Scion

The children of the Cuts who rule: the disinherited Heirs of Sallowreach, the Gut-line heirs being fattened for the Board, the lidless children of the Watch, the heirs of the Caul-lines in their membranes. A Scion has money, a name, a bloodline the god prefers, and a family that will not let them go. Requires Cut 3 or higher.

  • Calling Skills: Persuade, Lore, Godsign.
  • Talent — The Name: your family name opens doors. Once per session you may invoke it to gain an audience, a loan of up to 100 lacks, a bed, or the cooperation of a minor official, with no roll. The family will ask for something in return. Your Teeth add +1 each to the total when you Partake.
  • Gear: fine clothes, a signet, a horse or litter, a servant (Threat 1), a letter of introduction, 100 extra lacks.
StandingTitleGrants
1CadetAn allowance of 5 lacks a day
2HeirA household of your own
3Lord or LadyA seat in your land’s councils
4Head of a HouseThe house’s wealth and its feuds
5Great HouseA crown, a bench, a court, or a hill

Step Six: Skills

Distribute 18 points among the twenty-four skills. No skill may be raised above 3 with these points (Calling Skills may then go to 4). A skill at 0 can still be rolled; you simply add nothing for it.

RatingMeaning
0Untrained. You have seen it done.
1Novice. You can manage when it is easy.
2Trained. A journeyman’s competence.
3Expert. The best in a village.
4Master. The best in a city.
5Legendary. People travel to watch.
The Twenty-Four Skills
  • Hand — Blades (knives, swords, axes, cleavers, sickles), Brawl (fists, teeth, grappling, clubs), Shooting (bows, crossbows, slings, harpoons, thrown), Stitching (surgery, first aid, medicine, embalming, seaming the dead).
  • Gut — Endure (pain, poison, cold, exhaustion, disease), Labor (lifting, digging, hauling, breaking), Feast (eating the inedible, drink, drugs, tasting, cooking), Intimidate (threat by presence and size).
  • Lung — Athletics (running, climbing, swimming, dodging), Stealth (hiding, sneaking, shadowing), Wayfaring (travel, riding, driving, foraging, the Rim Road), Filch (pockets, locks, sleight of hand).
  • Eye — Search (finding, noticing, investigating), Lore (history, theology, the Cuts, the lands), Craft (making and mending things), Reckoning (numbers, ledgers, clocks, mechanisms, natural philosophy).
  • Tongue — Persuade (honest argument, charm, seduction, comfort), Deceive (lies, disguise, forgery), Haggle (prices, bribes, trade), Clause (law, contracts, the drafting of oaths).
  • Caul — Resolve (enduring horror, resisting compulsion), Rites (prayer, ritual, the doctrines, burial), Instinct (danger sense, reading people, the uncanny), Godsign (understanding and controlling the god in the blood).

Step Seven: Knacks

Choose two Knacks. Each is a narrow edge, a habit, or a scar that pays. More can be bought with Portions (see Advancement). Some have requirements.

KnackRequirementEffect
Bail-Lunged—Hold your breath for (Lung × 2) minutes; +2 to resist drowning and smoke.
Bone-Coin Nose—Tell counterfeit lacks, false seals and forged notes by smell (Routine 10).
Butcher’s Calm—Ignore Dread 1 from bodies and gore entirely.
Cold Supper—You need eat only every other day without penalty.
ConditionalTongue 3When lying, you may reroll one die, once per scene.
Corpse-Road Walker—+2 to travel and navigation rolls through fen, Uncovered or empty farmland.
Counting HabitEye 3Once per session, ask the Carver how many of something there are, and get the true number.
Dirty FighterBrawl 2Your unarmed attacks deal 2 and can blind for a round on a Helping.
Dowager’s PatienceCaul 3Once per session, take an action you were compelled not to take by a Want, without a roll.
Eats AnythingFeast 2You can eat spoiled, raw, or godtainted food: reduce any Taint from eating by 1.
Elder’s Ear—Old people, the Kept, and the Seated tell you things they tell no one else (+2 Persuade).
Fast HandsHand 3Draw and attack with a small weapon in the same moment; +2 to initiative.
Gallows Laugh—When you make the table laugh at something horrible in character, remove 1 Fray (once per session).
Good BonesGut 3+3 Flesh.
Hard Sleeper—You sleep without dreaming, wherever you are. (Useless in the Vigil.)
Hostage’s Smile—+2 to rolls to make captors like you or let their guard down.
Iron StomachGut 2+2 to Endure vs poison, disease, rot and drugs.
Kin-SenseCaul 2You always know when someone of your own blood is within a mile.
Light SleeperEye 2You cannot be surprised while asleep or resting.
Little Lies—One trivial falsehood per session is believed without a roll.
Mother’s HandsStitching 2Treat Injuries one step faster.
No Thank You—+2 to resist any offer, invitation, seduction, or temptation, mundane or divine.
Old Grief—Once per session, when you take Fray from the death or loss of someone, take 2 less. You have practice.
Pin-Cushion—Pain sharpens you: while below half Flesh, +1 to all Eye rolls.
Rope Knots—Your knots never come undone by themselves, even in Cradlewrack.
Second Chair—When an ally makes a roll you could help with, give them +2 (instead of the usual +1).
Scrap-Born LuckCut 1 onlyOnce per session, reroll a Lack.
Silent Supper—You can go a whole day without speaking and suffer no penalty; +2 Stealth in quiet places.
Smell of Cedar—You know how to look like you belong to a better Cut: +2 Deceive and Persuade among the rich.
Steady HandsHand 2No penalty for performing delicate work under pressure.
Strong BackLabor 2Carry double the normal load.
Table Manners—You know the grace and customs of all seven lands: +2 to first impressions anywhere.
UnflinchingResolve 3Once per session, automatically succeed on a Dread check of rating 3 or lower.
Vinegar Kiss—You carry the smells of rot well: animals and the Kept do not notice you unless you act.

Step Eight: Derived Traits

  • Flesh = 8 + Gut + Endure. Your physical endurance; see the combat chapter.
  • Guard = 10 + Lung + the best of Athletics, Blades or Brawl. The target number to hit you in melee. Ranged Guard = 10 + Lung + Athletics.
  • Armor from what you wear.
  • Hunger starts at 0.
  • Regrowth starts as set by your Cut. Note the Gifts you already have and any Wants that are active (High Cuts, starting in the Appetite, have their first Want active).
  • Fray starts at 0, unless the Carver rules otherwise. Some backgrounds (a Vigil-born, an Oathen Forsworn) may begin with Fray 2.
  • Want (Unfed only) starts at 3.
  • Portions (experience) start at 0.

Step Nine: The Four Questions

Mechanics describe what a Guest can do. These four answers describe who they are. Write them on the sheet. The Carver will use every one.

The Last Meal. What is the last meal you ate that you truly enjoyed, and who was at the table? Every Guest on the Table is hungry in some way, and this is the shape of theirs. Once per session, when your Guest acts to protect, honor or return to what that meal represented, gain +2 to the roll.

The Oath on the Dead. Swear an oath on the name of someone dead: a parent, a child, a friend, a victim. Write the name and the oath. (On my brother Wem, who was Reaped: I will find where they took him. On my mother, whom I finished: I will never touch another living thing with these hands.) See the rules for Oaths on the Dead. They bind across the Table, in ways that are subtler than Oathen’s but no gentler.

Who Waits at Home. Name one living person who loves you and is waiting for you to come back. Where are they? What would they think of what you are becoming? The Carver will put them in danger. That is a promise.

What You Will Not Do. Name one thing your Guest will not do, whatever happens. Eat a person. Kill kin. Lie under oath. Lie down. Sit at a laid table. When your Guest is pushed to do it, play it honestly; if they do it, they gain 5 Fray at once, and you must write a new line they will not cross.

Step Ten: Gear and Money

Take the starting gear from your Calling and the starting wealth from your Cut, and spend it in the Rim Market (Part Three). Everyone also begins with: a set of clothes suited to their land and station, a knife, a bowl, a spoon, a blanket, a water-skin, and three days of food they carried themselves.

Advancement: Portions

At the end of every session, each Guest earns Portions:

  • 1 for showing up and playing.
  • 1 for each of the following, if it happened: you learned a secret of the Table; you faced a horror of Dread 3 or higher; you acted on your Last Meal, Oath on the Dead or Who Waits at Home in a way that cost you; you made the table gasp, wince or laugh.
  • 1–3 for completing a goal or surviving a story’s end.

A typical session earns 4–7 Portions. Spend them between sessions:

ImprovementCost in Portions
Raise a skill by 1New rating × 2
Raise an attribute by 1 (max 5)New rating × 5
Gain a Knack6
Raise Standing by 1New rating × 3, plus a deed the Calling recognises
Remove 3 Fray2 (represents rest, rites, drink, company)
Treat a Derangement (see Fray)10, plus months of care

Cut cannot be bought. It is what you were born with. Regrowth cannot be bought, either: it comes on its own.

Example of Character Creation

Maya wants to play a Brinehollow Netwatch officer who has begun to doubt the job. She chooses Brinehollow (+1 Lung) and Common Cut (Cut 2, Regrowth 1, one Tooth, 40 lacks). She puts her 9 attribute points into Hand 3, Gut 2, Lung 3, Eye 2, Tongue 1, Caul 3, then adds the land bonus: Lung 4.

She chooses the Nightwarden Calling (Instinct, Search and Intimidate +1). With 18 skill points she buys Blades 2, Brawl 2, Athletics 3, Wayfaring 1, Instinct 2 (3 with Calling), Search 2 (3), Intimidate 1 (2), Endure 2, Resolve 3. She names her Guest Ressa Weir.

Her Knacks are Bail-Lunged and Old Grief. Flesh = 8 + 2 + 2 = 12. Guard = 10 + 4 + 3 = 17. At Regrowth 1 she has the Brinehollow Taste: salt on her lips at waking. Her Last Meal: smoked herring with her brother on the pier, the night before he was Called. Her Oath on the Dead: On my brother Ferrin, who walked in: I will never again drag anyone back from the water. Who Waits at Home: her sister-in-law, Ama, who keeps Ferrin’s chain on the bedpost. What she will not do: put a rope on a living person again.

That oath and that line are going to collide with her job by the second session. That is the point.

Chapter 12

The Grace Roll

On the Table, nobody asks if a thing can be done. They ask what it will cost, and who will be made to pay it.
— Rim Road saying

The rules of The Long Grace are short at their heart. One kind of roll settles nearly everything. Around it are wrapped the systems that make this world itself: what it costs to call on the god in your blood, how the god grows back, how the mind wears through, and how the dead hold you to your word.

When to Roll

Roll only when three things are true: the outcome is uncertain, failure would be interesting, and something is at stake. A Seamer stitching a cut in a quiet shop does not roll. A Seamer stitching a cut while the patient screams and the Kept in the next room are pounding on the wall to be let in, does.

When nothing is at stake, the Carver simply says what happens. When the outcome is impossible, nobody rolls: you cannot argue a Hush into giving back its silence.

The Roll

To attempt something uncertain, a Guest rolls 2d10 and adds one Attribute and one Skill. The Carver says which pair fits; players may suggest another and argue for it. The total is compared to a Difficulty.

Total = 2d10 + Attribute + Skill (+ modifiers) (+ Teeth, if Partaking)

DifficultyNumberExample
Routine10Climb a knotted rope; find an inn on the Rim Road; calm a frightened child.
Hard14Climb a wet pier-piling at night; pick a Seamer’s lock; lie to a Waker.
Grim18Stitch a severed hand back on in a moving cart; out-argue a Clausewright.
Dire22Climb a cliff of the Hanging Abbey in a gale; lie to a Tenanted judge.
Impossible26Talk a Sayer out of a sentence; outrun the Black Noon.

If the total equals or beats the Difficulty, the attempt succeeds. Otherwise it fails. A failed roll does not have to mean nothing happens: it may mean you succeed at a cost, too late, or with a complication, at the Carver’s judgment. Failure on the Table should always move the story somewhere worse, never to a dead stop.

Helpings

For every full 4 points by which a total exceeds the Difficulty, the roll earns one Helping. A Helping is an extra: more information, more speed, a better price, a quieter entry, a cleaner cut. In combat, each Helping adds +2 damage. A player can usually spend Helpings as they like, within reason; the Carver may offer a menu.

Example: Ressa (Eye 2, Search 3) searches a drowned house for the ledger of the Called. Difficulty Hard 14. She rolls 7 and 9: total 21. That beats 14 by 7, one Helping. She finds the ledger, and with her Helping she also notices that the last entry is written in her brother’s hand.

Grace and Lack

When the two d10 show the same number, the roll is an omen.

  • If the roll succeeds, it is a Grace. Something goes better than it had any right to: the strongest effect the situation allows, a Helping on top of whatever was earned, an enemy disarmed, a door that was going to be locked found open, a second piece of information. In combat, a Grace attack also inflicts a Mangling (see Combat).
  • If the roll fails, it is a Lack. The worst plausible complication happens: the weapon breaks, the lie is not only seen through but believed to be something worse, the patient’s wound opens further, the god notices.
  • Double 1s (“Licked Clean”) always fail, whatever the total, and always with a Lack.
  • Double 10s (“Second Helping”) always succeed, whatever the Difficulty (short of the impossible), and always with a Grace.
Lacks Worth Having

A Lack should never be the Carver punishing the player. It should be the world being itself. Good Lacks on the Table: your Tooth bites (gain 2 Hunger); somebody you love hears what you just said; the thing you did leaves a mark that a Cutwright will be able to read; the noise wakes something in the cellar; your knife slips, and now there’s blood on the bread; the rope you tied comes undone, in Cradlewrack, as everything does; you say “I promise” without meaning to, in Oathen.

Modifiers

Circumstances add or subtract from the total, usually by 2 (sometimes by 4 for something overwhelming). Good tools, time, and help add; darkness, injury, fear, cold and Wants subtract. Do not stack more than three modifiers. If the situation is that lopsided, change the Difficulty instead.

  • Help: another character who could plausibly assist gives +1 (or +2 with the Second Chair Knack). Only one helper counts, unless the task is physical and large (lifting a cart, pulling a Called man out of the surf).
  • Tools: the right tool is assumed; a fine one gives +1 or +2; no tool at all may make a task impossible or Grim.
  • Time: taking ten times as long gives +2. Rushing gives −2.
  • Injury, exhaustion, hunger: −2 per condition, as specified in their rules.

Opposed Rolls

When two characters act against each other (a lie against a suspicion, a chase, an arm-wrestle, a haggle), both roll. The higher total wins; on a tie, the defender (or whoever is keeping the situation as it is) wins. Helpings in an opposed roll are counted by how much the winner beat the loser by.

Long Tasks

For efforts that take hours or days (restitching a grandmother, deciphering a seating plan, crossing the Uncovered), the Carver sets a number of Helpings needed, typically 3 to 8, and a time per roll. The Guests roll until they reach the total or run out of time, and a Lack along the way costs something real.

Threat

Minor non-player characters do not need full statistics. They have a Threat rating from 0 to 5 that they add to all their rolls instead of Attribute + Skill (attack rolls are listed separately). A Rim Road innkeeper is Threat 1. A Netwatch lieutenant is Threat 3. Lady Corrow Vane is not a Threat-rated character.

Partaking: The Tooth

Anyone with a Cut of 1 or higher carries a god. Before any roll, a Guest may Partake: call on the god in their blood to lend them its strength, its senses, its terrible certainty. When you Partake:

  • Roll one Tooth (a d6, in a different color from your d10s) and add it to the total. A character of Cut 3 or higher may roll two Teeth if they wish. Teeth are rolled with the 2d10. They do not count for doubles.
  • Gain 1 Hunger for Partaking.
  • Gain 1 additional Hunger for every Tooth that shows a 1. The god bit back.
  • Describe how the god shows itself. Each land’s chapter describes its Tooth: a Sallowreach Guest’s hands go cold and their fingers seem one joint too long; a Fatlander’s mouth floods with saliva; a Brinehollower’s ears pop and their voice drops an octave; a Vigil-born’s eyes stop blinking; a Cradlewracker feels something turn over inside them; an Oathener hears their own heartbeat repeating their last words.

Partaking is powerful. A Tooth adds 3.5 on average, the difference between a Hard roll and a Grim one. It is also how the end comes. Every Guest who Partakes is choosing, roll by roll, to bring their god closer to the surface.

The Unfed and Blanks cannot Partake. The Unfed have Want instead.

Hunger

Hunger is a track from 0 to 10. It represents how awake and active the god in your blood is right now: the rise of appetite, compulsion, and wrongness in the body. Hunger rises when you:

  • Partake (+1, and +1 per Tooth showing 1).
  • Suffer a Lack while Partaking (+2).
  • Eat godtainted food or handle relics with Taint (see the Rim Market).
  • Spend time in a place where your god is strong, such as a Hush, the Trench or the Dilation (+1 per hour or more).
  • Give in to a Want (+1).
  • Refuse your Sop for too long (see below; +1 per day after the third).

When Hunger reaches 10, the god takes a step forward. Regrowth rises by 1 and Hunger empties to 0. Describe the change. Something in the body is different now, and it does not change back.

The Sop

Each land’s god can be quieted, for a while, by giving it a little of what it wants. This is the Sop: closing something in Sallowreach, eating in the Fatlands, bailing or submerging in Brinehollow, the dangerous blink in the Vigil, opening a door in Cradlewrack, keeping or making a vow in Oathen. Each land’s chapter defines its Sop precisely.

Performing the Sop takes a few minutes to an hour. It removes 1d6 Hunger. But the Sop is the god’s own habit. Each time a Guest Sops in a single day after the first, they must make a Caul + Resolve roll (Routine 10, Hard 14 for the third time, and so on), or the next Sop becomes a Want they cannot easily stop.

A Guest who goes three days without Sopping begins to gain 1 Hunger per day as the god grows restless.

Regrowth

Regrowth is a track from 0 to 12. It measures how far the god has come back in you. It rarely falls. The four stages, and the Brink before the last, are common to every land, though each land’s chapter describes what they look and feel like there:

RegrowthStageWhat Happens
0—The god is asleep. Blanks and the Unfed are here forever.
1–3The TasteSmall wrongnesses. Dreams, cravings, a tell in the body. Gain the land’s Taste Gift.
4–6The AppetiteCompulsions. The body wants what the god wants. Gain the Appetite Gift and the first Want.
7–9The CourseFlesh changes. You are visibly becoming something else. Gain the Course Gift and the second Want. Dread 1 to those who see you unclothed.
10–11The BrinkThe god is nearly here. Gain the Brink Gift. All Wants are Hard (14) to resist. Dread 2 to those who see your changes.
12The SeatingThe god is, in some real portion, present again, wearing you or making a place of you. The character is lost.

Gifts are the god’s power leaking through. They are real, useful and terrible, and they are listed in each land’s chapter. A Guest has every Gift from every stage they have reached.

Wants are compulsions. Each Want has a trigger (an open door, a closed eye, food left on a plate). When a Want is triggered, the Guest must either act on it or roll Caul + Resolve against Routine (10) in the Appetite, Hard (14) in the Course and Brink. Acting on a Want removes nothing and adds 1 Hunger. Resisting it successfully costs nothing; failing means acting on it anyway, or suffering 2 Fray if the player and Carver agree the Guest stood firm by sheer horror.

Can Regrowth Be Reversed?

Almost never. A Purger’s Grace can roll it back by one, once per stage. The relics of some lands can delay it. Orrum’s tables can stop it entirely, in the way that death stops a fever. There are rumours of a dozen cures on the Rim Road, and every land is certain that one of them works. None of them do. The Carver may allow a single, terrible, story-driven exception in a campaign. It should cost more than the character wants to pay.

The Seating of a Guest

At Regrowth 12, a Guest is Seated. Their god is, for a moment and in some portion, back in the world. What happens depends on the land: a Sallowreach Guest becomes a Hush; a Fatlander becomes a warm hill with, perhaps, a mouth; a Brinehollower’s Tenant takes the whole house; a Vigil-born lies down and becomes a sleeper who moves; a Cradlewracker bears what they were always going to bear, or becomes the door; an Oathener becomes a Sayer, whose every word is so.

The player and the Carver play out the Seating together as a final scene. It should be awful and it should be beautiful. Afterward the character is an NPC, a place, or a power, and the player makes a new Guest. A Seated Guest’s former companions should meet them again.

Fray and Dread

The Table breaks minds as surely as bodies. Fray is a track from 0 to 10 measuring how far a Guest’s composure has worn through.

Dread Checks

When a Guest encounters horror, the Carver calls for a Dread check: roll Caul + Resolve against a Difficulty set by the horror’s Dread rating:

DreadDifficultyExamples
1Routine (10)A rotting body. A Kept man restitched at the dinner table. Toothed wheat. Being Called by a stranger’s voice.
2Hard (14)Watching a murder. A Kept woman coming apart in your hands. The Reaping taking someone you have just met. A Tenanted stranger looking at you.
3Grim (18)A loved one Called, Tenanted, Reaped or Breaking. A ritual killing. Eating a person, knowingly. A face you know on a place card.
4Dire (22)A person becoming a place. A Hush swallowing a village. The god in your blood speaking. Kin-slaying by your own hand.
5Impossible (26)A Seating. A god’s face. The Host turning to look at you. Knowing that what you did changed nothing.
  • Success: gain 1 Fray (or none, on a Grace). You hold.
  • Failure: gain Fray equal to the Dread rating. On a Lack, add 2 more, and the Guest freezes, flees, screams, vomits or laughs, at the Carver’s choice, for a moment that matters.

A Guest only checks once against the same source in a scene, and the Carver may rule that a horror seen too often stops counting (a Seamer does not check for corpses). Guests may Partake on Dread checks. The god does not mind if you are frightened, and sometimes it is the god that makes you brave.

Fray Effects

  • Fray 0–4: steady.
  • Fray 5–7: Rattled. −1 to all Eye and Caul rolls. Sleep is thin, appetite strange, and you jump at doors.
  • Fray 8–9: Fraying. −2 to all rolls except to flee, hide or fight. You see things at the edge of the lamp. You are short with the people you love.
  • Fray 10: Break.

Breaking

When Fray reaches 10, the Guest Breaks. For the rest of the scene they are not in control of what they do: the player describes the Break with the Carver (running into the night, attacking the nearest person, curling under a table, laughing until they choke, saying every secret they have). Afterward, the Guest gains a Derangement and Fray drops to 3.

Roll on the table below or choose one that fits what broke them. Derangements are permanent unless treated. Each has a trigger and an effect; when triggered, roll Caul + Resolve (Hard 14) to master it for the scene.

d20DerangementEffect when triggered
1The Dead ManYou believe you are already dead: your flesh is rotting, your heart has stopped, you smell it. You feel no fear of harm and take no care of your body (−2 to Endure, +2 to Dread checks against death). Triggered by any reminder of your own mortality.
2The ImpostorsSomeone you love has been replaced by something wearing their face, their voice, their memories. You cannot be convinced otherwise. Choose the person. You cannot cooperate with them, and may act against them. Triggered by their kindness.
3Not My HandA part of your body is not yours: it belongs to someone else, or to the god. You will not use it willingly (−2 to rolls that need it) and sometimes it moves on its own. Triggered by exhaustion or Hunger 6+.
4Lost TimeYou lose minutes or hours. You come back somewhere else, with dirt under your nails and blood on your sleeve, and no memory. The Carver may narrate what you did. Triggered by Fray 5+ or by the Sop.
5The WatchersEveryone is watching you, reporting on you, planning against you. −2 to Persuade; +2 to Search for real threats. Triggered by being alone with strangers.
6The CountYou must count things: steps, teeth, the dead, the living. You cannot stop until you finish, and the number is always one short. Triggered by stress.
7The Voice at TableYou hear a voice that speaks in the tone of your god. It is reasonable. It gives advice. Some of it is good. Triggered whenever you Partake.
8The Hollow PlateFood tastes of ash, of rot, of people. You cannot eat without a Hard (14) Gut + Feast roll; you begin to starve in full larders. Triggered at every meal.
9The EchoYou repeat the last words spoken to you, under your breath, again and again. In Oathen this is lethal. Triggered by shouting or by oaths.
10The SeeingHallucinations: the Seeming without a city to share it. You see figures laying tables, the dead walking, your own body changing. −2 to Search. Triggered by darkness or exhaustion.
11Shut DoorsOpen things are unbearable: doors, eyes, mouths, wounds, books. You must close them. Triggered by any open door or eye. (In Cradlewrack this is a death sentence.)
12Kept GriefYou cannot let go of a dead person. You speak to them, set their place, keep their belongings, and, in Sallowreach, may keep them. Triggered by any reminder.
13The DevotionYou attach to a person, cause or god with absolute loyalty and will do anything they say. Choose the object. Triggered by their presence or their absence.
14Blood-HungerYou crave the taste of blood, of meat, of a particular kind of meat. Triggered by the smell of cooking or of wounds.
15The SplittingYou stand outside yourself and watch your body act. Calm, distant, unreal. +2 to Dread checks; −2 to Persuade and to anything requiring care. Triggered by violence.
16The UncleanYou are contaminated: by godsign, by others’ touch, by rot. You wash compulsively until you bleed. Triggered by touching another person or a body.
17The GaslightYou no longer trust your own memory. Others can convince you of anything you saw or did not see (−4 to resist being deceived about the past). Triggered by being contradicted.
18The RageSmall slights become murderous. Triggered by being mocked, cheated, or refused food. Roll or attack.
19The Guilt That Bends the RoomYour guilt is so heavy it warps what you see: the person you failed is everywhere, in faces and crowds and reflections. When triggered you gain 1 Fray. Triggered by success.
20The PullYou feel the god’s invitation in its fullest form: the sea, the Hush, the bed, the chair. You want to go. When triggered you must roll or move toward it. See Despair, below. Triggered by Fray 8+ or by being near the place.

Contagion

Madness on the Table is catching. It always has been: the Seeming of the Vigil is only the most organized form of it. When a Guest or NPC Breaks in the presence of others, every witness makes a Dread 2 check. Anyone who fails and is at Fray 5 or more also takes the same Derangement, in a shared form: they see what the Broken one saw, believe what they believe, count the same count. The Carver should make this feel like a cold draft moving through a room.

As the gods regrow, contagion grows stronger. In a place where a Seating has occurred, or near a Brink-stage noble, witnesses check at Dread 3.

Despair

Of all the Derangements, The Pull is the most dangerous, and the Table is full of people who have answered it: the Finishers singing their way into the Hushes, the Called walking into the surf, the sleepless of the Vigil lying down on purpose, the starving of the Fatlands crossing into the Fast to find a table where they can finally feel full.

When a Guest with the Pull is triggered and fails to master it, they move toward the god’s place and invitation. They can be stopped by their companions (a roll, a grip, a rope, a word, a reason). If they reach it and nothing stops them, the player and the Carver decide together what happens, out loud, with the table’s consent. This book never describes such an ending as a method or a release. It describes it as what it is on the Table: a loss that lands on everyone who loved them, and a little more of the god in the world. A Guest’s companions who witness it gain Fray as a Dread 4 horror, and the Carver should give the grief room.

Recovering from Fray

  • A night of real rest, safe, warm and fed (and awake, in the Vigil): remove 1 Fray.
  • A rite led by a Celebrant or performed sincerely: remove 2 Fray.
  • A vice: drink, rouse, poppy, brine tonic, gambling, sex (off-page), violence. Remove 1d6 Fray, but roll Gut + Endure (Hard 14) or develop a habit. Habits work like Wants.
  • Time with Who Waits at Home: remove all Fray, once per story, if they are still themselves.
  • Portions: 2 Portions removes 3 Fray between sessions.

Derangements can be treated with months of care, a Celebrant or Seamer who understands the mind, and 10 Portions. Some never go. Some of them, on the Table, are not wrong.

Oaths on the Dead

Every Guest begins with an Oath on the Dead, and any character may swear another. To swear on the dead, you speak the full name of a dead person, ideally where they lie, and promise something in their name.

  • The Strength of the Dead: once per scene, when you act directly to keep the oath, add +2 to a roll.
  • Keeping: when you fulfil an oath on the dead, remove all Fray and gain 2 Portions.
  • Breaking: if you deliberately break the oath, the dead come to collect. Gain 3 Fray immediately and suffer a Visitation, chosen by the Carver and shaped by the land where you swore: in Sallowreach the dead person, Kept, finds you; in the Fatlands you taste them in every meal; in Brinehollow their voice calls you from the water; in the Vigil they wait for you in every blink; in Cradlewrack you bear something with their face; in Oathen your body breaks to match the promise; in the Fast a place card bearing their name appears at every table you pass.

Swearing on the dead is not a light thing anywhere, and the Table is full of people who swore too easily. Grave-oaths sworn on the desecrated dead, over a body that has been opened or eaten or robbed, are said to bind twice as hard.

Health, Hunger, and the Body

Ordinary Hunger and Starvation

Every person needs about one day’s bread a day: one lack’s worth. Each day a character goes without food, they gain one level of Starving: −1 to all rolls per level, cumulative. At Starving 3, they cannot recover Flesh. At Starving 5, they lose 1 Flesh per day. A day of decent food removes one level. In the Fatlands, ordinary food never satisfies (see that chapter); in the Fast, nothing grows, and the Starving rules are the weather.

Cold, Exhaustion and Sleeplessness

Each night without shelter in Lack, or without sleep, imposes −1 to all rolls (cumulative, up to −4) until the character rests. The Vigil has its own rules for sleeplessness, which are worse.

Disease and Rot

Wounds left unstitched for a day may fester: roll Gut + Endure (Hard 14) or lose 1 Flesh per day and suffer −2 to all rolls until treated. In Sallowreach, festering never kills, and never stops.

Healing

  • First aid (Hand + Stitching, Routine 10, a few minutes, once per wound) restores 2 Flesh, +1 per Helping.
  • Rest: a full day of rest restores Gut in Flesh; a full day under a Seamer’s care restores double.
  • Injuries from the Mangling table heal according to their own entries, and some never heal.

Travel

The Rim Road is about 2,200 miles around. On foot a traveler makes about 20 miles a day on the road; by cart 25; by fast horse 40; by Company post-coach, changing horses at every waystation, 70. Waystations stand roughly every 15 to 25 miles, and a day’s walk off the road in any land is somewhere stranger.

Each day of travel through dangerous country, the Carver may roll on the land’s encounter table (see the bestiary), and one Guest may roll Lung + Wayfaring (Hard 14) to find a better route, avoid trouble, or make up time. Crossing into the Fast is a different matter entirely, and the rules for that are in its chapter.

Light and Darkness

The Table is lit by tallow, oil, rushlight and the candles of the dead. Darkness imposes −2 to Search and to attacks; total darkness, −4. In the Vigil there is no darkness, by law, and that is a horror of its own.

Chapter 13

Blood on the Cloth

There is no clean way to open a person. There are only quick ways and slow ways, and the slow ways are cheaper.
— Jem Crackle, the Cook’s Knife, to an apprentice

The Warden came at Halloway with a boathook, the long kind the Netwatch use for pulling the Called out of the surf, and she knew from the way he held it that he had pulled more people out of things than he had ever put into them. That was his mistake. He wanted to hook her, drag her, take her alive. She only wanted him to stop.

She let the hook go past her ear. It caught her coat at the shoulder and tore it, and she stepped inside the length of the pole, where it was no use to anyone, and put the cleaver into the meat where his neck met his collarbone. It went in with the sound a joint makes on the block: that wet, final chock of iron finding the gap in the bone. She felt it through the handle into her wrist. His breath came out of him in a long, surprised whistle, and something warm and copper-smelling ran over her knuckles and into her sleeve.

He sat down. He kept looking at her. He was trying to say something about his wife. She worked the blade free, the way you do, a little rock and a twist, and that was worse, because then the blood had somewhere to go.

She had butchered four thousand animals in her life. Her hands knew this. That was the part she would not be able to forget: how well her hands knew it.

Violence on the Table is fast, ugly and expensive. Fights are short. People who are hurt stay hurt. Guests who solve every problem with a blade will be dead, maimed, or something worse inside a few sessions, and they will deserve the stories told about them.

The Round

Combat is played in rounds of about three seconds. Each round, every combatant gets:

  • One action: an attack, a dash, a grapple, a first-aid attempt, a shouted plea, a Sop, a Partake-and-act, anything that takes real effort.
  • One move: a few steps, drawing a weapon, standing up, opening a door (in Cradlewrack it may already be open).

A character can give up their action for a second move. Talking a little is free.

Initiative

At the start of a fight, everyone rolls 1d10 + Lung + Eye. Act from highest to lowest. Ties go to the Guests. Those taken by surprise do not act in the first round. Initiative is rolled once for the whole fight, unless something dramatic resets it (a Hush opening, a pang, the lights going out in the Vigil).

Attacking

To attack, roll 2d10 + Hand + Blades (for edged weapons), Brawl (for fists, clubs, teeth, grapples) or Shooting (for anything thrown or loosed), against the target’s Guard.

  • Melee Guard = 10 + Lung + the best of Athletics, Blades or Brawl.
  • Ranged Guard = 10 + Lung + Athletics. Add +2 for partial cover, +4 for heavy cover. Firing into melee without hitting friends needs a Helping, or a friend is hit on a Lack.

If the attack total meets or beats the Guard, it hits.

Damage

Damage = weapon damage + 2 per Helping − the target’s Armor.

A hit that is reduced to 0 or less by Armor does no Flesh damage, but on a Grace it still inflicts a Mangling. Damage is subtracted from Flesh.

WeaponDamage
Fist, kick, bite1
Knife, awl, needle, sling2
Cleaver, hatchet, club, sickle, shortbow3
Sword, axe, spear, boathook, harpoon, crossbow4
Poleaxe, maul, greatcleaver, Tablebreaker’s axe5
Siege weapons, falling masonry, a Laden’s weight6+

Weapon qualities (Hooking, Ripping, Heavy, Reach, Silent, Brutal, and so on) are listed in the Rim Market.

Grace and Lack in Combat

  • A Grace on an attack inflicts a Mangling in addition to its damage (roll on the table below). Grace attacks are where people lose eyes and fingers.
  • A Lack on an attack means the weapon sticks, breaks, flies from your hand, or hits someone you did not mean to hit; or you overextend and the target gets a free attack against you.
  • A Lack on a defense (when you are rolling to resist a grapple, or the Carver calls for a roll to dodge something unusual) means you fall, drop something, or take a Mangling yourself.

Other Actions

  • Grapple: Hand + Brawl vs Guard. On a hit, the target is held: they can only try to break free (opposed Gut + Labor or Lung + Athletics) or attack with a small weapon at −2. A holder can choke (1 damage per round, ignoring Armor), drag, pin or bite.
  • Disarm: attack at −2; on a hit, no damage, the target drops their weapon.
  • Shove or trip: Gut + Labor or Hand + Brawl vs Guard; the target falls or is pushed back. Standing up takes a move.
  • Aim: spend an action aiming to gain +2 on your next ranged attack.
  • Full Defense: spend your action defending: +4 Guard until your next turn.
  • Flee: move away. Anyone engaged with you gets a free attack unless you win an opposed Lung + Athletics roll.
  • Partake: you can Partake on any combat roll. Many Gifts are combat abilities.

Fear in the Fight

A fight against horrors calls for a Dread check when the horror is first seen, not once per round. Seeing an ally Mangled is Dread 2. Killing someone for the first time is Dread 2 (Dread 3 for someone you knew, Dread 4 for kin).

Flesh, Ruin and Death

Flesh = 8 + Gut + Endure. A Guest at half Flesh or less is Bloodied: −1 to all rolls.

When Flesh reaches 0, the character suffers Ruin: they take an Injury (roll on the Mangling table) and collapse. They can crawl, whisper, and do nothing else useful. They are Dying.

A Dying character who takes any further damage is dead. A Dying character who is not treated within (Gut) minutes must roll Gut + Endure (Hard 14) every minute; failure means death. A successful first-aid roll stabilizes them at 1 Flesh.

In Sallowreach, nothing dies. A character who would die there becomes Kept: see that chapter. They keep their Injuries. They keep everything.

Damage on the Table, by the Numbers

An ordinary Guest has 10 to 14 Flesh. A knife does 2 to 6, a sword 4 to 8, a crossbow bolt at close range 4 to 10. Two or three solid blows will drop anyone. A Grace can end a fight at once. Armor matters enormously: boiled leather turns a knife into a bruise. The cheapest way to survive a fight is not to be in it. Carvers should let NPCs surrender, flee, bargain and beg, and they should do so often. On the Table, everybody is somebody’s kin.

The Mangling Table

Roll 1d20 when a Grace attack lands, or when a character suffers Ruin. Add +2 if the weapon is Brutal or the damage dealt was 8 or more. Every Mangling is also a Dread 2 horror for those who see it happen to someone they care about.

d20ManglingEffect
1–2Laid OpenA long shallow cut that unzips the skin and shows the yellow fat beneath. Bleeds freely: 1 damage per round until bound. Scar.
3KnucklesFingers broken or split to the bone. −2 to Hand rolls until healed (2 weeks). On a Lack later, one finger is lost.
4TeethA blow to the mouth: teeth spat out in pieces with the blood, lips torn. −2 to Tongue rolls for a week; permanent gaps.
5Rib-CrackYou hear it before you feel it: a green-stick crack, then the grinding. −2 to Lung rolls; every deep breath is a knife (4 weeks).
6HamstrungThe tendon behind the knee parts like a bowstring. Movement halved; cannot run. Without a Seamer’s Grim (18) repair, limp forever (−1 Lung).
7The EarTorn half off, hanging by a flap of gristle. −2 to hearing-based Search. Stitched back crooked, or lost.
8Gut-StuckA wound in the belly that lets out the smell of the bowel. Fever in 1d3 days unless treated (Grim 18 Stitching); −2 to all rolls while it festers.
9EyeThe eye is punctured, crushed, or hangs on its cord. Lost. −2 to Search and Shooting thereafter (−1 after a month of adjustment). Dread 2 to see.
10SkullThe scalp splits and the bone beneath dents like an egg. Stunned for 1d6 rounds; roll Gut + Endure (Hard 14) or lose memory of the last day.
11Broken ArmThe forearm bends between the wrist and elbow, where there is no joint. Unusable for 6 weeks; splint and pray.
12Broken LegThe shin snaps, perhaps through the skin, white and wet. Cannot stand. 8 weeks; a Lack in healing means a permanent limp.
13Severed FingersOne to three fingers gone, rolled away in the dirt. Permanent −1 Hand for fine tasks. Someone may pick them up.
14OpenedA deep wound across the abdomen. Loops of grey-pink bowel slide free and steam. Dying in (Gut) minutes unless held in and stitched (Grim 18). Survivors are weakened (−1 Gut) for a season.
15Severed HandOff at the wrist; the stump sprays in rhythm with the heart. Lose 2 Flesh per round until tied off. The hand twitches for a while afterward. In Sallowreach, much longer.
16JawThe jaw is broken, dislocated or torn half away: the tongue lolls in a ruin of teeth. Cannot speak clearly; can only take liquid. 6 weeks. (In Oathen, many count this as mercy.)
17ThroatA cut or crush to the throat. Blood in the windpipe; breathing is a gargle. Dying in (Gut) rounds unless treated (Dire 22). Survivors speak in a rasp forever.
18UnmannedA savage wound to the hip, groin or pelvis; the bone grates, the blood pools black. Cannot walk for 2 months; Gut −1 permanently. Dread 2.
19Severed LimbAn arm off at the elbow, a leg off at the knee: hacked through, the bone ends splintered and pale. Lose 3 Flesh per round until tied off. Ruin follows. A Seamer may reattach a limb from another body; it will not be quite yours.
20+ButcheredThe blow opens the body like a carcass on the hook: the chest split, the skull cloven, the head half off. The character dies at once, outside Sallowreach. Inside it, they continue, in that condition, indefinitely. Dread 3 to all who see.

Special Situations

Fighting the Kept

The Kept of Sallowreach cannot be killed. Reducing one to 0 Flesh drops it, and it goes on moving: crawling, biting, grasping with whatever is still attached. To stop a Kept enemy you must dismember it: each Mangling result of Severed Hand, Severed Limb or Butchered removes the use of that part. Burning helps; it does not finish. Hand-line touch and the Hushes are the only true ends.

Fighting Many

Mobs, the Forsworn of the Breakdowns, a Reaping crowd, the Finishers walking in: treat a mob as one character with Flesh equal to 5 × its number, Threat equal to 1 + one per 5 members (max 5), and damage equal to its best weapon + 1 per 5 members. Each 5 Flesh lost drops one member. Mobs break and run when they lose half their number, unless they are faithful, starving or Called.

Fighting Gods

You cannot. A Seated god has no Flesh to take. The rules for what you can do instead are in Things That Eat and Are Eaten.

Executions, Torture and Murder

Not every killing is a fight. When a Guest kills a helpless person, no roll is needed for the act. The roll is afterward: a Dread check at Dread 2 (Dread 3 for someone who begged; Dread 4 for kin). Torture extracts information on an opposed roll of the torturer’s Tongue + Intimidate against the victim’s Caul + Resolve, but the Carver decides how true the answers are, and the torturer makes a Dread 2 check each session they continue. Jack Tenterhook of the Vigil says the difference between his work as a wake-valet and his old job is the tipping. He is lying, and it shows on him.

Part Three
The Market and the Things That Eat
Coin, goods, relics of godflesh, and the horrors that walk the lands.
Chapter 14

The Rim Market

Everything on the Table has a price. The trick is finding out who is paying it.
— painted over the door of the Company counting-house at Toll Nine

The stall stood where the Rim Road bends at Gristmoot, between a man selling anchoring-rope by the fathom and a Seamer’s boy crying “Thread, wire, lacquer, fingers!” in a voice that had broken years ago and been stitched back wrong. It was a Fatlands stall. You could tell by the width of the counter, which was built to bear a forearm the size of a bolster, and by the smell, which was gravy, clove, and something under the clove that the clove was there for.

The stall-wife was called Mardy Haunch and she was, by the custom of her country, beautiful: she spilled over her stool on both sides like risen dough over a tin. She was eating while she sold. She was always eating while she sold. She had a sausage in one hand and a knife in the other, and the sausage was a yard long and coiled on the board in front of her like a sleeping dog, and every so often it moved.

“It is not moving,” said Mardy Haunch, to the customer. “That is settling.”

The customer was from the Vigil. You could tell by the eyes, which were red to the rims and had stopped bothering to blink, and by the long pin she wore through the web of her left hand so she could twist it when the world went soft. She had a nudger with her, a small boy on a lead, whose whole job was to kick her ankle every twenty breaths. He was very good at it. He did not look up from her ankle once.

“Price,” said the Vigil woman.

“For the yard? Eleven lacks.”

“Eleven.” The Vigil woman put three little black tabs on the counter, pressed and stamped with an open eye. “Rouse. Good rouse. Crane’s strain, not the Slope stuff. Four hours of waking each.”

Mardy Haunch looked at the tabs the way a cat looks at a painted bird. “What am I going to do with four hours of waking, my love? I sleep like a ditch. Coin.”

“I have six lacks in coin.”

“Then you have six lacks of sausage.” Mardy raised the knife and the sausage, quite distinctly, tightened its coil away from it.

“Settling,” said Mardy, and put the knife down.

At this point a third party arrived, which is how all real haggling on the Rim Road goes. He was an Oathener, tall and dry and dressed in canyon-red, with a little brass plate at his collar that said PRICE-WITNESS, LICENSED, and he spoke very slowly, the way a man walks across a frozen pond. “If it would be of use,” he said, “and if neither party objects, and barring weather, I might, as I now intend, assist.”

“Nobody asked you,” said Mardy.

“That is so,” said the Oathener, which cost him nothing, because it was true. He looked at the sausage. He looked at it for some time. “I would observe, without asserting anything as to its composition, that the casing bears a mark.”

It did. A little way from the end there was a faded blue pattern pricked into the skin. Anchors. Two anchors, crossed, and under them, in a sailor’s crude letters, the beginning of a name: SAL. The rest of the name was round the other side of the coil.

There was a silence of the kind you get at a market when everyone within six stalls has stopped pretending not to listen. The rope-seller had stopped measuring. The Seamer’s boy had stopped crying fingers.

“That,” said Mardy Haunch, with tremendous dignity, “is a pig that went to sea.”

“I would not say otherwise,” said the Oathener, very carefully, “since I cannot.”

The Vigil woman leaned in, red eyes unblinking, close enough to read. The boy kicked her ankle. She did not notice. “Turn it over,” she said.

“Turn it over yourself. Four lacks, then. For the yard. And the tabs.”

“Three lacks and the tabs, and you turn it over.”

“Five and I don’t.”

The Oathener coughed, gently. “If it would help to settle the matter, and as a neutral party, I might say that in my judgment, as I now hold it, the item has a value, and that value is not nothing.”

Both women looked at him with loathing. He received it calmly. He was paid a crumb a word, and he had been very economical.

In the end the Vigil woman paid four lacks and two tabs, and Mardy Haunch threw in a heel of toothed bread, which bit the boy, and wrapped the coil in a sheet of oiled paper and tied it with string, and did not turn it over. The Vigil woman walked off up the Rim Road towards the lamp-glow on the eastern horizon, carrying the parcel against her chest like a baby, and three stalls down she stopped, and unwrapped one end, and looked.

Nobody saw what the rest of the name said. But they saw her stand there a long while. And they saw her, at last, wrap it up again and keep walking, because it was a long road and she was hungry and four lacks is four lacks.

“Lack keep away,” said Mardy Haunch to the next customer, and smiled, and ate.

On the Table everyone needs something that only an obscene neighbour can sell. The sleepless need oil, brine and pain. The undying need perfume and thread. The starving heartland needs everything, and hates whoever brings it. The Rim Road is the ring of highway that carries all of it, three thousand miles of rutted stone around the Fast’s border, owned by the Rim Road Company, tolled at every bridge and lined with inns, wells, shrines, gibbets and markets. Most of what player characters buy, they buy on the Rim, from someone who is lying to them about where it came from.

This chapter is a working market. It sets out the money of the Table and what it is made of; how to find something for sale and how long that takes; how to argue the price down; what living costs in each land; and long lists of weapons, armour, clothes, tools, food, drugs, beasts, beds and services. It closes with the things that are not supposed to be for sale at all: relics cut from the gods, and the merchants who deal in them.

Using This Chapter

Prices are given in lacks (L) and crumbs (c). Ten crumbs make a lack; twenty lacks make a platter. Prices assume a Rim Road market in a good season. Use the Availability rules to decide whether an item is on the stall at all, the Haggling rules to settle what the characters actually pay, and the Taint rules whenever the thing they bought was once part of a god.

The GM should not let shopping become bookkeeping. Track money closely when it is scarce and it matters (in the Fast, in a siege, in debt to an Oathener). Otherwise let characters live at a lifestyle and roll only for the purchases that make a story.

The Coin of the Table

We pay for bread with bone. Nobody thinks this is strange. Nobody has ever asked whose.
— Meek Garrity, from a suppressed lecture

The Lack

The lack is the one coin honoured everywhere on the Table: a disc of salt-cured bone the width of a thumb-joint, a finger’s width thick, pierced at the centre so it can be strung, and stamped on one face with the Plate (a full moon) and on the other with an empty circle. By law and by custom it is worth one day’s bread. When the price of bread rises, people do not say that bread is dear. They say the lack is thin.

Nobody minted the first lacks. In the years after the Gorging, when the famine broke and the crops rose in a week, the peoples of the Table had a great deal of bone lying about from the meal, and the oldest tradition holds that the first coins were cut from the gods themselves: from Ummer’s ribs, from Dromm’s vast spine, from the knuckles of Ossel. Those First Lacks, if any survive, are not money. They are relics (see Relics & Godflesh). The coin in your purse is ordinary bone. That is the official position, and it is almost true.

How Bone Becomes Coin

Since 212 A.G. the only lawful mint is the Rim Road Company’s Cure-House at Saltbridge, on the Rim where the Fatlands road meets the Brinehollow road. Every lack struck in the last four centuries passed through it. The process is old, simple and filthy.

  • The bone. It comes from the Chute, the Fatlands’ great export depot, in sealed carts stamped BONE: MIXED. The Renderers’ Union sells the Company the long bones of everything slaughtered in the south. Everything slaughtered in the south includes the cattle, the swine, the orchard-pigs, the drover-herds of Sal Trotter, and the Fatlands dead, who are served at their own wakes and whose bones the family is paid a few crumbs to send on. The Company does not sort. Coin-cutters say you can tell a cattle lack from a person lack by the grain; the Company says that is superstition, and fines anyone who says it twice.
  • The boil. The bones are boiled white in copper vats for three days and three nights. The fat is skimmed and sold back south as tallow. The steam from the Cure-House can be smelled from the next toll, and the people of Saltbridge are famous for their good skin and bad dreams.
  • The cutting. Coin-cutters, most of them Scraplings bound to the Company for twenty years, saw the long bones into rounds on treadle saws and punch the centre hole. A good cutter gets nineteen lacks from a man’s thigh. The cutters keep tally-sticks of their work and are paid in their own product, one lack in fifty.
  • The cure. The rounds are packed in salt for a full season. The salt is Brinehollow salt, and since the sea retreated, most Brinehollow salt is boiled out of the water Brinehollowers cough up at dawn and dusk, collected in parish buckets and sold by the barrel. Every lack on the Table is cured in somebody’s lungs.
  • The stamp. A hot iron die burns the Plate and the empty circle into the faces. The empty circle has been on the coin since the first Company issue; the Company’s charter says it represents “the bread to be bought.” Some old coin-cutters say it is a chair seen from above.

A genuine lack is dense, faintly translucent at the edge when held to a lamp, cool to the touch, and tastes strongly of salt. Merchants bite coins. On the Rim this is not a figure of speech.

Crumbs

A crumb is a tenth of a lack: a bone bead the size of a pea, pierced and cured like its parent, cut from the knuckles, ribs and offcuts that will not make a full disc. Crumbs are strung in tens on a knotted cord called a loaf. Paying a lack in crumbs is legal but rude, and a merchant may count every bead in front of you while you wait. Children are paid in crumbs, beggars ask for them, and every Oathen price-witness charges by them.

Platters

A platter is a sealed Rim Road Company tablet of polished bone, the size of a palm, worth twenty lacks. Each is cut from a single shoulder blade, stamped with the Company’s ring-road seal, numbered, and closed with a bead of red wax impressed by the signet of Jessamy Quill, Notary of the Rim Road. The Company has sworn, in Oathen, before Quill, that it will redeem every unbroken platter for twenty lacks at any Company house on the Rim. Because the oath was sworn in Oathen, it cannot be broken without the Company’s sworn officers coming apart. This is why the platter is trusted more than any coin, and why the Company guards Jessamy Quill more closely than any king guards a crown. If she dies, every platter in circulation becomes a pretty piece of shoulder.

Weighing and Clipping

A true lack weighs as much as forty grains of untoothed wheat. Money-changers carry hanging scales and a pouch of reference grains, and in the Fatlands, where the wheat has teeth, they carry grains from the Rim and guard them like jewels. Shaving a lack (clipping) is a hanging offence in every land except Sallowreach, where the offender is shaved in turn, very slowly, by the same amount. Clipped coins are accepted at nine crumbs, or at eight if the clipping shows.

Counterfeits

Bone is everywhere, so forging lacks is the commonest crime on the Rim. The common fakes and their tells:

  • Horn and hoof. Pressed and dyed. Too light; burns with a stink when touched with a hot needle. Detected on a Routine (10) Eye + Reckoning roll.
  • Unsalted bone. Bone that skipped the season in brine. Tastes of nothing. A merchant who bites coin finds it at once.
  • Kept bone. Cut from the Kept of Sallowreach, whose bodies never finish rotting. These coins are perfect in every respect but one: they never stop decaying. In a few weeks a Kept lack goes greasy and grey and smells faintly of the fen. In a purse it sweats. A purse of Kept coin attracts flies. Hard (14) to spot when fresh.
  • Wrack bone. Bone from Cradlewrack Parts. A coin cut from a Part, it is whispered, is still growing; it thickens by a hair a month, and in a year will not fit a string. Hard (14) to spot.
  • Blank bone. The rarest and most sinister fake: lacks cut from the bones of Blanks or the Unfed. They are said to be the only coins with no god in them at all. Collectors pay twenty times face value. They are almost always proof that somebody was killed for their skeleton.

Passing false coin knowingly is punished by the Company with a fine of ten times the face value and the loss of the passing hand’s thumb, and by most lands with worse.

Whose Bones?

The question every player eventually asks is answered differently depending on who is asked. The Company says: cattle. The Renderers’ Union says: whatever comes. Mistress Brisket Annalow, if she can be made to say anything, says that since the Reaping doubled the Chute ships more bone than the herds could possibly account for, and that the Company has never once complained about the quality. A character who studies lacks for long (Grim 18 Eye + Lore) can learn to read the grain, and from then on will know which coins in their purse were people. They will still spend them. Everybody does.

Sworn Notes

Oathen does not mint. It does not need to. In Oathen, a written promise to pay, sworn aloud before witnesses and signed, is backed by the only security that cannot run away: the issuer’s own body. These are sworn notes, and they are the paper money of the eastern half of the Table.

A sworn note reads something like this: “I, Halde Vosk, of Tacit, as I now intend and barring weather, will pay the bearer twelve lacks on demand at my house in the third gallery, and if I do not, let my left hand answer.” The issuer reads it aloud in front of a licensed Clausewright, signs it, and the Clausewright witnesses it with a thumbprint in ink. The note then circulates exactly like coin.

The collateral clause is what gives the note its value. It names what breaks if the issuer defaults: a hand, an eye’s sight, the use of a knee, the voice, a set of teeth. The Rule of Oathen does the rest. The moment the issuer refuses or fails to pay a bearer who has made lawful demand, the named part breaks, at once, with a sound, wherever the issuer happens to be. Notes backed by large collateral (“let my heart answer”) are not legal in Oathen, since a break is never fatal by itself and a heart that opens like a cupboard and goes on beating is considered bad for trade.

  • Valuing a note. A note is worth its face value only if the issuer is solvent, whole, and findable. Oathen notes trade at full value in Tacit, at a crumb in the lack discount on the Rim, and at two or three crumbs in the lack in the far west, where the issuer is weeks away. A note by an issuer known to be close to default trades at half. Speculators in Tacit watch issuers’ bodies through spyglasses from the opposite canyon wall, and a limp is news.
  • Forsworn paper. Notes issued by the Forsworn of the Breakdowns are backed by what they have left. A man whose ribs already stand open like a book has little to pledge. Brakk’s people issue notes against parts that are already broken; these are worthless and are traded as jokes, souvenirs and insults.
  • Sureties. A merchant who lacks good body can hire a Surety to co-sign: the Surety pledges a part of their own body as second collateral, for a fee of one lack in ten. Ona Fell’s notes are the best paper in the canyon. She has two hundred and eleven other oaths in her, and her signature still trades at par.
  • Default abroad. The break happens wherever the issuer is, because the oath is in the issuer. A note sworn in Tacit and defaulted in Lastgate snaps a wrist in Lastgate. Foreign issuers who swear notes in Oathen are bound like natives. A non-Oathener who signs a note outside Oathen is not bound at all, and their notes are not called sworn notes but “dry paper,” worth what the issuer’s honesty is worth.
  • The new terror. Writing has begun to bind on its own. Two clerks in Tacit have broken this year over notes they copied but never swore. The Bench of Clauses has said nothing. The discount on Oathen paper has quietly doubled.
Default — What Happens

When a character who issued a sworn note fails to pay on lawful demand, the named collateral breaks: treat it as an Injury from the Mangling table chosen to match (a hand that will not close; an eye gone milky; a knee reversed), with no roll to avoid it, and a Dread 2 check for anyone who sees it happen. The character is now Forsworn in that matter, and every Oathener who sees them knows it. Paying the debt afterwards does not mend the break. Nothing does.

Regional Money

Every land uses the lack, and every land also uses something else, usually something only that land could think of. A traveller who wants to be treated as a fool pays in lacks everywhere. A traveller who wants local prices learns the local money.

Sallowreach: Licenses, Minutes and Breaths

The only thing truly scarce in Sallowreach is ending, and so death is the money of the north. The Mortuary Court sells a death-license, entitling the bearer to one Closing by a Hand-line Closer, for about four thousand lacks. Few families can raise that, so for three centuries the Court has also issued fractions of a license. A minute of Closing is a sixtieth part of a license, a narrow lacquered slip of coffin-wood bearing Regent Grue’s signature and the number of the license it belongs to. A breath is a twelfth of a minute: a black wax token stamped with a closed eye. Families save minutes for generations, in jars under the floor, towards the day great-great-grandmother can at last be finished. Lend a man a minute and he will thank you. Give a man a full license and he will weep. Minutes are the closest thing in Sallowreach to inheritance; they pass because their owners do not.

The Fatlands: Meat Scrip

The Board of Plenty pays wages, rents and taxes in meat scrip: printed slips of greased paper, each redeemable at any Board store or at the Chute for a stated weight of meat. The common denominations are the pound, the stone and the side. Meat scrip is the most honest money on the Table in one sense (it is backed by something you can eat) and the most horrible in every other, because its value tracks the supply of meat, and the supply of meat rises every Carving with the Reaping. In a heavy Reaping year the scrip falls by a third in a month. Pell Hogget’s tally-keepers chart the scrip rate alongside their count of the missing, and the two lines match.

Brinehollow: Bail-Tokens

A bail-token is a small disc of cast lead, stamped with a bucket, issued by Brinehollow parishes to anyone who bails the infirm at dawn and dusk. Each token is good for one cup of sweet water at an Admiralty cistern or one bailing done on your behalf. Because both are always wanted, the tokens circulate as small change. Children like Tolly Brack earn more in tokens than their parents do in coin. A Netwatch tally, a larger lead token stamped with a hook, is paid to the patrol for every Called person dragged home alive; Netwatch tallies are worth ten bail-tokens and are always suspected of being for bodies that were not, strictly, alive.

The Vigil: Rouse-Tabs

The Vigil’s small money is a rouse-tab: a pressed lozenge of black rouse stamped with an open eye, nominally good for one hour awake. Wages on the Slope are paid in tabs. Because the dose required rises every year, the tab is the only currency on the Table that suffers literal inflation of the body: a tab that held an hour in 600 A.G. now holds perhaps twenty minutes, and the Apothecary-General’s office restamps the official value each season. Tabs cut with Brinehollow brine (see Drugs) are worth more on the Slope, because they work better, and are worth nothing to anyone who knows why.

Cradlewrack: Naming-Rights

In Cradlewrack, no child is named until it is a year old and plainly a child. Until then, the right to name it belongs to whoever bore it, and that right can be sold. A naming-right is a Tally-office certificate giving the holder the sole right to name a particular birth when the year is out. Rich families buy naming-rights to fill a branch of the family tree; the poor sell them for bread. Because nobody knows what a birth will turn out to be, naming-rights are speculation in the purest form: a right to name a healthy boy is worth a fortune, a right to name a hand is worth nothing, and a right to name something the Attendance does not permit is void. Kest has a naming-exchange, under the Tally hall, where rights are bought and sold by the hour as rumours come down from the birthing-rooms.

Oathen: Sworn Notes

As above. Small coin in Oathen is still the lack, and the price-witness is still paid in crumbs, but anything over a platter changes hands as paper.

The Fast: Ration Chits

The Unfed do not touch bone coin. They say the lack is cut from Godeaters and cured in Godeater lungs, and they are right, and they will not have it in their houses. Inside the Fast the only money is the ration chit: a square of unbleached cloth stamped by the Pantry with a single empty bowl, entitling the bearer to one day’s ration at the Pantry window in Wanting. Chits are issued, never earned; the Abstinent give them out by household, by name, by list. A family left off the list has nothing to trade. The chits cannot lawfully be sold, and are sold constantly. In Lack season, when Mother Stint Avery begins cutting the lists, a chit fetches three lacks from a Crumb-Runner, who will be spat at for buying it.

Barter

Most of the Table does not live on coin. Scrapling villages run on barter, and on the Rim a great deal of trade is goods against goods, with lacks used only to settle the difference.

  • Fair barter. Goods trade at their listed price if both parties need them. Goods the buyer does not need are taken at half their value. Goods the buyer badly needs (oil in the Vigil, perfume in Lastgate, sweet water in Brinehollow, anything edible in the Fast) are taken at one and a half times or double.
  • Regional goods travel well. A good carried from its home land to a distant one is worth half again its home price on arrival, before any haggling. This is the whole business of the Rim Road.
  • Bartering with Partaking. A character may not Partake to haggle with goods unless the god they carry is one the other party fears; the Tooth is felt, not seen, and merchants on the Rim know the look of a customer who is getting help.
  • Barter in the Fast. The Unfed accept no gift and give none. A barter in the Fast must be declined three times by both parties before it is agreed on the fourth asking. Skipping the ritual voids the trade, and the offended party will not deal again.

Finding Things

Anything can be bought on the Rim Road. Not everything can be found.
— Toll Nine proverb

Availability

Every item in this chapter has an Availability rating. To find an item that is not simply sitting in front of the characters, one character makes a Grace Roll: Eye + Haggle against the difficulty below, modified by where they are looking. Other characters may help in the usual way. A character may Partake on the roll; the Tooth makes merchants talkative, or makes the searcher notice the stall behind the stall.

RatingDifficultySearch timeTypical goods
CommonRoutine 10an hourbread, knives, rope, lamp oil, perfume, rouse
UncommonHard 14half a dayswords, crossbows, mail, Kept-candles, laudanum
ScarceGrim 18a dayplate, Brinehollow tonic in the Fatlands, a Tucker
RareDire 22a weekgodflesh, a Sayer’s word, Blank parts
Uniquespecialan adventurenamed relics; never found by rolling alone
  • Success means the item is for sale, at listed price, in this market. Each Helping may be spent to find a better example (one extra quality, or no hidden flaw), to find it cheaper (one step of price in the buyer’s favour, see Haggling), or to learn something about the seller.
  • Grace means the seller is eager, or there is a second one, or the merchant offers something better that they “weren’t going to show anyone.”
  • Failure means it is not here. The character may try again after the search time has passed again, at +2 difficulty for every retry in the same market.
  • Lack means the item is found, and it is wrong: stolen and recognisable, Tainted and undeclared, a fake, or sold by an informer. The GM chooses, and does not say which until it matters.
  • Unique items are never found with a roll. They are the end of a trail, the price of a favour, or the reward of an adventure.

Black Markets

Every city on the Table has a market that is not on the Company’s ledgers. In Lastgate it is the undercity under the lowest pilings, where Marrow Jack’s boys sell limbs off drying racks. In Sated it is behind the rendering yards. In Lowmark it is out on the Uncovered at low fog. In the Vigil it is the Slope, which is a black market with houses on it. In Kest there are no locks, so the black market is simply wherever you are when somebody shuts the door. In Tacit it is conducted entirely in Handtalk, which is held not to bind, and which lately does.

Finding a black market needs a contact or a Hard (14) Eye + Search roll. Contraband bought there costs one and a half times the listed price, or double if the goods are capital crimes in that land. Selling there pays half the listed price, since the fence carries the risk. A Lack on any black-market roll means the Wakers, the Netwatch, the Bailiff’s men or the Echo-Wardens were already watching.
