Haggling

Listed prices are opening prices. When a character wants to argue, the buyer rolls Tongue + Haggle opposed by the seller’s Tongue + Haggle (or Threat, for minor merchants). The higher total wins. Ties favour the seller; it is their stall.

Price moves in steps of one-tenth of the listed price. The winner shifts the price one step in their favour, plus one step for each Helping (count Helpings from the loser’s total, not from a fixed Difficulty). Price cannot fall below half or rise above double the listed price by haggling alone. A Grace for the buyer adds a small thing thrown in (a heel of bread, a name, a warning); a Lack for the buyer means they have offended the seller, who will not deal again today and will tell the next stall.

  • Regional tempers. Sallowreach merchants have centuries of patience and are at +2 to resist haste. Fatlanders haggle while eating and are at −2 if the buyer refuses to eat with them, +2 if the buyer finishes the plate. Brinehollowers stop mid-haggle to bail and are not to be hurried. Vigil sellers are short-tempered and hallucinating; a buyer who pinches them first is at +1. Cradlewrack sellers knock on the counter before every offer.
  • Haggling in Oathen. Every offer in Oathen is a promise. A buyer who says “I’ll pay six” has sworn it. Oatheners haggle in conditionals (“If six were mentioned, it would not be refused”) and a foreigner who does not is at −2 and is also likely to break something. A buyer who hires a licensed price-witness (1 crumb a word, a good one uses twenty) haggles at +2 and swears nothing.
  • Haggling in the Fast. No price may be accepted until it has been declined three times. A character who forgets is at −4 on any further dealing that day.
Helpings and Price at a Glance

Opposed Haggle: the winner moves the price one tenth in their favour, and one more tenth per Helping of margin. Floor half, ceiling double. A buyer who Partakes and rolls a 1 on the Tooth has let the god show at the counter: the seller sees it, and the price goes up a step for fear, or down two for awe, as fits the god.

Taint

Never eat the god twice. Once is history. Twice is a habit.
— Purgation catechism

Some goods are made from the gods. Bread from toothed wheat is grown in Ummer’s flesh. Bottled brine is the Fathom coughed up by its eaters. A Kept-candle is Ossel’s long refusal to finish, rendered into tallow. These goods carry Taint: the residue of the god, which goes on working in whoever uses them.

Taint is written as a rating from 1 to 5 and a kind: Hunger, Regrowth, or Dread. An item may carry more than one kind (for example, “Taint 2 Hunger, 1 Dread”). Taint triggers on use: once each time the item is eaten or drunk; once per scene it is wielded in anger, or burned, or opened; once per day it is worn against the skin; and once each time a relic’s power is called on.

  • Hunger Taint. The user gains Hunger equal to the rating, exactly as though they had Partaked. No roll. If this takes Hunger to 10, Regrowth rises as normal.
  • Regrowth Taint. The user makes a Caul + Resolve roll against the matching difficulty: Taint 1 Routine 10, 2 Hard 14, 3 Grim 18, 4 Dire 22, 5 Impossible 26. On success, they gain 1 Hunger. On failure, they gain 1 Regrowth directly. On a Lack, they also gain the item’s land’s Want for a day, even if it is not their land.
  • Dread Taint. The user makes a Dread check at the rating’s Dread level, because the thing is horrible to use (a candle that whimpers; a loaf that bites back). Repeated use of the same item lowers Dread Taint by 1 after the first five uses, to a minimum of 1. One gets used to things.

Foreign gods. Godflesh from a land not your own carries a god you did not eat. Taint from a foreign god is not reduced by any Gift of your own Regrowth, and on a failed Regrowth Taint roll the gained point of Regrowth is marked as foreign: the GM may spend a foreign point at any time to give the character that land’s Taste-stage tell for a scene. Characters who mix gods in their blood are the reason the trade in cures never ends and never works.

The Unfed and the Blank. A character with Cut 0 ignores Hunger Taint; there is nothing in them to be hungry. Regrowth Taint is worse. Each failed Regrowth Taint roll gives a Cut 0 character one mark of Seasoning; at three marks, the meat has found what it was looking for, and the character gains Cut 1 in that god’s line, permanently. Tobias Wether and the Reckoner called Scour each have three marks.

Declaring Taint. In the Fatlands the law requires godflesh to be declared and stamped. Nowhere else does. A seller who knows the Taint will rarely say so; a Hard (14) Eye + Lore roll identifies the kind and rating of an item’s Taint, and a Grim (18) roll identifies which god.

Purging. A Purgation emetic (see Drugs) taken within an hour of eating Tainted food removes the Hunger it caused. Nothing removes Regrowth that Taint has given.

Cost of Living

The rich smell of cedar. The poor smell of themselves.
— Lastgate saying

A character’s lifestyle covers food, lodging, clothes and small expenses. Pay it by the day, the week (seven days) or the season (ninety days, at a tenth off).

Arms and Armour

There is no gunpowder on the Table. There are a great many hooks.
— Netwatch drill-sergeant’s opening remark

Damage is listed in brackets. Attack with melee weapons is Hand + Blades (or Brawl for fists, clubs and grapples). Ranged weapons use Hand + Shooting. Weapons marked with a land are Common there and one step rarer everywhere else.

Weapon and Armour Qualities

  • Brutal. Each Helping on a hit adds +3 damage instead of +2.
  • Concealable. Finding it on a body takes a Hard (14) Eye + Search roll.
  • Entangling. On a hit with at least one Helping, the target is held instead of taking the Helping’s damage: they cannot move away and are at −2 Guard until they spend an action and succeed at a Hard (14) Gut + Athletics roll.
  • Fragile. On a Lack, the weapon breaks.
  • Heavy. Needs Gut 3 or more to use without penalty; otherwise −2 Attack. The wielder is at −1 Guard.
  • Hooking. On a hit with at least one Helping, the attacker may give up the Helping’s damage to drag the target one pace, pull them off a ledge or mount, tear away a held item, or knock them prone (the target may resist with a Hard 14 Lung + Athletics roll).
  • Light. Can be used in the off hand; +1 Attack against a held or prone target.
  • Noisy. Everyone within a long stone’s throw hears it used. In the Vigil, this is considered good manners.
  • Parrying. +1 Guard against melee attacks while held ready.
  • Piercing. Ignores 1 point of Armor.
  • Reach. Strikes from two paces away. A foe closing to arm’s length is attacked first.
  • Ripping. If the hit deals 3 or more damage after Armor, the wound bleeds: the target loses 1 Flesh at the end of each round until someone succeeds at a Routine (10) Hand + Stitching roll. In Sallowreach a Ripping wound never closes without stitching, ever.
  • Silent. Makes no sound in use; attacks from hiding gain +2.
  • Slow. Reloading takes a full action.
  • Stunning. On a hit with a Helping, the target loses their next action unless they succeed at a Hard (14) Gut + Endure roll.
  • Thrown. Can be thrown up to ten paces with Hand + Shooting.
  • Two-Handed. Needs both hands.
  • Waking. A Vigil quality. A creature struck cannot blink, sleep or fall unconscious for the rest of the scene, even at 0 Flesh, and feels everything.
  • Tainted. The item is made from godflesh and carries Taint as listed (see Taint).

Lack keep away.
— said before eating with any stranger, everywhere

What's in the Barrel?

Chute barrels are stamped with their origin, and then stamped over, and then stamped over again. When a character opens one, roll a d20.

d20Contents
1Pork. Honestly pork. Everyone is suspicious.
2Brined beef, the good stuff, with a brass Board tag. One joint has a healed fracture set by a surgeon.
3Orchard-pig: fat, sweet, and with a bone pit at the centre of every chop.
4Mutton that is still warm, two weeks out of Sated.
5Drover-herd beef, Sal Trotter’s brand. The shins are very long. The hooves are not hooves.
6Salt tongue, eighty of them, in neat rows. Several are pierced for earrings. No, for bits.
7Mixed offal and a wedding ring.
8Bacon with a birthmark shaped like a hare. Someone in Low Tilth will know whose.
9Sausage, a single coil, tattooed in blue: crossed anchors and a name.
10Brawn in jelly. The jelly has a heartbeat for an hour after opening.
11Corned beef stamped with Ivo Stockpot’s notch. He would not eat this.
12Fatlands field-meat: a joint with roots growing through the marrow. Taint 2 Hunger.
13A whole ham with a face on the rind. Pleasant. Smiling. Eyes closed.
14Good beef, and at the bottom a sealed letter: “If you are reading this, tell my sister Merrin I was Reaped at Low Tilth on the ninth of Carving.”
15Tripe that continues to digest whatever is put in with it.
16Salt pork and forty teeth, sorted by size. Granny Cracknel will want them.
17Empty but for brine, and the brine is cold and pulls gently west.
18A Gut-lines cut: marbled, enormous, Taint 3 Hunger. Worth twenty times the barrel.
19Meat that a Fast-born character cannot be persuaded to look away from.
20Something alive, packed in salt, curled up, and very glad of the light.

Addiction

Each time a character uses an addictive drug, they roll Gut + Endure against its Addiction difficulty. On failure, they gain one point of Need for that drug. At 1 Need they want it; at 3 Need they are addicted. An addicted character who goes a day without a dose is at −1 to all rolls, and −1 more for each day after, to −4; each day without also adds 1 Fray. Need falls by 1 for each full week without the drug, while suffering. A Lack on the Addiction roll adds 2 Need.

Rouse is special. In the Vigil, nearly everyone is addicted, and the dose rises. A character addicted to rouse must double the dose after each season of use to get the same effect. Dr. Aldous Crane knows where the curve ends. It is eleven years off, and a character who works the arithmetic for themselves (Grim 18, Eye + Reckoning) takes a Dread 2 check.

The Inn at the Crossroads

In the last three years Company inn-keepers on the Rim have reported finding tables laid in their common rooms at dawn: a white cloth, warm bread, a chair pulled out, a place card. The Company’s standing instruction is to burn the table and not read the card. Not all inn-keepers obey. A few have started renting the chair.

Relics and Godflesh

Every land believes another land’s curse might cure its own. Nothing has ever worked. The trade never slows.
— The Rim Road, in a sentence

Relics are pieces of the Providers, or of people far enough into the Regrowth that the difference no longer matters. They are never Common. Most are illegal somewhere. All are Tainted. The prices given are what a dealer would ask, if a dealer could be found who was willing to sell.

A Hand-Line Finger

Cost: 1,200 L · Avail.: Rare · Taint: 2 Regrowth (Ossel), Dread 2

A grey finger with nine joints, taken from a Hand-line noble in the Course, still cold. Touched to a lock, a lid or a door, it closes it, and nothing opens it again without breaking it. Touched to a candle, the candle finishes. Touched to a person outside Sallowreach, it does nothing, and the wielder takes a Dread 2 check from the way it flexes. Capital crime in Sallowreach. The Mortuary Court counts its nobles’ fingers.

A Bottled Hush

Cost: 2,500 L · Avail.: Rare · Taint: Dread 4

A stoppered jar of air from the edge of Dunmere Hush. Unstoppered, it makes a silence ten paces across for one minute: no sound carries, flames go out, flies drop. Any Kept inside it finishes, completely and properly. The Finishers will kill for one. The Court calls every jar a stolen license. The jar is always slightly too heavy.

A Biting Loaf

Cost: 20 L · Avail.: Scarce · Taint: 1 Hunger, 1 Dread

Toothed-wheat bread baked with the teeth left in. Set on a windowsill or in a doorway, it bites anyone who enters uninvited (attack +4, damage 1, Ripping). Granny Cracknel bakes them for widows. After a week, the loaf has grown a second row.

A Jar of Tenanted Brine

Cost: 400 L · Avail.: Rare · Taint: 3 Regrowth (Dromm)

Water coughed at dawn by one of the Tenanted. Held to the ear, it can be heard talking, slowly, in a voice like a hull settling. A character who listens for an hour may ask one question about the sea, the Trench, or the Tenant, and is answered truthfully. They must then pass a Grim (18) Caul + Resolve roll or walk west the next night.

A Lash from the Eye of Iss

Cost: not for sale (offers start at 10,000 L) · Avail.: Unique · Taint: 4 Regrowth (Iss)

A black hair a yard long, stiff as wire, one of the few that survived the Eye-lines’ meal. Laid across a sleeper’s lids in the Vigil, it lets them sleep and wake again, once, safely. The eye in the long room will have seen them. The Warden-Prime knows where every lash is, and there are three.

A Caul-Scrap Veil

Cost: 600 L · Avail.: Rare · Taint: 2 Regrowth (Vey)

A square of membrane cut from a Caul-line noble, stitched to a hat-brim. Through it the wearer sees a few heartbeats ahead, blurred: once per scene, reroll any one die. Each day it is worn, roll a d10; on a 1, the veil has grown into the skin of the brow. Duchess Morwen’s veil has lately gone red. So have the scraps.

A Sayer's Word Sealed in Wax

Cost: not for sale (20,000 L if it were) · Avail.: Unique · Taint: Dread 3

A ball of gold wax the size of a walnut, sealed by the Bench of Clauses, containing a single word spoken by a Sayer into it before the bit went back in. Crack it, and the word is so. Known words in private hands: Stop, Shut, Mend, Mine. Nobody knows the scope of any of them. One is rumoured to say Enough.

An Orrum Crumb

Cost: 150 L · Avail.: Rare · Taint: Dread 2; see text

A crumb of bread from one of the Host’s tables, picked up off the cloth by a Tablebreaker before the axe fell. While carried, the holder’s Hunger cannot rise above 5 and they never feel hungry. If it is ever eaten, the character is a guest, and must pass an Impossible (26) Caul + Resolve roll or sit at the next table they see, forever. It smells of fresh bread for six hundred years.

A Place Card Bearing Your Name

Cost: not for sale · Avail.: Unique · Taint: Dread 3

A stiff cream card, a fine hand, your name spelled correctly. Nobody sells these; they are found. While a character keeps it, every host on the Table must offer them a seat (+4 Persuade for hospitality), and wherever they sleep, a table is laid by morning. Burning it does nothing. It is on the next table.

Granny Cracknel's Matched Teeth

Cost: 80 L a set · Avail.: Scarce · Taint: 1 Hunger, 2 Dread

A full set of teeth milled from toothed wheat, matched by Granny Cracknel to someone she knew. Held in the mouth for a night, they give the holder that person’s last meal and last sight in a dream. Pell Hogget has bought eleven sets from Low Tilth. The last sight is always the same field at dusk.

Ilse Marl's Chart

Cost: not for sale · Avail.: Unique · Taint: Dread 3

Forty years of transcriptions of the Tenanted’s low-water song, laid end to end: a chart of the Uncovered, with depths no sea has ever had there. A navigator using it crosses the Uncovered without rolling and can find the Trench and a stone table with eight chairs. Studying it for a week allows a character to hum the song; anyone Tenanted who hears them stops and turns.

A Shard of Hallowboard

Cost: 3,000 L · Avail.: Rare · Taint: Dread 2

A hand-sized fragment of the eight-sided stone table of the Refusal, always clean, always faintly warm. No table of Orrum’s can be laid within a hundred paces of it. The Abstinent say Hallowboard has never been chipped; therefore this is a fake, or Hallowboard is lying. A Reckoner who sees it in Godeater hands will kill to return it.

A First Lack

Cost: 1,000 L · Avail.: Rare · Taint: 1 Regrowth (one god, by grain)

A coin cut from a Provider’s own bone in the first year after the Gorging, cured in no salt at all. Worn on a cord, it gives +1 to Godsign rolls involving its god. Spent, it gives the merchant who takes it that god’s Taste for a month. They circulate anyway; somebody always mistakes one for change.

Ossel's Knucklebones

Cost: 2,000 L · Avail.: Rare · Taint: 2 Regrowth (Ossel), Dread 1

Five dice cut from a joint of the Closing Hand. Thrown for a question about when something will end, they answer truly. Thrown for a person, they show the number of years before their death; in Sallowreach they always roll blank.

Dromm's Ear-Stone

Cost: 700 L · Avail.: Rare · Taint: 2 Regrowth (Dromm)

A pale stone from the Fathom’s inner ear, hauled up at Longslab. Its holder always knows which way the sea is and how far, and feels pressure days a full day early. In the last year it has begun to point down.

A Dowager Clod

Cost: 250 L · Avail.: Rare · Taint: 2 Hunger

A clod of warm earth from the Dowager Hills, cut from a Seated Gut-line matriarch. Planted, anything grows from it overnight, plump and red-veined. If the matriarch is consulted first, she may agree. If not, the crop has her opinions.

A Thief's Kept Hand

Cost: 120 L · Avail.: Scarce · Taint: Dread 2

Taken by Marrow Jack from a Kept pickpocket who was asleep on a shelf. Worn in a glove harness, it gives +2 Filch. Its owner, still in Lastgate, can feel everything it does, and is trying to find you.

A Dormitory Pillow

Cost: 1,500 L · Avail.: Rare · Taint: 3 Regrowth (Iss)

Smuggled out from under one of the Counted. A Dream-Diver who sleeps on it goes down and returns without a tether, once per dive, for an hour. Owning it in the Vigil is a capital crime. It is still warm, and it still smells of someone.

Bed One's Words

Cost: not for sale · Avail.: Unique · Taint: Dread 4

Matron Cecily Dorm’s notebook of what Aveline Morne’s lips have shaped. Most of it is a baker’s daughter’s recipe for bread. The last page is a list of names, and they are being crossed off in an order the Matron cannot see the reason for. One is a player character’s.

A Living Part in a Jar

Cost: 200 L · Avail.: Scarce · Taint: 2 Regrowth (Vey), 1 Dread

A Cradlewrack Part, healthy and warm: an ear, a hand, a length of spine. It turns in the jar toward other Parts and toward the Assemblers’ Barn, a compass to the figure. The Assemblers pay double. The Attendance seizes it and the buyer.

A Yard of Living Cord

Cost: 300 L · Avail.: Rare · Taint: 2 Regrowth (Vey)

Cut, with permission, from one of the Uncut. Tie it between two people and for a day they share damage: each hit is split between them, and so is every Dread check. The cord pulses. It wants to grow back to the one it came from.

A Sayer's Gold Bit

Cost: 5,000 L · Avail.: Rare · Taint: none

Garl Tome’s work, worn and then outgrown by a Sayer. Fitted to any mouth, it prevents speech from binding: Oathen’s rule does not touch the wearer, nor does a Sayer’s word they hear. The wearer cannot eat or speak clearly. The Bench wants all of them back.

An Echo-Stone of Sworn Gorge

Cost: 50 L · Avail.: Scarce · Taint: Dread 3

A pebble from Sworn Gorge that has soaked up the echo. Held to the ear, it repeats the oath of 419 A.G., too faint to understand. Anyone who listens for a full minute is bound by it. Nobody knows what they have sworn. Halvar Stane buys them to grind into sand.

A Puddle of Old Wet Tom's

Cost: 40 L · Avail.: Scarce · Taint: 1 Regrowth (Dromm)

A corked flask of water that followed Old Wet Tom down a corridor. Poured out, it makes a puddle much deeper than the floor. Things can be dropped into it and are gone. Something in it can be heard, very far down, asking for the cork back.

Wren Hollowell's Hair

Cost: 900 L · Avail.: Rare · Taint: none

A lock of the Fasting Girl’s hair, sold by someone who got close. A Blank relic: worn at the throat, it lets the wearer ignore Hunger Taint and gain no Hunger from the first Partake each day. Owning it is proof of having dealt with the Blank trade. The Thin kill for it, the Board pays for it, and the girl wants it back.

A Dunmere Bird

Cost: 60 L · Avail.: Scarce · Taint: Dread 1

A sparrow that fell at the edge of Dunmere Hush, perfectly dead and perfectly whole, uncorrupting. In Sallowreach it is the only finished thing most people have ever seen, and collectors keep them under glass. Kept who hold one weep without moisture.

The Scarecrow's Straw

Cost: 30 L · Avail.: Scarce · Taint: 2 Hunger, 2 Dread

A handful of straw from the Scarecrow of Low Tilth, taken at night by a dare. Scattered in a field, it shows on the next dusk which person will be Reaped there. Held in a pocket, it tells the land where you are.

Merchants of the Table

Never buy from a merchant who says the grace first. He wants something.
— Rim Road advice

These dealers can be dropped into any market scene. Each has a specialty: items in that line are one step more available from them, and they will buy such goods at three-quarters of the listed price instead of half.

Mardy Haunch, Sausage-Wife of Gristmoot

Mardy Haunch Threat 3 · Flesh 14 · Guard 10 · Attack +3 (cleaver 3, Ripping) · Armor 1 (suet) · Dread 0

Stock: Fatlands meat, toothed bread, Chute barrels, marrow-brandy. She has the widest stall on the Rim and has never once stood up behind it. Everything she sells is settling. She buys tattooed casings at a premium and will not say who for; it is Hob Gristle, who is trying to give them back to their families.

Abelard Myrrh, Perfumer of the Lower Pilings

Abelard Myrrh (Kept) Threat 4 · Flesh 9 · Guard 9 · Attack +2 (awl 2) · Armor 0 · Dread 1

Stock: cedar, vinegar, smoke-oils, Kept gauze, Seamer’s lacquer. His own nose rotted off in 340 A.G. and he blends entirely by memory, which is perfect. For 40 L he will make a scent from a dead person’s clothes that convinces any Kept who smells it that they are home and loved. The Court has asked him to stop selling it to the Lofts. He has not.

Nan Pickering, Limb-Broker

Nan Pickering Threat 3 · Flesh 11 · Guard 11 · Attack +4 (shelving hook 3, Hooking) · Armor 1 · Dread 2 (her drying-racks)

Stock: Kept limbs, seamed parts, Thief’s Kept Hands, Seamer’s kits. She buys from Marrow Jack and sells to back-alley seamers in Lastgate’s undercity. Every limb on her racks is labelled with its owner’s name, because she is honest. Some of the owners come to visit. She charges them admission.

Mags Weir, Salvage Queen of the Uncovered

Mags Weir Threat 4 · Flesh 13 · Guard 12 · Attack +5 (harpoon 4, Hooking) · Armor 1 (oilskin) · Dread 0

Stock: wreck goods, salvage-tins, Netwatch gear, Dromm’s Ear-Stones, Tenanted brine. She sells from a beached hulk two miles out on dry seabed. Her newest salvage came from a wreck that sank before the Gorging: a crate of silverware in services of eight. She has sold seven settings. The eighth keeps coming back to the crate.

Lucan Spill, the Oilman

Lucan Spill Threat 4 · Flesh 12 · Guard 11 · Attack +4 (sword 4) · Armor 2 · Dread 0

Stock: lamp oil by the cask, mirror-lanterns, lamp-flasks. He is the supplier who doubled the price to the Vigil, and Garron Ashlock would kill him if killing him would not stop the oil. His new oil burns brighter and smells of low tide. It is rendered on the Uncovered from things with too many ribs, and the lamps that burn it have begun to drip seawater.

Dovey Pinch, Pin-Seller of the Slope

Dovey Pinch Threat 3 · Flesh 9 · Guard 13 · Attack +4 (Waker’s needle 2, Waking) · Armor 0 · Dread 0

Stock: pins, pin-gloves, Waker’s needles, rouse-tabs, hired nudgers by the hour. Seventy, sharp-eyed and pricked all over, she sells pain as a convenience. Her needles are recovered from dead Wakers, and each still remembers the last person it kept awake; if you stick yourself with one, you see their face.

Tamsin Keyless, Lock-Pedlar

Tamsin Keyless Threat 3 · Flesh 10 · Guard 12 · Attack +3 (hatchet 3) · Armor 0 · Dread 0

Stock: locks, bolts, bricks, mortar, knocker’s rings, counterfeit Agnes Latch locks. Her copies hold for a night, sometimes two. She does not mention that they hold only from the outside, and that what she sells to frightened mothers in Kest is not a way to keep things out but a way to keep them in.

Ruth Ninefold, Name-Broker of Kest

Ruth Ninefold Threat 5 · Flesh 10 · Guard 10 · Attack +2 (knife 2) · Armor 0 · Dread 0

Stock: naming-rights, Tally extracts, Attendance birth-fees on credit, living Parts in jars. She owns the rights to name two hundred births. Several were taken to the Lying-In. One was bought from a clay-digger at the rim of the Dilation, and its year is up at the next pang.

Silas Amend, Paper-Broker of Tacit

Silas Amend Threat 5 · Flesh 9 · Guard 10 · Attack +3 (quill-knife 2) · Armor 0 · Dread 0

Stock: sworn notes at a discount, Surety introductions, spyglasses, wax tablets. He speaks only in conditionals and watches issuers’ bodies from the opposite cliff. He has quietly bought every note ever sworn by a single senior Clausewright of the Bench, and intends to call them all on one morning.

Nay-Saying Hobb, the Declining Grocer

Hobb Threat 3 · Flesh 8 · Guard 11 · Attack +2 (knife 2) · Armor 0 · Dread 1 (his shelves)

Stock: ration-bread, Unfed greys, frost-markers, Tablebreaker’s wedges. Wanting’s only shop, run by an Unfed elder who declines every sale three times as custom requires. Sometimes he declines a fourth. His shelves are fuller than the Pantry’s, and he cannot say who restocks them overnight. He does not sell the bread that appears on the top shelf. He throws it into the wind.

Factor Orsolya Tare, Mistress of the Cure-House

Orsolya Tare Threat 5 · Flesh 11 · Guard 11 · Attack +3 (knife 2) · Armor 1 · Dread 0

Stock: platters at par, new-minted lacks by the barrel, clipped coin bought by weight, First Lacks under the counter. She runs the Company’s mint at Saltbridge and smells of boiled bone. Last month a coin-cutter brought her a fresh-cured lack with letters in the grain, as though the bone had grown them. It was a name. She has had the batch held back, and the Renderers’ Union keeps asking where it went.

Mister Cutlery

Mister Cutlery Threat 6 · Flesh 13 · Guard 13 · Attack +6 (Clausewright’s quill-knife 2, Silent) · Armor 1 · Dread 1

Stock: relics and godflesh of every land, laid out on velvet in a silverware case. A soft-voiced man in a silk mask with a silver fork embroidered on it, he travels the Rim in a black coach and sells to nobles. He will buy back anything he sold at triple its price, provided the seller names exactly where it came from. He is cataloguing the gods for the Second Table, one portion at a time.

Strange Encounters at Market

Roll a d20 whenever the characters spend time in a Rim Road market, or when a shopping scene needs something under the clove.

d20Encounter
1A Fatlands child is selling teeth by the cupful, sorted by village. She knows which village each cup is.
2A Kept auctioneer in Lastgate is selling himself by the limb, to settle a debt from 300 A.G. The bidding is brisk.
3A coin a character spent an hour ago is back in their purse. It is greasy and smells of the fen.
4A Vigil customer blinks mid-haggle and comes back from the long room three stalls away, holding a knife, with no idea why.
5A Brinehollow stall-keeper stops to bail. The brine she coughs into the bucket is moving in a slow circle.
6An Oathener, asked the price, says “Too much” without thinking. His purse splits open at his belt.
7A drover herds Sal Trotter’s cattle through the market. One of them, passing, says a character’s name.
8Someone has set a table at the market cross: white cloth, warm bread, a chair pulled out. Two Tablebreakers are running towards it.
9A Cradlewrack pedlar’s crate has given birth. Nobody knows to what. It is under the cart.
10A Price-witness offers his services, then quietly declines to witness a character’s purchase, and will not say why.
11The Company’s toll-men are weighing every lack in the market. Clipped coin is confiscated, and so are three thumbs.
12A Netwatch patrol drags a Called man through the stalls on a hook. He thanks every merchant he passes, courteously, by name.
13A Seamer’s boy offers a character a finger “that matches yours exactly.” It does. Down to the scar.
14Wick Tallow’s candles on a stall all lean toward one shopper. The chandler’s man goes pale and closes the stall.
15A Reckoner is buying nothing, watching a Gut-line merchant’s stall. She has been there since dawn.
16A Wreckwife sells her Tenanted husband’s clothes. He is helping her fold them.
17A Purgation preacher hands out emetics and begs the crowd to throw up the god. Some do, on the spot. The Bailiff’s men arrive.
18A Fast pilgrim, starving, offers everything she owns for a single Orrum crumb. Someone has one.
19A Cutwright with calipers measures customers’ skulls for free, and quietly writes certain names in a separate book.
20A stall that was not there an hour ago sells only one thing: place cards, in a fine hand. The one on top has a character’s name on it. The stall-keeper is very tall, and stoops under the awning, and is warm.
Chapter 15

Things That Eat and Are Eaten

Everything on the Table is either sitting at it or lying on it. Learn which you are before the knives come out.
— Tablebreaker saying, Wanting

REPORT OF THE THIRD NIGHT WATCH, NETWATCH, LOWMARK PIER-SECTION FOURTEEN. Entered by Lt. Sable Reef. 9th of Carving, 641 A.G. For the Admiralty Clerk of Losses. Not for the Bench.

Weather: salt rain from the second bell, fog off the Uncovered from the third. Pressure rising. Two of my hookmen bled from the ears before midnight and were sent to bail.

At the fourth bell the count came up short in Ropewalk Row. Widow Carse called her neighbour’s name through the wall three times and got no answer, and then, she says, got an answer from the wrong side, from the floor. We broke the door. Bed empty, anchor-rope sawn through from underneath. Not cut. Sawn, as if by something with a very small and patient mouth. The cellar was full to the fourth stair with water that had no business being there at that hour and smelled of a harbour I have not smelled since I was a girl. Weed on the stairs, still moving. I wrote the time.

We took the shore road at the run. Found the Called at the end of the old breakwater, which ends now in nine miles of dry seabed, and which she was walking down as if the water were still there to receive her. Woman of forty, nightdress, barefoot, feet cut to ribbons on the shell and not caring. Hookman Dabb put the boathook through the back of her collar as taught and she did not fall. She kept walking and dragged him. A woman of nine stone dragged a man of fourteen stone forty yards on his knees across the shingle. When I got the second rope on her she turned her head and looked at me, and I am obliged to record that her face was perfectly calm and she was weeping out of her nose. Brine. A good deal of it.

We netted her and sat on her. She bailed in the net, unasked, a bucket and a half, and some of what came up was alive and went scuttling under the planking. Dabb stamped on two. He says the third had a face. Dabb has been on the Watch four years and I do not think he is a man for faces, so I have written it down.

At the fifth bell, while we were roping her for the cart, the Uncovered sang. I have heard it before. Everyone on the Watch has, and none of us mention it at muster. It comes up out of the dark where the sea used to be, low, a sound like a hull grinding on a bar, and it has a tune if you let it. Hookman Persey let it. He put his hook down very carefully, the way you put down something you mean to come back for, and he started walking west. We got the rope on him at the tideline and he fought us harder than the woman had. He was crying and saying he was sorry, he was so sorry, they had been waiting such a long time.

On the walk back we passed something standing upright in the mud about a furlong out. In the lamp it looked like a wreck’s keel with the ribs still on. It was not a keel. It had more ribs than a keel and they were opening and closing. We did not stop. I note for the Clerk that it was nearer the pier at the sixth bell than at the fifth, and that the Watch’s standing orders do not cover it, and request that they be made to.

Called recovered: two, one of them my own man. Called lost: none tonight. Injuries: Dabb, bitten on the ankle by something under the planks, wound weeping salt, he swears it is nothing. Persey sleeps roped in the guardhouse. When I looked in on him at dawn the bucket beside him was full to the brim and he had not coughed once.

I would like it entered that I am not asking what the Called are walking toward. I am asking how much longer we are meant to pretend we are the ones doing the pulling.

S. Reef, Lt.

The Table is not short of monsters. It is short of anything else. Every land ate a god, and every land is now host to the slow return of what it swallowed, and that return does not confine itself to the bloodlines of the nobility. It gets into the soil, the weather, the drowned, the sleeping, the unborn and the overheard. It makes things. Some of those things were people a week ago. Some were never people at all, and some are people still, and are the worst of the lot.

This chapter is the GM’s larder. It gives rules for running adversaries in the terms of the Grace Roll, then walks the seven lands one by one, presenting the horrors native to each with full statistics and the long, unpleasant detail that makes them worth meeting. After the lands come the human adversaries, who outnumber the monsters and do more harm. Then come the Seated Gods, the endings of campaigns, and a frank discussion of why nobody at the table should expect to win against one. The chapter closes with random encounter tables for every land and for the Rim Road between them.

Running Adversaries

Threat and the Quick Line

Most adversaries do not need a full stat block. A Netwatch hookman, a field of toothed wheat or a mob of the Forsworn can be run from a single quick line, which gives everything needed at the table: Threat, Flesh, Guard, Attack, Armor and Dread. Threat is a flat bonus the adversary adds to every 2d10 roll that is not an attack: a Search to find a hidden player character, a Stealth to creep up on the camp, a Resolve against a Hush-walker’s silence. Threat 1 is a frightened farmhand. Threat 3 is a trained professional. Threat 5 is the best in the land at their work. Threat 7 and above belongs to things that are no longer working at anything human.

Attack is the full bonus added to 2d10 against the target’s Guard. Damage follows the core rules: the listed weapon damage, plus 2 for each Helping (every full 4 points the roll beats Guard), minus the target’s Armor. Doubles on an adversary’s roll produce a Grace or a Lack exactly as for player characters, and the GM should describe both with relish. A Netwatch hook that rolls a Grace has hooked a player character’s collar and is dragging them. A Seated guest that rolls a Lack has knocked over the salt, and the whole table turns to look at who did it.

Full Stat Blocks

Important adversaries, monsters with Gifts and anything with a name receive a full stat block. These use the same six attributes as player characters (Hand, Gut, Lung, Eye, Tongue, Caul) and the same skills. Humans rarely exceed 5 in an attribute. Monsters, the Laden, the Tenanted and the deep Regrowth may run to 6, 8 or 10, and a Seated fragment of a god ignores the scale entirely. Flesh, Guard and Attack are calculated by the core formulas where the creature is anything like a body; where it is not (a field, a tide, an echo), the block says so and gives what is needed instead.

Dread Ratings

Every adversary carries a Dread rating from 0 to 5. The first time in a scene that a character perceives the thing clearly, they make a Dread check: Caul + Resolve against the difficulty the rating sets. Failure adds Fray equal to the rating; success adds 1; a Grace adds nothing. Many entries specify what, exactly, triggers the check, since a Tenanted judge in a courtroom is Dread 0 until her lower voice finishes her sentence before her upper one does.

DreadDifficultyTypical horror
0noneAn armed man, a thin dog, an honest threat
1Routine 10A Kept beggar, a toothed ear of wheat, a corpse
2Hard 14An Unstitched Kept, a Forsworn’s opened ribs, a blink-murder
3Grim 18The Sump-thing rising, a Tenanted loved one, a table set for you
4Dire 22A Laden hill speaking, a crowning opening, a god’s attention
5Impossible 26A Seating, the Host’s face, any Seated god

Some horrors carry a rising Dread, written as “Dread 2/4”. The first number applies on sight; the second applies when the thing does what it does (a Hush-walker’s silence reaching the character, a Seeming turning to look at the one who imagined it). Others carry Contagion: anyone who sees a character Break in the creature’s presence must make the Dread check again, and on failure takes on the same Derangement the Breaking character did. The Table’s madness travels best in crowds.

Godsign-Powered Creatures

Anything with the god in it can Partake. Creatures with a Cut are listed with it, and with a Hunger track exactly like a player character’s. Before any roll, the GM may Partake for the creature, adding one Tooth (a d6) or, for Cut 3+, two Teeth. Each Partake adds 1 Hunger, and every Tooth that shows a 1 adds 1 more. When a creature’s Hunger reaches 10, it empties and the creature’s Regrowth rises by one. For a monster this is not bookkeeping. It is escalation: the Sump-thing pulls three more drowned bodies into itself and gains Flesh, the Laden hill’s mouth opens wider, the Waker gone mad stops blinking. Each entry describes what a Regrowth rise does to that creature. Players learn quickly that a monster which gambles on its Teeth is a monster that gets worse, and that sometimes the best tactic is to make it Partake.

Godsign creatures also have Sops. A creature that performs its Sop removes 1d6 Hunger, exactly as a player character does, and the Sop is always something the players would rather it did not do: close a child’s eyes, eat the farmhand, take one more of the Called. Interrupting a Sop in progress is often the only way to break a creature’s momentum.

Monster Special Abilities

The following abilities recur through the chapter. They are written in the core rules’ terms and can be lifted onto any creature the GM builds.

  • Unending. The creature does not die from Ruin. At 0 Flesh it is Undone: it stops acting for 1d6 rounds, then recovers 1d6 Flesh and resumes, unless it has been dismembered, sunk, Closed, or moved out of Sallowreach. Every Kept thing has this ability within Sallowreach’s borders.
  • Swarm. The creature is many. Blades and Brawl attacks deal only 1 damage regardless of Helpings; fire, smoke, flood and area effects deal double. A swarm reduced below half Flesh disperses and re-forms elsewhere next scene.
  • Hooking / Grapple (X). On a hit with one or more Helpings, the target is held. Escaping is a Gut + Athletics or Lung + Athletics roll against difficulty X. A held target cannot move and suffers −2 to all rolls.
  • Engulf. Against a held target, the creature’s next hit pulls the victim inside it. Engulfed characters take the creature’s damage automatically each round, ignoring Armor, and make a Dread check each round they remain.
  • Fray Aura (N). At the start of each round within the creature’s reach, every character must pass a Caul + Resolve roll against difficulty N or take 1 Fray. This is in addition to the first sight Dread check.
  • Pull (N). The creature calls. Characters with the relevant Cut must roll Caul + Resolve against difficulty N each round or spend their action moving toward it. Resisting is not free: every success adds 1 Hunger, because the god in the blood wants to go.
  • Rooted. The creature cannot move, but cannot be pushed, knocked down or held. It usually has enormous Flesh and a reach measured in fields.
  • Tide (N). The creature’s influence rises and falls. On the GM’s turn, roll a d10: on N or less it acts twice this round. Things in Brinehollow and the Vigil have this.
  • Binding. The creature’s words count. When it speaks a sentence about a character and that character fails a Tongue + Clause roll (difficulty set in the entry), the sentence becomes physically true. Found only in Oathen and in very bad places elsewhere.
  • Hosting. The creature offers. Any character who accepts anything it offers (food, a seat, shelter, “Come in”) must roll Caul + Resolve against the listed difficulty or stay. Refusing three times grants +2 to the roll; thanking it imposes −4.
  • Armor (type). Some armor is not leather. Waxed flesh, bone lattice, compressed water and layered fat all count. Where an armor ignores a damage type (fat ignores blunt, water ignores blades), the entry says.
  • Helping Effects. Many creatures list what their Helpings do in place of or alongside extra damage. A Flyfront that scores two Helpings does not deal +4 damage. It gets into the mouth.
  • Grace and Lack Effects. Some entries list special results when the creature’s own roll comes up doubles, or when a character’s roll against it does. A character who rolls a Lack against a Hush-walker hears, for one awful second, nothing at all.

Putting Things Down

Killing is not the same in every land. Outside Sallowreach, a creature at 0 Flesh suffers Ruin and further damage kills it, as for any character. Inside Sallowreach nothing dies, and the only ways to finish anything are a Hand-line’s Closing touch, a Hush, or carrying the thing across the border, where it drops at once. Many creatures in this chapter have a Weakness or an End entry, which describes the one way the people of that land have found to stop them. Some of those Ends are worse than the monster. Some are not ends at all, only delays, and the entry will say so.

The GM’s Larder: Pacing Horror

Every creature in this chapter is built to be survivable at first sight. The Dread check, not the attack roll, is where most of them do their damage. Use that. Let the players see the Sump bubble in patterns for a full session before anything comes up.

The best monster fights on the Table end without a death and with a cost: a player character’s Hunger maxed out to win a single roll, a companion who Broke and is now certain their sister has been replaced, a field that now knows their name. Track those costs and bring them back.

When a creature’s Hunger fills and its Regrowth rises mid-fight, describe the change before you describe its next action. The moment of transformation is the scene.

Remember that every creature here began as a meal, a mourner, a farmer or a child. Somebody on the Table loved it. Somebody is still bringing it dinner. Put that person in the scene.

Sallowreach: What Will Not Finish

Every monster in the north began as a person or a thing that tried to end and was refused. They are not malicious, mostly. They are in pain, and they have been in pain for a very long time, and pain that long becomes a kind of weather. Remember that within Sallowreach all of these have Unending unless noted.

The Sump-Thing

Weighted sacks go into the Sump by the hundred each year: the Kept too far gone for stitching, the unclaimed, the inconvenient. The sacks rot. The weights do not. Over decades, in the black peat-water forty feet down, the bodies find each other. Rotting flesh that cannot finish rotting goes soft as dough, and soft things press together under the fen’s weight until there is no telling where one grandfather ends and the next begins. A Sump-thing is what happens when a few hundred of them agree to come up.

It surfaces first as bubbles in patterns: rings, then spirals, then the shape of a hand spread flat under the water. Then the smell, which is not the sweet Sallowreach rot but something older, sulphurous and vinegary, a pickle-jar opened after a century. Then the mound breaks the surface, a slick dark heap twenty feet across, hair and sackcloth and peat-tanned leather stretched over a lattice of knitted bone, and out of it, everywhere, faces. Pressed flat. Mouths working. Some still have the twine of their labels around their necks. The sound it makes is a choir of drowned people trying to say their names through a lungful of fen, which comes out as a long wet gargle with words in it.

It wants to be finished, and it has learned that it cannot be, so it has settled for company. It drags the living down. Victims are not eaten. They are added. A week later a new face surfaces in the mound, and it is still screaming, and it will scream for centuries. Families who lose someone to a Sump-thing sometimes row out to listen for them, and sometimes hear.

Tactics: it rises under boats and walkways, grapples with dozens of arms, and sinks. It is slow on land but can drag itself up a bank like a slug of wet meat. It does not flee. It has nowhere else to be.

Sump-Thing — the Many Drowned
AttributesHand 3 · Gut 9 · Lung 1 · Eye 2 · Tongue 0 · Caul 5
Cut & RegrowthCut 2 (the scraps of a hundred Hand-line servants) · Regrowth 4 (the Appetite) · Hunger 3
SkillsBrawl 4, Endure 5, Stealth 4 (underwater only), Instinct 3
BodyFlesh 40 · Guard 12 · Armor 2 (peat-tanned hide; blades deal −1 more) · Threat 4
AttacksMany Hands +7 (3, Grapple 18; it can attack three targets a round); Draw Down against a held target +7 (Engulf: 3 per round, drowning)
AbilitiesUnending. Swarm-of-bodies: severed arms keep grabbing for 1d6 rounds. Fray Aura 14 when it surfaces. Each character Engulfed for 3 rounds is Added and lost; their face appears next scene.
Regrowthwhen Hunger fills, it pulls 1d6 bodies from the bottom and gains 10 Flesh. At the Course its hands go grey and long and its grip begins to Close what it holds (each held round, a held character must pass Caul + Resolve 18 or lose 1 point of an attribute permanently, as some part of them finishes).
SopAdding a living person. Removes 1d6 Hunger.
Dread3 (when it surfaces); 4 (on recognizing a face in it)
EndIt cannot be killed. It can be cut apart and its pieces carried out of Sallowreach on the Rim Road, which takes a caravan, or lured into a Hush, which takes a sacrifice. The Seamers have a standing bounty of 600 lacks per recovered face.

Hush-Walkers

Edda Thrush walked out of Dunmere Hush. She was the first. She is not the last. A Hush-walker is a person who entered a Hush and did not finish, or a Kept body from inside a Hush that was somehow refused even there and stood up. They come out of the silence carrying it with them. A Hush-walker has no smell at all, which in Sallowreach is the most alarming thing about it: one notices a gap in the stink of the world, a person-shaped absence of rot, before one notices the person. Their skin is clean and pale and perfectly still, unrotted, every fly that lands on them dropping dead and unmoving. They walk slowly. Their feet make no noise on boards. Their mouths move.

Within ten paces of one, sound stops. Not quiet: stopped. A scream comes out as breath. A drawn blade makes no ring. A heartbeat cannot be heard in one’s own ears, and this is what breaks people: the body insists the heart has stopped. In that silence something is listening, the way Edda Thrush insists something listens through her. Victims who stay in the silence too long simply end. They sit down, close their eyes, and are properly, completely dead, with no rot afterward and no flies, and their families tend to envy them. Hush-walkers wander toward Hand-line estates. Nobody is sure if they are drawn there or sent.

Hush-Walker — the Silence That Got Up
AttributesHand 2 · Gut 4 · Lung 2 · Eye 4 · Tongue 0 · Caul 7
Cut & RegrowthCut 3 (Hand-line, by contact) · Regrowth 10 (the Brink) · Hunger 0 (it does not hunger; it does not Partake)
SkillsInstinct 5, Search 4, Resolve 6
BodyFlesh 14 · Guard 12 · Armor 0 · Threat 5
Attacksa slow, gentle touch +4 (Closes: target makes Caul + Resolve 18 or suffers Ruin at once and, outside of Sallowreach’s protection, dies)
AbilitiesThe Silence (10 paces): no sound; Tongue rolls impossible; Partaking costs double Hunger as the god in the blood strains toward the stillness. Each round in the Silence, Caul + Resolve 14 or take 1 Fray and lose the next action to listening. NOT Unending: a Hush-walker reduced to 0 Flesh lies down and is finished, and the ground under it becomes a Hush a yard across.
Dread2 on sight / 4 on entering the Silence
EndDamage it enough. The problem is getting near enough to do it, and the hole it leaves behind. Pim Sorrel’s touch makes them kneel.

The Flyfront

Flies are Sallowreach’s weather, and a Black Noon is its storm. A Flyfront is a mass of carrion-flies thick enough to put out lamps, rolling across the fen at walking pace with a sound like frying fat. It is not a creature in the ordinary sense, but it behaves as one: it hunts. Everything in Sallowreach rots and never finishes, so the flies never finish breeding, and the oldest fronts are centuries old, and have a direction. They come down on the living because the living are warm and wet and still have their soft parts. Within a minute a person is black with them, flies in the eyes, the ears, the nostrils, the throat, a thick crawling paste that has to be scraped off with a knife. The Kept caught in a front come out the other side with their faces gone to lace. The living come out choking up maggots for a week. Justice Ever Lathe’s colony is said to have come from a front, which raises questions about what fronts want.

Flyfront Threat 3 · Flesh 30 · Guard 15 · Attack +6 (crawl 1; every Helping instead adds 1 Fray as they get into the mouth) · Armor 0 · Dread 2 · Swarm; lamps within it go out; Eye rolls −4; fire, smoke and vinegar deal double; a character with two Helpings scored against them is Choked and can do nothing but cough next round.

The Unstitched

The Seamers’ Guild holds Sallowreach together with gut-thread, wire, lacquer and resin. When a Kept body’s stitching fails all at once, from neglect or a lapsed fee or a Seamers’ slowdown, what results is an Unstitched: a person who has come apart along every seam, held together only by habit and old tendon. They lurch. Their arms swing loose from shoulders that are only hooked on. Their jaws hang. Their bellies, sewn shut a dozen times, open like purses with every step and have to be held closed with both hands, so their arms are never free, so they use their teeth. They smell of everything Sallowreach smells of, all at once, concentrated. Most Unstitched are not violent, only desperate: they come at the living begging for thread, for a needle, for someone to hold their face on while they get the wire through. Some, after enough decades of it, have stopped asking. Marrow Jack’s victims are often Unstitched, and come looking for their parts.

Unstitched Kept Threat 1 · Flesh 12 · Guard 10 · Attack +4 (teeth and loose hands 2, Grapple 12) · Armor 0 · Dread 2 · Unending; any Helping against it severs a limb, which keeps fighting on its own (Threat 0, Flesh 3, Attack +2, 1).

The Undone Closer

The Hand-lines sell death by touch, and the touch grows. Osric Vane in his lead mittens is the famous case. An Undone Closer is the case nobody contained: a Hand-line noble deep in the Course whose mittens came off and who went out into the fen. The hands are the thing. Grey, cold, damp like the underside of a stone, the fingers lengthened to a span and a half and jointed nine and ten times, so that they fold and unfold like a spider settling. They move independently of the face above them, which is often weeping. Everything the hands touch finishes: a candle gutters and will not relight, a conversation stops mid-word and cannot be restarted, a person sighs and slumps and is done. The Closer cannot stop touching. It is the Want, gone total. Victims are found laid out tidily, eyes shut, hands folded, and the village around them strangely silent, birdless, every door closed. Hunting one is the Mortuary Court’s most secret duty, because every Undone Closer is a cousin.

The Undone Closer — a Hand-line Out of Its Mittens
AttributesHand 6 · Gut 3 · Lung 3 · Eye 2 · Tongue 2 · Caul 5
Cut & RegrowthCut 5 (Hand-line) · Regrowth 9 (the Course) · Hunger 7
SkillsBrawl 4, Stealth 3, Instinct 4, Rites 3
BodyFlesh 13 · Guard 17 · Armor 1 (fine ruined coat) · Threat 4
AttacksClosing Touch +10 plus Teeth (on a hit, target makes Caul + Resolve 18 or suffers Ruin and is Finished, truly dead even in Sallowreach; each Helping raises the difficulty by 2)
AbilitiesThe hands may act separately: two Closing Touch attacks a round. Closing the World: once a scene it may touch a door, lamp or voice and end it. Wants: must close every open eye it sees, even a friend’s, even its own child’s.
Regrowthwhen Hunger fills it reaches the Brink and its touch spreads; the ground it stands on begins to Hush. At 12 it becomes a Hush, and a village goes silent.
SopClosing a living thing. 1d6 Hunger.
Dread2 / 3 when the face speaks and apologizes
EndIt can be Closed by another Closer, which the Court prefers, or killed outside Sallowreach, which the Court cannot allow anyone to see. The hands, severed, live on in a box, and are worth a fortune.

The Tallow-Saint

Wick Tallow renders the unclaimed into candles that feel themselves burn. A Tallow-Saint is a candle that did not want to be one. Sometimes, when a great many candles made from one family are burned together in one room, the tallow remembers itself, runs, and gathers on the floor into a figure of soft yellow wax five feet high, faceless, wicked through its crown and burning. It smells of mutton fat and singed hair. It drips as it walks, leaving a trail of puddles that harden into the shapes of footprints, then of hands. Its light is very steady. People in the room with one find they can read by it perfectly, and that the words on the page have changed into the names of the dead. It wants to be put out, and nothing put out stays out in Sallowreach. So it hunts for darkness and for breath to snuff it, and it presses its burning crown into the mouths of the living.

Tallow-Saint Threat 2 · Flesh 16 · Guard 11 · Attack +5 (burning embrace 3, Grapple 14; held targets take 2 fire each round) · Armor 2 (wax; blunt weapons deal only 1) · Dread 2 · Unending until its wick is pinched out (Hand + Filch 18 while Grappled with it); water hardens it for 2 rounds; Dark Sallowreach rooms make it act twice.

The Fatlands: The Crop That Stands Up

In the Fatlands the monsters are agricultural. Nothing there is anything but crop, and that includes what eats the crop. Fatlands horrors are warm, wet, slow, enormous and hungry, and the smell that precedes most of them is gravy.

The Laden Hill with a Mouth

Many of the best fields in the south are somebody’s great-grandmother. Most Seated Laden are quiet hills, warm to the touch, generous with barley. Some keep a mouth. Old Mother Rind is benign, more or less. Not all are. A hungry hill is a low green mound a hundred paces across, its turf rising and falling with slow breath, and in its side, at about the height of a cart, a mouth: lips of soft red loam, a tongue the size of a ploughshare, and teeth that were once teeth and are now stones, old roots, and the skulls of what it has eaten, pushed out through the gums like new growth. Its breath is hot and smells of ripe silage and stomach. It speaks, in the voice of the woman it was, and it is polite, and it is very, very hungry. It wants to be fed by its family, as is right. When its family stops coming, it calls out to passersby by the names of grandchildren. The ground around it is soft for a long way. The roots under that ground move.

The Hungry Hill — a Gut-Line Matriarch, Seated
AttributesHand 3 · Gut 10 · Lung 0 · Eye 3 · Tongue 4 · Caul 6

The Scarecrow of Low Tilth

Nobody put it up. It stands in the far field with its back to the village, and each Carving it is a few furrows closer. Last year someone saw it turn around. Pell Hogget’s tally does not attribute the Reaping in Low Tilth to the scarecrow, but he has noted that the missing were all last seen nearer its side of the field.

Up close it is a figure seven feet high, cross-armed on a stake that it does not need. Its coat is sacking. Its stuffing is not straw, though straw sticks out of it. Its head is a sack, tied at the neck, and the sack is damp, and it is warm, and if pressed it gives like a full stomach. Under the hat, where the face is painted, the paint is very old, and very good, and the face is smiling. When it moves, it moves only while nobody in the field is looking at it, and then very fast, and the sound of that is a dry, rushing crackle like a scythe through tall wheat. The taken are not found. In the following spring, the stuffing in the scarecrow’s arms has new fingernails in it.

The Scarecrow of Low Tilth — Nobody Put It Up

EndBurn it on its stake by daylight with every eye in the village on it. What runs out of the ashes is fat, and it screams in many voices. Next Carving there is a scarecrow in the far field, and nobody put it up.

The Toothed Field

Wheat with teeth in the ear has been a superior strain since 204 A.G., by ruling of the Board. A toothed field in its late Plenty is tall as a man, gold and red, and every ear is a small jaw of white milk-teeth set in a husk that clicks open and shut in the wind. On a still day it is quiet. On a windy one, a toothed field sounds like a crowd chewing. Harvesters wear leather to the shoulder. Anyone who falls in a toothed field in late Plenty is in serious trouble: the ears turn toward warmth like flowers to the sun, and every ear takes a nip, and there are millions of ears. Victims come out lacework, bleeding from a thousand pinpricks, and the wheat they fell in is the best of the crop that year, heavy and pink in the grain. Granny Cracknel says the teeth in a field that has fed well are adult teeth.

Toothed Field (per acre) Threat 2 · Flesh 40 · Guard 8 · Attack +5 (nipping 1 to everyone inside; every Helping adds a Bleed of 1 per round until bound) · Armor 0 · Dread 1 / 2 when the ears turn · Swarm; Rooted; fire spreads through it at a run and it screams; Lung rolls inside are Hard.

Two-Legged Cattle

Sal Trotter walks herds to market that the buyers call cattle. They are heavy, docile, and pinkish-white, with broad flat faces and soft lowing voices. On the road, when nobody watches, they stand up. Upright they are the height of a tall man, bellies swinging, forelegs tucked like hands, and they walk easily and well. They do not talk. They hum, sometimes, a hymn with a tune most Fatlanders know from childhood. Some have scars where a brand would be, and the scars are in the shape of letters. Nobody in the Renderers’ Union will say where the bloodstock comes from, but the Reaping takes people every Carving and the herds are larger every spring. Most cattle are harmless. A herd that has been mistreated, or that smells its own kind in a slaughterhouse, becomes a stampede on two legs, and it knows how to open gates.

Two-Legged Cattle (herd of 20) Threat 2 · Flesh 30 · Guard 11 · Attack +6 (trampling 4 to all in its path) · Armor 1 · Dread 1 / 3 when they stand up and one of them says a name · Swarm; a single beast is Flesh 14, Attack +4 (3), harmless unless cornered.

Rootkin

Tansy Lard dug up a root with her mother’s birthmark on it. She was not the first. Rootkin are what the Reaping leaves in the soil: swollen root vegetables the size of a sleeping child, pale and veined and warm, with features. Most are lumpen. Some are exact. Their eyes are closed. Pulled up, they flinch and leak a pinkish sap that smells of the person they resemble. Eaten, they are delicious and their eater dreams the dead person’s memories for a week. Left in the ground, they grow. A Rootkin bed left unharvested through a full year sends up shoots with hands on them, and those hands pull down whatever leans too close. The Cullmasters harvest Rootkin by night and sell them to the Renderers’ Union by weight.

Rootkin Bed Threat 1 · Flesh 20 · Guard 9 · Attack +5 (grasping shoots 2, Grapple 14, then dragged underground at 1 per round) · Armor 1 (soil) · Dread 2 / 3 when a character recognizes a face · Rooted; harvesting one is a Hard Labor roll and a Dread check.

The Reaping

The Reaping is not a monster. That is the Board’s official position, and it is technically correct: no single thing takes the Fatlands’ missing. The land does. On dusk in Carving, out in the far fields, the soil softens. The furrows deepen, slowly, so slowly a farmhand will not notice until her boots are below the surface. The rows of wheat lean in. The air thickens with the smell of fresh bread and fat. And then the ground opens, wetly, the way a mouth opens around a spoon, and closes again, and the furrow is smooth, and the crop in that furrow will be very good next year.

Run the Reaping as a hazard with a clock. Each character in a far field at dusk in Carving rolls Lung + Wayfaring each round against a rising difficulty (Routine 10, then Hard, then Grim, then Dire). Failure means they are held to the ankle, then the knee, then the waist; a fourth failure and they are gone. Allies can pull them free with a Gut + Labor roll at the same difficulty. Partaking for the Fatlands’ Gut-line, ironically, helps: the ground recognizes kin and loosens its grip for a round, though it costs Hunger as always. A Cullmaster’s assigned workers are marked with a strip of red cloth at the wrist. The ground knows the cloth. Remove it, and the difficulty drops by 4.

The Reaping has Dread 3 the first time it is seen to take someone, and Dread 4 when a character realizes the field is breathing in time with them.

Brinehollow: What the Sea Left Behind

Brinehollow’s horrors are patient, heavy and courteous. They press. Many have Tide, and all of them smell of a harbour at low water: weed, salt, rot and cold iron.

The Tenanted

A Tenanted is not hostile. That is what makes it so hard. It walks out of the surf weeks after its Calling, heavier, calm, with the same face and the same memories, and someone else looking out. It knows your name, your nickname, the way you take your tea. It is kinder than the person was. Its skin is cool and faintly grey, its hands are always damp, and its breath, if you are close enough, smells of deep water, a clean mineral cold. Its weight is wrong: floorboards creak under a slight Tenanted girl as if under a cart. When it is angered, which is rare, it does not raise its voice. It presses. The air in the room thickens, ears pop, windows bow, and a man who has crossed a Tenanted judge has been found with his ribs gently folded inward, as if the sea had leaned on him.

The Tenanted — Someone Else Looking Out

EndCut it and it bleeds seawater by the gallon, more than its body can hold. Drained dry it lies down, an empty skin. Somewhere in the Trench, it is said, the water it held goes on.

Ribwalkers

On the Uncovered, among the leather weed-forests and the wrecks standing upright, there are things with too many ribs. Salvagers call them Ribwalkers. A Ribwalker is a cage of long curved bones, thirty or forty pairs, opening and closing like a slow bellows, mounted on legs that might once have been the ribs of something else. There is no head. There is meat inside the cage, a grey sack that pulses, and there is usually a salvager’s boot or two. They move toward water, any water, at a creaking stalk, and they open their ribs wide over anything wet and alive and close them, and squeeze, and drink. The squeezed come out flat, dry as leather, with their bail-buckets still on their belts. Some salvagers swear the Ribwalkers are what the Admiralty’s fallen sailors become. Hask Tarn will not say.

Ribwalker Threat 3 · Flesh 22 · Guard 13 · Attack +7 (rib-cage closing 4, Grapple 18; held targets lose 2 Flesh per round as the water is pressed out of them) · Armor 3 (bone lattice) · Dread 2 / 3 when it closes on someone · Tide 4; drawn to a character who has just bailed.

The Dowager Below

Lady Ondine Vasht lives in the flooded cellars of the palace in Lowmark, and the cellars have had to be extended twice. She is far into the Course and has not been seen whole in years. What can be seen of her, through the black water by lamplight, is a vast grey shape folded into the vaults, skin like a drowned sail, hair that drifts across the floor of three cellars, and eyes the size of serving platters, dark and wide and wet, which open one at a time in different rooms. She is still a grandmother. She still has opinions about the prince’s marriage. She speaks through the water: the surface of every cistern in the palace trembles with her words. She would like her grandson to come down. She has been asking for years. The servants who go down to feed her return with less of their breath every time, and some do not return.

The Indoor Tide

In every cellar in Brinehollow, water rises twice a day and drains away. An Indoor Tide is when it does not stop. It comes up the stairs at night, black and cold, bringing kelp and silt and small crabs and the smell of an open harbor. It rises through the kitchen, through the parlor, up the bedroom stairs to where the family sleeps anchored, and it does not care that the house is a mile from the shore. It has a current. It pulls toward the west wall. People found after an Indoor Tide are found tidily, laid face down on the west side of rooms, lungs full, hands reaching. Treat it as a hazard: each round the water rises a step, Lung + Athletics rolls to move against the current start at Hard and rise to Dire; anchored characters are safe until it reaches their mouths. Lung-line characters feel the Pull 14 every round. The Tide has Dread 2 as it rises and Dread 3 when someone sees a shape swimming through the drowned parlor that was not there when the water came in.

The Called Procession

The Deepening walks in willingly, in procession, with lanterns. Sometimes the Called do too, without the lanterns: twenty, forty, a hundred people in nightclothes walking west at night in perfect silence, eyes open, bleeding brine from the nose, singing very low the same tune the Uncovered sings. They are not hostile. They will not stop. Anyone who stands in their way is walked over. Anyone with a Lung-line Cut who watches them pass must roll against the Pull.

Called Procession (40) Threat 2 · Flesh 40 · Guard 10 · Attack +5 (trampling, grasping 2, Grapple 14: the grabbed are carried along) · Armor 0 · Dread 2 / 3 on seeing someone known among them · Swarm; Pull 14 on Lung-lines; roping individuals out takes a Gut + Labor 14 roll each.

The Vigil: What Happens When You Close Your Eyes

The Vigil’s horrors arrive in blinks. Many of them happen, or are seen, in the second between one waking moment and the next. All of them are worse for an exhausted character: a character who has not taken rouse in the last hour suffers −2 on Dread checks in this section.

The Blink-Killer

Inspector Hale Grimmer has forty cases. The method is the same in each. A blink-killer is an ordinary citizen of the Vigil (a cook, a nudger, a clerk) who blinks for two seconds, mid-sentence, standing at a market stall, and in those two seconds goes to the long room with the eye, and something there uses them. They come back holding a knife they did not pick up, standing behind a stranger, and the stranger is open from hip to collarbone in one perfectly straight line, and the blink-killer does not remember any of it. The cut is the same each time: the line a midwife or a butcher would use to open a body for inspection. Blink-killers are not monsters. They are anyone. That is the horror. The stat below is for the second in which they are something else.

The Blink-Killer — Two Seconds Under

Dread2 on the murder / 3 when a character realizes they themselves have lost two seconds
EndKeep everyone awake. The Wakers’ needles are the only defense the city has.

A Seeming Made Solid

After enough waking, everyone hallucinates, and when a whole street sees the same thing, it is entered as news. When a whole street sees the same thing for long enough, it becomes true. A Seeming made solid is a hallucination that has been agreed on by too many exhausted minds: a horse with a man’s face walking down the Slope, a staircase that goes on past the roof, a tall figure laying a table in the street. It has weight, smell and heat. It does what the people imagining it fear it will do. It is precisely as strong as their certainty and it smells like rouse, burnt and bitter, because it is made of their attention.

Seeming Made Solid Threat 4 · Flesh equal to 2 × the number of witnesses · Guard 14 · Attack +7 (it does whatever it was imagined doing; damage 4) · Armor 0 · Dread 3 · it gains +1 to all rolls for every frightened witness; characters who succeed at Eye + Reckoning 18 can disbelieve it aloud, and each disbeliever strips 4 Flesh from it; if no one is looking at it, it stops existing until someone does.

Sleepwalking Counted

Sixty thousand beds, numbered, in rows, completely silent. The Counted breathe in time. In the last year, some have begun to get up. A sleepwalking Counted rises with its eyes closed, its lips moving, and walks in the direction the eye in the dream faces. It does not wake. It cannot be woken. It is warm, unaged since the night it lay down, nightclothes faded to cobweb, and wherever it walks people around it begin to yawn, then to nod, then to blink. Matron Dorm sends them back to their beds with an orderly on each arm. Odile Farthing’s son, in bed 40,112, has grown to a man’s size and is smiling. When he walks, he walks with his arms open.

Sleepwalking Counted Threat 3 · Flesh 16 · Guard 12 · Attack +5 (embrace 2, Grapple 16; a held character must pass Caul + Resolve 14 each round or blink) · Armor 0 · Dread 2 / 3 when its lips form a character’s name · Fray Aura 14 (as yawning); cannot be harmed by pain; returning it to its bed ends its walk.

The Waker Gone Mad

The Wakers’ job is to hurt people for their own good, and they are skilled after three centuries. A Waker gone mad has decided that nobody is safe, ever, unless they are in pain. He is usually an old Waker, on triple rouse, lidless or near it from long effort, his eyes gone red and cracked and leaking. He carries a rattle and a sheaf of long steel needles. He has stopped distinguishing between a citizen who is nodding and a citizen who might nod later. He goes door to door at the third bell. He pins people’s eyelids open with fish-hooks. He drives needles under nails so that no one in the house can doze. In his cellar there are people he has been keeping awake for weeks, tied in standing frames, weeping and hallucinating, and he feeds them rouse by the spoon and sings to them.

The Waker Gone Mad — For Your Own Good

Dread2 / 3 on finding the cellar
EndHe will kill himself with rouse within a month. The question is how many people he keeps awake before his heart stops.

The Yawn

On Yawn days, the Wakers double their patrols. The Yawn is not a creature; it is contagion. Lukas Marre once put down a market square. When a yawn is spreading through a crowd it moves like a rumor, mouth to mouth, and every person who catches it must roll Caul + Resolve 14 or blink. In a crowd of the exhausted the first blink becomes ten, the ten become a hundred, and the hundred do not all come back. Treat a Yawn as a hazard with Dread 1 that becomes Dread 3 the moment a character sees someone fall and not rise. The Glass House exists because of it.

Cradlewrack: What Comes Through

Nothing in Cradlewrack is born right, and it is all healthy. Cradlewrack horrors are new, wet and determined. Many are drawn toward each other, toward the Sill or toward the Dilation, and they are getting bigger.

Wandering Parts

A single living hand. A warm ear. A length of spine that crawls. The Parts are born healthy and drawn toward each other, and when they are not caught by the Attendance’s knife or the Assemblers’ sacks, they wander. They move in the night, at the speed of a crawling infant, through doors that drift open: a hand walking on its fingertips, a pair of lungs that inflate and deflate to roll themselves along, a jaw that pulls itself forward by its teeth. They are warm and blood-pink and smell of milk and iron. They seek each other, and when two fit, they join with a wet click and a seam that heals in an hour. A cluster that has found six or seven partners is called a Gathered, and it is the size of a dog and the shape of no animal, and it is hungry, and it wants the parts it is missing. It will take them from whoever has them.

Parts (handful) Threat 1 · Flesh 3 · Guard 12 · Attack +3 (clutch, bite 1) · Armor 0 · Dread 1 / 2 when a hand holds yours · they pass any door or lock.

Gathered Threat 3 · Flesh 20 · Guard 13 · Attack +6 (grasp and tear 3, Grapple 16; on a held target with two Helpings, it takes a part: the character suffers an Injury from the Mangling table and the Gathered gains 5 Flesh) · Armor 0 · Dread 3 · it grows each scene it is left alive.

The Refused

The Attendance’s knife is called the Second Opinion, and there is no appeal from it. Except sometimes, as Sabeth Thorne found, the knife hesitates. A Refused is a born-grown thing that was meant to be cut and was not, and that has lived since in hiding, and has grown up knowing what it was supposed to be. It may look like a tall woman with a seam across her throat, or a man of thirty born mid-stride with a second face asleep in his chest. It knows it was judged. It remembers the midwife’s face. Refused are clever, careful, and very often kind, until they meet a midwife. Then they settle the account.

Fenn's Get

Josiah Fenn, a shepherd, labored for three days and delivered something that stood up, looked at him, and walked out of the door. He has followed its tracks for eight years, and they are getting larger. Fenn’s Get is twelve feet tall now. It walks the high red hills on legs too long, with a lamb’s soft white face on a man’s long skull, and its wool is matted with blood from the flocks it lies down among. It is not cruel. It is newborn and enormous, and it does not understand why things break when it holds them. It has a shepherd’s crook it has made from a whole ash tree. It has been seen, at dusk, sitting at a distance from Fenn’s camp, watching its father, and making the bleating sound that lambs make for their mother.

Crownings

The earth dilates, slowly, over weeks, into a perfect round opening, and people gather at the rim to see what comes up. A crowning is a hazard, a festival and a monster’s birth in one. The rim is soft, red, wet, warm as flesh; the hole is perfectly round and descends into darkness that pulses. The air above it is humid and smells of iron and birth-water. Every pang, the crowning widens a hand’s breadth. Then, at the end, something comes up. Roll on the table below when it does, and run the crowd. The rim itself is Dread 2 on sight; the moment of emergence is Dread 4.

d6What is born from the crowning
1Waters: a flood of warm salt fluid fills the valley to the rooftops in an hour.
2A house: whole, furnished, with a family at table who believe they have always lived there.
3A Gathered of three hundred Parts, hungry for the Assemblers’ figure.
4A hill, which stands up, which is a person. Use the Hungry Hill, Lung 3, and mobile.
5A door in a frame, standing alone, ajar. It is identical to the Sill’s.
6Nothing. The hole closes. Three days later, every pregnant woman for ten miles goes into labor at once.

Doorborn

A locked chest once gave birth. So did a well. Doorborn are the offspring of thresholds: thin grey things with jointed limbs like hinges, born from any door, gate or lid that has been shut too long. They come out at night into a sleeping house, unfolding from a cupboard or a bricked room, and they open things: windows, cradles, mouths, eyes, wounds, chests. They do it with care, with long fingers like keys. Victims are found opened neatly along every seam a midwife knows, still alive, and very surprised. Agnes Latch’s doors keep them in for up to nineteen days.

Doorborn Threat 4 · Flesh 12 · Guard 16 · Attack +6 (opening fingers 3; with two Helpings, a held door, lock, or a character’s oldest scar is opened, Bleed 1 per round) · Armor 1 · Dread 3 · passes any door; cannot cross a threshold that has been knocked on and answered from the far side.

Oathen: What Was Said

In Oathen, the monsters are made of words and the people the words broke. Nearly every horror here can be avoided by saying nothing. The difficulty, as every Oathener knows, is that silence is also a kind of answer.

The Forsworn Mob

The Breakdowns are full of people whose bodies keep the record of their sins: legs folded backwards for a fled duty, hands off at the wrist for a short measure, ribs opened outward like a book for a broken marriage vow. Most of them are no danger to anyone. A Forsworn mob is what happens when a Clausewright’s ruling goes against the Breakdowns once too often. They come up the canyon stairs in a mass of crutches and wheeled boards and open chests, slow, loud (the only loud thing in Tacit), shouting plain words because they have nothing left to break, and they drag down whoever made the promise they blame. They know where every breakable promise is. They shout their victims’ oaths back at them, verbatim, and wait to see what snaps.

Forsworn Mob (30) Threat 3 · Flesh 36 · Guard 11 · Attack +6 (crutches, clubs, bare broken hands 3) · Armor 0 · Dread 2 · Swarm; once a scene the mob may shout a character’s own past promise back at them (Tongue + Clause 18 or the character must act at once as if renewing it).

The Living Echo

An oath repeated is an oath renewed, and a canyon will repeat anything. Most echoes die. A living echo does not. It is a sworn phrase trapped in deep rock long enough to have learned to move. It travels down gorges after people, riding the stone, faint at first, a voice two bends behind; then nearer; then from the wall just beside one’s ear, in the voice of whoever first swore it, often dead for centuries. Anyone who hears it whole is bound by it. Halvar Stane hunts them. The one in Sworn Gorge is the oldest, and he has made out two words.

A Living Echo — the Words in the Rock
