BodyFlesh 20 (it has no body; damage is done by noise, see End) · Guard 18 · Armor special · Threat 6
AttacksRepetition +11 against Tongue + Clause (Binding; a character who fails is sworn to the echo’s oath, which the GM writes, and breaks as an Oathener breaks if they ever act against it)
AbilitiesRides Stone: it moves as fast as sound through rock; cannot cross open air or soft soil. Every Repeat: each round, it may Bind another listener. Characters who stop their ears entirely (wax, cloth, Hard Endure) are immune, and deaf.
Dread2 / 4 when it speaks in a character’s own voice
EndEcho-Wardens kill echoes with silence: they collapse a gorge, pack its walls with felt, or shout a contradicting oath into it and take the break themselves. Blades and arrows do nothing. Loud counter-speech deals 1d6 damage per round to it and to the speaker.

A Sayer Unbitted

Lady Imre Dath says one sentence a year. She has begun to write her own. A Sayer is a Tongue-line in the last stage, and what they say is. A Sayer unbitted, without the gold, is the most dangerous creature on the Table that is still, technically, a person. Their mouths are usually a ruin from decades of the bit: lips scarred into a permanent shape, teeth filed or missing, tongue thick and pale. They speak slowly, savouring it, because they have not been allowed to speak in years. Each word lands like a hammer on an anvil, with a sound in the bones. Things they describe become so. They are usually frightened. Fear makes them say what they are afraid of.

A Sayer Unbitted — What Is Said, Is
AttributesHand 1 · Gut 2 · Lung 2 · Eye 4 · Tongue 9 · Caul 6
Cut & RegrowthCut 5 (Tongue-line) · Regrowth 12 (Seated in speech) · Hunger 7
SkillsClause 6, Persuade 4, Lore 4, Resolve 4
BodyFlesh 9 · Guard 12 · Armor 0 · Threat 6
Attacksnone needed
AbilitiesSaying: once per round, the Sayer speaks one sentence. If it is about the world, it is true from that moment. If it is about a character, that character may roll Tongue + Clause 22 (Dire) to wriggle out on a technicality the Sayer did not cover; otherwise it is true. A Sayer cannot unsay. Each Saying costs 1 Hunger; at 10 Hunger, the Sayer’s next sentence happens to an entire valley.
Wantsto speak, to finish sentences, to be heard.
Dread3 when the bit comes off / 5 on hearing it undo something that cannot be undone
EndRe-bit it. A bit fitted by Garl Tome holds. Getting close enough means speaking to it first, and it will answer.

The Oath-Made

A man once swore to his wife, “I promise you a son.” Ilan exists anyway. The Oath-Made are people created by promises: sons sworn into being, soldiers promised to a cause, a lover sworn to come back that came back. They are real, warm and often loving. They also exist only for as long as the promise is kept, and they know it, at some deep level, and when the promise begins to fail (the one who swore it dies, or wavers, or forgets) they begin to fade. Fading Oath-Made become frantic: they cling, they demand, they extract new promises at knifepoint from anyone near. A fading Oath-Made who gets a stranger to swear “I will look after you” lives on, bound to that stranger. Forever.

Fading Oath-Made Threat 3 · Flesh 12 · Guard 14 (hard to see clearly) · Attack +5 (desperate grip 2, Grapple 16) · Armor 0 · Dread 2 / 3 when a character realizes they cannot remember its face · Persuade 6 to extract a promise; if it succeeds, the character is bound to it as by an oath.

The Defaulted Surety

Ona Fell can survive one more default. A Surety carries other people’s oaths in their body for a fee. A Surety who exceeds their limit breaks all at once, every carried oath snapping in a single afternoon: bones, joints, ribs, a heart, a tongue, two hundred breaks in a minute. Most die. A few are left standing, a twisted heap of folded and refolded limbs that should not be able to stand, crawling in a way that hurts to watch, and they have nothing more to lose. They hunt the original swearers whose debts they paid, every one, by name. They cannot be bound by oath any more. There is no room left in them.

Defaulted Surety Threat 4 · Flesh 22 · Guard 13 · Attack +7 (grasping broken limbs 3, Grapple 18) · Armor 1 · Dread 3 · immune to Binding; knows the name of every oath it carried; a character whose oath it held suffers −4 to all rolls against it.

The Fast: The Host and Its Table

The Fast has no Regrowth. It has a whole god, unhoused, laying tables. Its horrors do not attack, mostly. They offer. Every entry in this section has Hosting, and every one is best survived by saying “No, thank you” three times.

Orrum's Tables

They appear in empty houses, at crossroads, in the middle of a field at dusk: a table of old dark wood, cloth laid white, candles lit, places set, the food steaming. The smell arrives first, a mile off: baking bread, roast fat, apples in butter, everything one’s mother ever cooked on a feast day. It is warm around a table, gently warm, the warmth of a kitchen after a long walk. There is a chair pulled out. Lately there is a card at the place with a name on it, spelled correctly. Treat a table as a hazard with Hosting 18. Any character who smells a table rolls Caul + Resolve 14 or moves toward it. Any who sees their own place card rolls Dread 3. Any who sits rolls Caul + Resolve 22 to rise again; Lent Ashby is the only one known to have managed it. Tablebreakers smash tables with axes before anyone can sit: a table has Flesh 20, Guard 0 and Armor 2, and as it breaks it bleeds gravy and its candles cry out like children. A table smashed by a character with any godsign in them adds 2 Hunger, because the god inside wanted that food.

The Seated

The Seated remain at table for decades, eating from empty plates, smiling, alive long past any natural span. They are skeletal and radiant. Their clothes have rotted to rags around them; their skin is paper over bone; their forks move. They are perfectly sane, and they want company. Brother Hallow Crust describes each course in detail, the soups, the roasts, the jellies trembling in their moulds, and people who listen too long pull out a chair. The Seated never attack. They invite. They are very good at it.

The Seated Threat 5 (Persuade) · Flesh 4 · Guard 6 · Attack none · Armor 0 · Dread 2 / 3 when one of them is someone known · Hosting 18: describing a course is a Persuade +11 roll against the listener’s Caul + Resolve; failure costs 1 Fray and three failures pull out a chair. Lifting one from its seat kills it, gently, still smiling.

Welcome Ardent, the Steward

He walks a mile ahead of Orrum, laying the tables. He was the first of the Unfed to accept, six hundred years ago, and the only guest who was offered a position. He looks like a tall, thin, tired man of fifty in a waiter’s long apron, gravy-stained, with a cloth over his arm and very clean white gloves. His smile is genuine and exhausted. He smells of bread and old candles. He does not fight. He sets places, folds napkins, writes place cards in a beautiful hand, and asks politely whether you will be joining the Host this evening. He would like, very much, to be relieved. He has begun to look for a replacement.

Welcome Ardent — the Steward
AttributesHand 4 · Gut 3 · Lung 5 · Eye 5 · Tongue 6 · Caul 7
Cut & RegrowthCut none (he was never fed a god; he was hired by one) · no Hunger · no Regrowth
SkillsPersuade 6, Craft 5 (setting a table), Lore 6, Instinct 6, Wayfaring 6
BodyFlesh 30 · Guard 21 · Armor 0 · Threat 7
Attacksnone. He does not fight. A character who attacks him finds their blow lands on a table that was not there a moment before.
AbilitiesHosting 22. The Card: he can write any character’s name on a place card; that character feels the Pull 18 toward the nearest table every night until the card is burned. Ahead of the Host: Orrum is always a mile behind him. Cannot Die While Employed. Wants: a successor. He will offer the position to the character who refuses him most gracefully.
Dread2 / 4 when he speaks a character’s mother’s name
EndNone. His contract can be negotiated. Jessamy Quill has been asked to witness it. She has not yet said yes.

The Host

Orrum has no stats. Nobody living has seen it clearly and returned whole. The descriptions agree only that it is very tall, that it stoops under doorways, and that it is warm. It does not attack. It hosts. Run the Host’s approach as a sequence of signs, each a scene or more apart. Each sign is a Dread check of rising difficulty, and at each sign the characters may still leave.

SignWhat the characters perceiveDread
1Company: frost melting in a line across a field; the smell of bread with no source1
2Chimneys smoking in empty houses; a hearth already lit where they mean to shelter2
3A table, laid, with their names; Welcome Ardent bowing in the road3
4A tall shape stooping under the lintel of a house a field away, looking in4
5It is in the room. It is warm. It pulls out a chair.5

At the fifth sign, any character who has accepted anything in the Fast must sit. Others must refuse three times aloud, each a Caul + Resolve roll at Dire 22. A character who refuses all three times and does not thank it is left alone, and the Host, very gently, sets their place anyway, for next time. Do not let the players kill it. There is nothing to kill. Spare Tolland has seen it stop and wait for him to catch up, and has come to think it is lonely, and that is the most dangerous thing anyone has ever said about it.

The Lit House

Never enter a house where the hearth is already lit. A Lit House is the Host’s ambush: a ruin that, at dusk, has its windows glowing, its door ajar, its fire crackling and a kettle on. Inside, everything is warm, clean and laid out, and the door does not open from within once a guest has crossed the threshold until they have eaten. The walls sweat butter. The floors creak with a sound like a stomach. The rooms rearrange themselves so every corridor leads back to the kitchen. Hosting 18 to resist eating each hour; Dread 2 on entering, 3 when a character finds the bones of earlier guests tidily stacked in the larder, clean and polished, every one with a napkin.

Human Adversaries

Most blood spilled on the Table is spilled by people. The templates below each give a quick line for the rank and file and a full stat block for a veteran or leader. Adjust Cut to the land: a Netwatch sergeant is a Lung-line commoner, a Second Table diner is whatever the highest Cut of their country is. Remember that every human with a Cut can Partake, and that a desperate soldier will.

The Seated Gods

No land has reached a full Seating. Three are close. This section is for the night one of them gets there.

When a Regrowth completes, the god does not return whole. A god eaten by ten thousand mouths and scattered through six centuries of blood comes back as a Seated fragment: a portion of itself, wearing a person or a place as a body, and growing. It is enough. A fragment of a Provider is the largest thing that has walked the Table since the Night of Seven Tables, and its arrival ends the campaign as it was. What follows is not a fight. The entries below give a fragment’s Seat (what it wears), its Reach (how far it extends, and how fast it grows), its Presence (what happens to everyone in reach, each round or each day), its Hands (the creatures from this chapter that now act for it), and What Can Be Done. None has Flesh. Every one is Dread 5, and Fray Aura 22, and anyone of its land’s Cut within its Reach feels the Pull 22 every round.

Ossel Seated — the Closing Hand
Seatthe Hand-lines, all at once; the Mortuary Court’s chamber becomes a Hush with a figure in it whose hands are folded.
ReachDunmere Hush and every other Hush join; grows a mile a day across Sallowreach.
Presenceeverything in Reach finishes. The Kept lie down by the thousand, glad. The living who fail their Dread check stop, mid-breath, and are done. Sound ends. Then the fen begins to end, and the fog, and the land.
HandsHush-walkers, Undone Closers, every Finisher.
What Can Be Donecarry people out. Every Kept who can be got across the border before the Hush arrives drops dead at once, which is at least an ending they chose. Pim Sorrel may be able to ask it to wait.
Ummer Seated — the Laden
SeatChairman Obb Tullow, rooted through his cart, swelling until Sated is built on his shoulders.
Reachevery field in the Fatlands, and every barrel of their meat on the Rim Road.
Presencethe Reaping all at once, by day and by night. The soil takes anyone standing on it who fails Lung + Wayfaring 22. Everyone who has eaten Fatlands meat in the last year, anywhere, feels Fatlands Hunger: +1 Hunger per day, and the Feast Want.
HandsHungry Hills, the Scarecrow, Rootkin by the million, the two-legged cattle, all standing up.
What Can Be Donestop eating. The Thin have practiced. Wren Hollowell feels no hunger at all and may walk where no one else can.
Dromm Seated — the Fathom
Seatthe Tenanted, every one, standing up in courtrooms across the land and walking west; and the Dowager Below, who rises.
Reachthe Trench, then the Uncovered, then Lowmark’s nineteen miles of pier. The sea comes back, all at once, from inside the people who were holding it.
Presencepressure. All rolls in Reach −4. Each round, every character with a Lung-line Cut must bail (Gut + Endure 18) or drown on dry land. The Called number in the tens of thousands.
HandsRibwalkers, the Called Procession, the Indoor Tide in every house on the Table that has ever drunk Dry Jonah’s tonic.
What Can Be Doneget high and get inland. Dagna Hull’s Follow may survive the water’s return. Father Ebb says the chain is not what holds him.
Iss Seated — the Lidded
SeatAveline Morne, the Sleeper in Bed One, sitting up. The eye in the long room opens.
Reachthe Dormitory, then the Vigil, then everyone on the Table who has ever slept, which is everyone.
Presencesleep. Every character must roll Caul + Resolve 22 every hour or blink, and a blink now lasts until the Seated fragment is satisfied. The Counted wake together, sixty thousand of them, breathing in time, and walk.
Handsthe Counted, blink-killers in every street, Seemings made solid wherever the exhausted gather.
What Can Be Donestay awake for as long as it takes. Nobody knows how long that is. Sallowreach’s Kept do not sleep. Castellan Dray’s terrible proposal may become the only sane one on the Table.
Vey Seated — the Opening
Seatthe land. Cradlewrack’s highlands are delivered of something out of the Dilation, as the Sill’s door swings open, and the Assemblers’ figure stands up with a voice and a left hand.
Reachevery threshold on the Table. Every door opens.
Presencebirth. Every character must roll Gut + Endure 18 each day or go into labor with something that is not a child. Wounds reopen at dawn. Locks, seals and graves fail; things begin.
Handsthe Gathered, Doorborn, Fenn’s Get (now the size of a hill), and whatever the crowning produced.
What Can Be Donethe Barren Order’s answer is to begin nothing. Ambrose, the Eldest Infant, says that when he reaches the cradle it will be time, and may know for what.
Tolm Seated — the Witness
Seata Sayer, unbitted at last, speaking without stopping; or the Ledger, four miles of carved vows, beginning to read itself aloud.
Reacheverywhere a word in Oathen has carried, which means every treaty and every Rim Road Company contract on the Table.
Presenceevery word binds. Every thought binds. Characters with any Tongue-line Cut cannot think a lie without breaking. Every contract sworn before Jessamy Quill comes due at once, with interest, in the body of each signatory.
Handsliving echoes, every Forsworn, the Defaulted, and the Rain, which falls now only on those who have kept their word.
What Can Be Donesay nothing. Cassian Wry can lie and stay whole; in a world that has become a promise, a liar is the only free man left.

Orrum has no Seated fragment. It was never eaten. It is whole, and it is coming. Some scholars of the Table have begun to ask why a god with all its strength would spend six centuries laying places, and for whom. The Hallowboard table has eight sides. One side, the Hostwatch reports, is always laid, and always empty.

Why You Cannot Fight a God

The players will want to. Tell them, in the fiction, why they cannot. The Providers did not fight when they were eaten; that is recorded everywhere and explained nowhere. Returning, they do not fight either. A Seated god is not hostile any more than weather is hostile. It is a condition of the world reasserting itself. Its Presence affects everyone in Reach without a roll to hit. It has no Flesh to reduce. Attacking a fragment’s Seat (cutting down Obb Tullow, smashing Aveline Morne’s bed) is possible and accomplishes exactly what killing a single fold of a flooding river would.

What player characters can do is choose how the world meets the god. Every campaign-ending threat above should be run as a set of choices, each with a terrible cost.

  • Refuse it. The Fast’s answer: accept nothing it offers, and endure. This works, partly, for the godless, and for those who can bear starvation. For everyone with a Cut, refusal means fighting the god in their own blood every round of their lives. Each refusal costs Hunger. Hunger fills.
  • Feed it. Every god has a Sop. Feed the Sop on a national scale (the Cullmasters’ answer, the Second Helping’s, the Finishers’) and the fragment quiets. It grows, too.
  • Bind it. Go to Oathen and have it sworn. A god’s word outlives the god; the Kept Rain proves it. A Seated fragment can be negotiated with, through a Sayer, in a Clausewright’s language, before Jessamy Quill. It will keep its word. The question is what it asks in exchange.
  • Carry it out. The rules of a land stop at its border. A Seat that can be moved (a person, a child, a hand) can be carried across the Rim Road. Then the god is somewhere new, and its rules come with it.
  • Eat it again. The Second Table’s answer. It worked once. It bought six hundred and forty-one years. The party that eats a Seated fragment becomes the next Seat, and their children carry it, and the Long Grace begins again.
  • Hide. The Providers held still once, and nobody knows why. Characters who ask that question loudly enough, in the right places, may find out what a god is afraid of. That is a matter for the Secrets chapter, and for the GM.

Roll when the characters travel, camp, or linger too long in one place. Each table is weighted toward the uncanny; a GM who wants a quieter road should reroll results above 7.

The Last Word on Monsters

Every land on the Table believes another land’s curse might cure its own. Monsters travel along the same road the cures do. A Tenanted judge can turn up in Sated. A Hush-walker can stand at the border and watch the living cross. The Host has been seen at crossroads in three lands already.

Use this chapter as a menu, not a map. Everything here was once fed, and everything here is still hungry, and the Grace is ending.

Part Four
Setting the Table
For the Carver alone: running horror, building campaigns, the secrets of the world, and an adventure to begin with.
Chapter 16

The Carver's Knife

At a feast on the Table, the one who carves decides who eats first, who gets the best of it, and who is served the part that nobody wants. It is a position of honor. It is never a position of love.
— Dame Suet Marrable, to a new Carver at the Unending Dinner

From the commonplace book of a Rim Road storyteller, found at Thimble Cross after the snows.

They always ask me for the one about the god that smiled. I tell it the same way every time. I lower the lamp. I let the fire burn down until their faces are only the parts the coals can reach: noses, wet eyes, the shine on the lips. I wait until somebody coughs, and then I wait for them to be ashamed of having coughed.

The trick is not the monster. Anyone can describe a monster. The trick is to describe the kitchen first. The bread on the board, the knife beside it, the knot in the wood under the bread that looks like an eye. The child asleep in the corner with her thumb in her mouth. You make them love the kitchen. Then, when the knife moves on its own, they do not scream because of the knife. They scream because of the bread, and the knot, and the child.

I have told that story four hundred times. Last winter, on Tablenight, I told it in this very room, and when I got to the end there was a place laid at the back table that nobody had laid, and a chair pulled out, and a card with my name on it.

I am writing this down because I have decided not to tell it again.

This chapter is for the Carver: the player who runs the game. It explains how to run horror on the Table, how to use the rules without letting them get in the way, how to build a campaign around the Regrowth, and how to make sure everyone at the table leaves wanting to come back, even though their characters will not.

The Carver's Duties

You have five jobs. Everything else is technique.

  • Describe the world so the Guests can see, smell and taste it.
  • Play everyone else: the Regent and the beggar, the god and the dog.
  • Apply the rules fairly, and know when to put them away.
  • Keep the table safe, with Lines, Veils and the Grace, and with your own attention.
  • Make the world move. The Grace is ending. The gods are growing back whether the Guests act or not. Show them the clock.

Running Horror on the Table

Make Them Love the Kitchen

Horror is the violation of something cared for. If the Guests do not care about anything, nothing can be violated. Spend the first half of every story making them care: a warm inn, a Kept grandmother who tells filthy jokes through her stitched jaw, a Fatlands cook who sings while she skims the drip from the stockpot, a Netwatch sergeant who calls his patrol “my ducks”. Let the Guests eat, rest, joke and plan. Let Who Waits at Home write them letters. Then take it away.

All Five Senses, and Then One More

The Table is a world of bodies. Describe it through the body. For every horror you run, ask:

  • What does it smell like? The sweet wrongness of the Breath in Sallowreach; the rendering-yard stink of the Belch; salt and kelp and the cold-mineral smell of a drowned man’s lungs; lamp-smoke and sour rouse-sweat in the Vigil; iron, wet clay and birth-water in Cradlewrack; the hot stone and dry silence of Oathen; and, in the Fast, bread, always fresh bread, from nowhere.
  • What does it sound like? Flies in fronts. Teeth in the wheat. Bailing coughs at dawn. Bells every quarter hour. The pang, felt through the floor. The crack of a body breaking to match a broken word.
  • What does it feel like? Warm ground that rises and falls. Cold grey fingers with one joint too many. A floor that slopes so you cannot rest.
  • What does it taste like? Everything on the Table is food, or was. Make them taste it.
  • What does it look like? Last. Sight is the least frightening sense, because it is the one we trust.
  • And the sixth sense, the god: what does the Guest’s own blood do, in the presence of this? Does their Hunger stir? Does their Tooth itch? Does the thing in front of them seem, horribly, like family?

Gore With a Purpose

This book is graphic, and your table may want it graphic. That is allowed and it can be powerful. The rule is: gore should always carry meaning. A body opened on the Table is never just a body. It tells the Guests what the god wants, what the land costs, what was done and by whom. A Mangling is a story in a wound. When you describe the bowel sliding free of a Netwatch officer’s belly, make sure the Guests also see the wedding knot tied into his anchoring rope.

When the table’s appetite is satisfied, cut away. Restraint is a tool too. The door closing on the Cullmaster’s dusk shift, and the sound of the wheat moving in a field where there is no wind, can be worse than anything you say.

Tragedy, Not Spectacle

Some of this book’s horrors are deliberately human: suicide, contagious despair, kin-slaying, the murder of the helpless. Run them as tragedy. That means:

  • The camera stays on the people left behind: the cut rope on the bed, the extra place at the table, the note in a careful hand, the neighbors who stop calling names through the wall.
  • Nobody is a punchline, and nobody’s death is a reward.
  • The god benefits. Every loss is a little more of it in the world. That is the horror, more than the act.
  • You never describe how. You describe after.

The Clock Is Always Running

The Grace is ending. Use clocks: the Cradlewrack interval shortening, the Vigil’s empty beds, the Pantry’s four months of grain, the Brinehollow waterline, the Sallowreach Hushes spreading toward the Hand-line estates. Write each one on a card where the Guests can see it. Advance them between sessions whether the Guests act or not. Horror is helplessness, and the slow tick of a number going down is helplessness made visible.

No Rescue, but Many Mercies

The Table cannot be saved. That is the premise. But individual people can be: for a night, a season, a life. A Guest who cannot stop the Reaping can still get one family across the border before the dusk shift. A Guest who cannot cure the Vigil can still sit up with a dying nudger through her last hour. Those small mercies are the only victories the Long Grace offers, and they should feel enormous. Do not take them away cheaply. Take them away expensively, much later, when the Guests have forgotten to guard them.

Using the Rules

When to Call for Dread

Call for a Dread check the first time the Guests encounter a horror, and whenever something they love is harmed. Do not call for Dread so often that Fray becomes accounting. If a Guest is a Seamer, corpses do not frighten her; what frightens her is a corpse that thanks her. Calibrate to the character.

Pacing Hunger

The Tooth is the most important choice a player makes. Make it tempting: put the Guests in positions where +3.5 is the difference between saving someone and failing them. Make it visible: describe the god coming forward every time they Partake. Make it count: when Hunger fills and Regrowth rises, stop the game for a moment and describe the change together. A Guest who reaches the Course should feel the weight of it. In a typical campaign of twenty sessions, a Guest who Partakes freely will reach the Course; one who Partakes recklessly will reach the Brink.

When the Seating Comes

Treat a Guest’s Seating as the finale of their story, not as a failure. Talk with the player beforehand. Give them a last scene: a last speech, a last kindness, a last act of terrible power. Then let the god have them. Bring them back later as part of the world, and let the other Guests visit what is left. The Dowager Hills are full of grandmothers who were once someone’s companions on the road.

Fudging and Fairness

Roll in the open whenever you can. The Table is a cruel place, and the dice are the most honest thing in it. If a Guest dies to a bad roll in a meaningless fight, that is a sign you should not have run a meaningless fight. Make fights matter, warn players when they are walking into death, and let the dice fall.

Saying Yes to the God

Players will look for loopholes: Kept characters who use their undying bodies as shields; Oathen Guests who swear things into existence; Brinehollowers who try to bargain with their Tenants. Let them. The gods are not interested in rules-lawyering, but they are very interested in being invited in. Every loophole a Guest finds is a door the god can walk through. Say yes, and then show them who else came through it.

Building a Campaign

Choose a Center

Campaigns on the Table work best when they are anchored to one place and one thread, at least to start. Choose:

  • A land. Begin in one land, and let the Guests learn its rules intimately before they travel.
  • A thread. Pick one of the Threads Between the Lands: the Deadwatch, the Host on the Road, Brine in the Rouse, the Missing Hand, the Sayer’s Sentence, Eight Chairs. It will pull the Guests across borders when they are ready.
  • A clock. The land’s own crisis, ticking.
  • A patron. Someone who pays the Guests or protects them, and who will betray them.

Campaign Frames

The Caravan. The Guests are the crew of a Rim Road Company caravan: Factors, Wardens, a cook, a Seamer, a Cutwright on assignment. Each story is a waystation, a cargo, a border. The Company’s contracts are sworn in Oathen and cannot be broken; it is only a matter of time until one of them requires something unthinkable.

The Survey. The Guests work for the Cutwrights’ College, mapping where each god is regrowing fastest. They travel the lands, read bloodlines, and slowly discover that their own ledgers are being used by the Second Table to plan a menu.

The Purge. The Guests are a Purgation cell. At first they fast and bleed and pray. Then they are asked to burn a house with a family inside it. What do they believe, and how far will it take them?

The Watch. The Guests are Nightwardens in one city: the Netwatch of Lowmark, the Wakers of the Vigil, the Loft-Wardens of Lastgate. Each story is a case. The cases get worse. The city’s secret, which the Guests are paid to protect, is the worst of all.

The Household. The Guests serve or belong to a single noble family in the last stages of the Regrowth: a Hand-line house where the hands have started to grow; a Gut-line estate where the matriarch is putting down roots; a Caul-line household where the heir has been carried for forty years. Domestic, claustrophobic, unbearable.

The Pilgrimage. The Guests are travelers bound for the Fast, for reasons of their own: to find the Host, to find a cure, to find someone who was invited and never came home. The Rim Road is the journey. Hallowboard is the end.

Escalation

A campaign on the Table should move through four movements, like the Regrowth itself:

MovementSessionsWhat Happens
The Taste1–4The Guests learn one land. Small horrors. Personal stakes. The god in their blood barely stirs.
The Appetite5–10A thread pulls them across a border. They discover the scale of the Regrowth. They begin to Partake to survive.
The Course11–18The powers of the Table notice them. A Guest is changed beyond hiding. Someone they love is lost. A land’s crisis breaks.
The Seating19+The end of the Grace in one land, or all of them. The Secrets of the Table come into play. Somebody sits down.

Making the Guests Matter

The Guests cannot save the world. They can decide who sits at the table when it ends. Let their choices shape the shape of the catastrophe: whether the Vigil buys the secret of Keeping, whether the Assemblers’ figure gets its hand, whether Lady Imre Dath is unbitted and what she is told to say. A campaign on the Table is a story about which awful thing happens, and who is to blame for it.

The Carver's Tools

Read-Aloud Text

Read-aloud passages in this book are set in the same style as in-world documents. Read them slowly. Pause before the last line. Then stop, and let the silence do the work. Do not explain. The Guests will ask.

Handouts

The Table is a world of documents: death licenses, Cutwright ledgers, contracts forty pages long, place cards, the Tally, the Long Count, a seemer’s report. Give your players paper. A handwritten place card with a Guest’s name on it, set at their seat before the session starts, will do more than any monster.

Names

Every land has its naming customs, listed in its chapter. When you need a name in a hurry: Sallowreach names are soft, mournful and old (Bettany, Osric, Henna, Tam); Fatlands names are hearty and edible (Suet, Brisket, Tansy, Hob); Brinehollow names are wet and coastal (Kessa, Sennet, Hask, Tolly); Vigil names ring like bells (Ilvane, Maud, Pip, Rook); Cradlewrack names are rustic and beginning (Orla, Lark, Juniper, Hinge); Oathen names are clipped and few-syllabled (Ket, Brakk, Rue, Ona); the Unfed name their children for the Refusal (Forbear, Abstain, Decline, Stint, Tarry, Nay, Want, Spare).

Twenty Things the Carver Can Do When Nothing Is Happening

d20The Table Moves
1A Kept relative arrives with a message and a missing hand.
2Someone the Guests met last session is found Reaped, Called, Seated, or Broken.
3A place card with a Guest’s name on it, at a table that was not there an hour ago.
4A pang, felt from three lands away.
5The Guests’ patron asks for something small and wrong.
6A Cutwright arrives to read a Guest’s bloodline, by order.
7A Reckoner has a list. One of the Guests is on it, or someone they love is.
8Bread smells in a house where nobody bakes.
9The Rim Road is closed by the Company: no reason given, Wardens on the bridges.
10The Seeming of the Vigil shows something the Guests did.
11A Forsworn begs a Guest to carry an oath for a single night.
12The Purgation burns a house nearby; there are children’s shoes outside.
13A barrel bursts on the road, and the meat inside has a tattoo the Guests recognise.
14The sea has dropped another mile; the salvage rush begins.
15Someone yawns, and the yawn moves around the room like a hand.
16A door that has been bricked up is found open.
17A Blank is being auctioned in the market square.
18A Guest’s Tooth bites in their sleep: gain 1 Hunger and a dream of the god.
19A Second Table invitation, on heavy paper, addressed to the highest Cut among them.
20A tall figure is seen far off, stooping, laying a table in an empty field.

Safety, Again

You have read the content warning. You have discussed Lines and Veils. You have explained the Grace. Now do one more thing: watch the people at your table, not just their characters. If someone has gone quiet, check in at the break. If someone laughs too hard at the wrong moment, it may be how they are coping. If a scene you planned starts to land on something real in someone’s life, stop it, and do not make them explain.

The Table is a world without rescue. Your table is not. Be the Carver who makes sure everyone gets fed.

Chapter 17

The Ninth Chair

A good host lays one place more than he expects. A great host never asks who it is for.
— carved over the hearth at Thimble Cross, Rim Road Company waystation, 402 A.G.

From the station ledger of Thimble Cross, kept by Warden Josse Haverick of the Rim Road Company, under oath. Entries for the last week of Lack, 641 A.G.

Seventh day before Tablenight. Snow since noon, if it is snow. It does not melt on the hand. It sits on the skin and goes soft, like lard left by a stove. Convoy of the Renderers’ Union arrived at dusk out of the south, eleven wagons, forty-four barrels, Cullmaster’s seal on the lead wagon. Teamster Crumm reports the white has followed them up the road from the Chute for six days. Reports one drover lost on the road. Reports it as wolves. I have entered it as wolves.

Sixth day before. Road closed both ways. The white lies a hand deep on the yard and has veins in it. Stores: flour for nine days at half bread. Guests: twenty-two, family four, myself. One drover missing from the yard at dusk. No tracks. A smell of baking where he stood.

Fifth day before. There is a table in the common room. It was not there at midnight. I sat up with the lamp and the ledger and I did not sleep and I did not see it come. It is long and dark and set for nine and the cloth is whiter than anything I have seen in my life. The bread is warm. Nobody has touched the bread. There are cards at the places. One of them has my name on it. I have entered it in the inventory under Furniture, Not Company Property. I do not know what else to enter it under.

Fifth day before, later. Mistress Thimble has polished the table. Nobody asked her to. She says she could not help it. She says a table like that ought to be kept nice.

Tablenight eve. I am still bound to hold this station until relieved. I wish it entered that I was never relieved.

An Introductory Adventure

The Ninth Chair is an introductory adventure for The Long Grace, written for three to five new characters of mixed lands and playable in two or three sessions of four to five hours. It takes place in the last week of Lack, 641 A.G., at a Rim Road Company waystation called Thimble Cross, where the great ring road bends between the warm meat-plains of the Fatlands and the gold, empty edge of the Fast. A storm of something that is not snow strands the characters there with a convoy of Fatlands meat, a houseful of strangers, and a long table that nobody carried in.

It is a siege, a murder mystery, and a famine, all at once, and it ends on the longest night of the year. It is designed to teach the core of the game: the Grace Roll, Dread and Fray, Hunger and Partaking, the way each land’s curse travels in the blood of its people, and the first rule every child of the Fast learns, which is that there are invitations you must not accept.

It is also designed to hurt. The adventure’s climax is a sacrifice that the community demands, that somebody gives, and that buys nothing at all. Players should leave the table understanding, in their stomachs, what kind of world this is: a world in which the gods are not angry and cannot be bargained with, in which good people do the brave thing and it does not matter, and in which the Host, the only god never eaten, is kind.

Content and Care

This adventure contains graphic gore and transformation, cannibalism, the desecration of graves, a ritual murder, a killing within a family, an inherited bloodline curse with implied incest between adults, contagious madness, and a suicide. Talk with your players before you begin. The suicide in Day Three is written to be played as grief, never as spectacle: its method is never described and need never be, and the scene is about who finds the body, what was in the note, and what the people left behind begin to say to themselves afterward. Use the tools your table prefers to step around anything that cuts deeper than the game should. Horror works best among people who trust each other.

The Secret Truth

Read this section before anything else. Nothing in it should reach the players directly. All of it can reach them in pieces.

Four Things Are Happening at Once

The Reaping has followed the convoy. Forty-four barrels of Fatlands meat came up the Rim Road under the seal of Cullmaster Hedley Brawn. Thirteen are notched with a small knife-mark under the stamp, and they hold the harvest of the Dusk Acres: Rootkin, field-grown meat with faces, and, packed in brine among them, the remains of people the Fatlands soil took and then, being a generous field, gave partly back. The soil of the Fatlands is the flesh of Ummer, the Laden, and that meat is still, in a sense the Board would rather not examine, ground. It has carried its weather with it. Marbling, the Fatlands’ first frost, the whitening of the fat in the soil, has followed the wagons north for six days and settled over Thimble Cross like snow. Where the marbling lies, the ground is Fatlands ground. And on Fatlands ground in the dark of the year, at dusk, people are Reaped.

The Host has come to dinner. Orrum, the only god never eaten, has been walking out of the Fast along the Rim Road, laying tables where people are hungry. Thimble Cross is the most perfect invitation it has ever been offered. The inn is starving. The convoy’s hunger is the bottomless hunger of the Fatlands. And the family who keep the inn are bound, by a Company charter sworn in Oathen two hundred and thirty-nine years ago, to “turn no traveller away, nor refuse any guest, while the blood of Thimble endures.” A house that cannot refuse is a house the Host can enter. On the night after the convoy arrives, a table appears in the common room, laid for nine. On Tablenight, the longest night of Lack, the Host will come to sit at its head, and everyone who takes their place will be Seated: alive, smiling, eating from empty plates, never to rise.

The guests are not innocent. A poacher means to sell a caged Unfed woman to the Second Table, two of whose nobles are here under false names to measure the Host’s table for carving. A Purgation preacher is looking for a high-Cut throat to open. The innkeeper is about to feed his guests his own mother. A Vigil courier on her last rouse is seeing things, and the things are catching.

The ninth chair is not for anyone here. Orrum’s newest tables on the Rim Road are always laid with one place more than there are guests to fill it. That place has a chair pushed in square to the table, and at Thimble Cross, for the first time anyone has recorded, it has a card. The card bears no name. It bears a single mark in the oldest form of Table-speech, the root word that means both “to worship” and “to eat,” with a stroke beneath it that scholars read as “after,” or “last,” or “late.” The people of Thimble Cross will come to believe that the ninth card names someone who must be given to the Host so that the rest may be spared. They will argue about who. They will choose. Someone will sit in the ninth chair. And the Host will come anyway, lift the volunteer gently out of a chair that was never theirs, lay a new place for them, and go on with dinner. The ninth chair was not laid for any guest of Thimble Cross. Welcome Ardent, the Host’s steward, sets it at every table himself, and in six hundred years he has never once seen who it is for.

What the Ninth Chair Is (Do Not Say)

The ninth chair is the place every old carving keeps for the Eighth, the figure chiseled out of the world’s history. This adventure never says so, and neither should you. If players connect the empty chair to the eighth place in old carvings, to the stone table under the sea with eight chairs, or to the eight sides of Hallowboard, let them. Do not confirm it. Welcome Ardent does not know. The Host, if it knows, does not discuss its guest list. The horror of the climax is that the chair belongs to someone who has not arrived, that everyone at Thimble Cross can feel it waiting, and that nothing they offer fills it.

Background

Thimble Cross

Thimble Cross stands where the Rim Road, coming north out of the Fatlands, bends hard west to skirt the edge of the Fast. A rutted track, the Hungry Lane, leaves the bend and runs north into the gold country of the Unfed, toward the hearthless town of Wanting; it is used by Crumb-Runners, Hostwatch trackers, and nobody else. The station is old, solid, and plain: a two-storey inn of grey fieldstone with a slate roof and seventeen chimneys, a walled yard, a long stable, a smokehouse, a toll house with a Company bell, and, behind a low wall, a little graveyard of nine stones.

It was founded in 402 A.G. by Hadley Thimble, a Crumb-Runner who had spent her life carrying grain into the Fast on her back and been spat on for it by the people it kept alive. She left the Fast, married a Fatlands drover, bought the crossing, and swore her charter with the Rim Road Company in Oathen before the Company’s notary of the day. The charter granted the Thimble blood the keeping of the station in perpetuity in return for a single clause, which Hadley, who had grown up among people who refused everything, insisted on writing herself: that the keepers of Thimble Cross shall turn no traveller away, nor refuse any guest, while the blood of Thimble endures.

Promises sworn in Oathen follow the body that swore them, and the bodies that come after it, if the drafting says so. Hadley’s drafting said so. Her descendants cannot refuse a guest without their bodies breaking to match. Mistress Hepzibah Thimble barred the door once, in her youth, against a leper in the rain, and two fingers of her right hand folded backwards to the wrist with a sound like kindling; she wears them that way still. And because the charter binds only “the blood of Thimble,” and a Clausewright consulted in 488 A.G. opined that a mixed line might be argued to have ended, the Thimbles have for five generations kept their blood carefully, narrowly, at home. Company ledgers list Absalom and Hepzibah Thimble as husband and wife. Three lines higher on the same page, in an older hand, they are listed as born to the same mother. Guests notice the family’s sameness: the same pale-lashed grey eyes, the same small chin, the same strawberry birthmark at the throat, the same habit of laying an extra spoon. Guests do not ask.

The Convoy

The convoy is eleven wagons of the Renderers’ Union under Teamster Abel Crumm, carrying forty-four barrels north from the Chute toward the Vigil, where Fatlands salt pork is bought by the ton to feed a city that eats hourly to stay awake. It travels under the seal of Cullmaster Hedley Brawn, who rides with it to see the far-field barrels safely sold, because the Board is beginning to worry about inspection at the Vigil border and wishes its paperwork to be beyond reproach. The convoy’s manifest lists forty-four barrels of “pork, salted, first quality.” The thirteen notched barrels were packed at the Dusk Acres under Brawn’s eye. Abel Crumm knows they are notched. He has not let himself know why.

Six days ago, as the wagons climbed out of the warm country, the ground behind them began to whiten in long, branching veins. Each night the marbling crept a little further up the road. One drover was lost on the second night. Crumm entered it as wolves, as the Board’s forms require. On the evening before the adventure begins, the convoy reached Thimble Cross, and the marbling came with it, and in the morning it was lying a hand deep over everything, and it had begun to fall from the sky.

Why Now

Tablenight is the anniversary of the Gorging, the night six peoples ate their gods and one did not. Orrum has been patient for six hundred and forty-one years. This year, the Hostwatch say, it is walking faster. Its steward, Welcome Ardent, usually lays a table a mile ahead of his master and waits for him. At Thimble Cross, for the first time, the Host has not waited for its steward. The table was laid before Ardent arrived, and that frightens Ardent more than anything has frightened him in six centuries.

Running The Ninth Chair

Structure

The adventure runs across seven days, from Day One (six days before Tablenight) to Day Seven (Tablenight itself). A day-by-day timeline gives what happens if the characters do nothing; the characters will, of course, do something, and the timeline bends around them. Scenes are written to be dropped in when the moment is right. Roughly:

SessionDaysWhat It Is About
OneDays One to ThreeArrival, the table, the cards, the first Reaping, hunger, the suicide
TwoDays Four to SixThe graveyard, the kin-slaying, the ritual killing, the madness, Ardent
ThreeDay SevenThe demand, the sacrifice, the Host, the endings

For a two-session game, compress Days Four to Six into a single long night of discoveries, and begin the second session on the morning the consensus forms.

The Shape of Dread

Thimble Cross gets worse in a particular order: first strange, then hungry, then frightened, then cruel, then devout. Pace the Dread checks accordingly. The first session should cost each character perhaps 4 to 6 Fray; by the climax most should be within reach of Breaking, so that the arrival of the Host can tip one or two over the edge. Contagion of madness is a central mechanic here: when anyone Breaks, everyone who sees it makes a Dread 2 check, and the inn’s own population is Breaking too.

The Count

From Day Two, Merrit Sloe, the Brinehollow bail-girl, begins the count, as is the custom of her country: each morning she walks the upstairs corridor and calls every name through every wall, and waits for an answer. Use the count to open every day after the first. It tells the players who is gone without needing a scene, and the silences after names are the adventure’s heartbeat. Keep a list. Cross names off where the players can see you do it.

Hunger at Thimble Cross

The inn’s stores run short at once. From Day Two, everyone at Thimble Cross is on half bread. From Day Four, there is no bread. A character who does not eat a proper meal on a given day gains 1 Hunger at dawn whether they have Partaken or not (Unfed characters, trained to it, ignore the first two days). From Day Four, a hungry character suffers −1 on all Hand and Lung rolls per full day without food, to a maximum of −3. Hunger gained from starvation counts toward Regrowth like any other. Fatlanders, whose hunger was never in the stomach, gain 2 Hunger a day instead of 1, but suffer no penalty: they are used to it.

Eating from the Barrels

The convoy’s forty-four barrels are the only food at Thimble Cross worth the name. Thirty-one are honest salt pork. Thirteen are notched (see the Convoy Manifest handout). Meat from a notched barrel is the best thing any character has ever eaten: sweet, yielding, rich, with a fat that melts at blood heat and coats the tongue for an hour. It removes all starvation penalties. It does not remove Hunger. Instead, a character who eats it must roll Gut + Feast against Hard 14. On a failure they acquire the Laden Taste until the end of the adventure: they gain 1 Hunger every time they see food, smell cooking, or watch someone else eat, and they must make a Caul + Resolve roll (Hard 14) to stop eating once they have begun. A character who eats from a notched barrel three times dreams the memories of the person the meat once was, and must make a Dread 3 check on waking. A Fatlander who eats it suffers nothing new at all, which is the worst thing about it.

The Marbling

The marbling looks like snow until you are close to it. Then it looks like the white veining in a cut of beef, branching and rejoining across the ground, with a pinkish translucence between the veins that gives slightly underfoot. It smells of cold fat and, faintly, of bread. It does not melt in the hand. It softens. It falls from the sky in soft white flakes that land on the skin and cling, greasy, and must be scraped away with a knife-back. Where it lies, the ground is Fatlands ground. Between sunset and full dark, anyone standing on marbled ground alone may be Reaped (see the Reaping, below). Each day the marbling covers more: on Day One the road and the yard; on Day Three the stable floor and the graveyard; on Day Five the cellar; on Day Seven the boards of the common room, everywhere except the strip of floor beneath the Host’s table, which stays bare and warm.

The Reaping at Thimble Cross

The Reaping here obeys its Fatlands rules. A character alone on marbled ground between sunset and full dark first notices a stillness (Eye + Search, Routine 10). Then the ground leans in, the smell of new bread rising from it (Dread 3 to witness; Dread 2 for a Fatlander). Then it softens: the character must succeed at Caul + Resolve (Hard 14; Grim 18 if their Hunger is 6 or more) or stop wanting to leave. Companions may drag a character free with Gut + Labor against Grim 18, but each round in the soil deals 1d6 Flesh as the ground begins, gently, to digest. A character Reaped is gone. What is pulled out after full dark is a shape of clothes and the smell of bread. Never use the Reaping as a surprise kill on a player character; describe it slowly, and give their friends the chance to pull.

Portions and Advancement

At the end of each session, award each character 5 to 10 Portions of experience, as described under Aftermath. A character who survives the whole adventure should have earned between 15 and 30.

The Cast

Twenty-odd people are snowed in at Thimble Cross, and every one of them is hungry. The major figures below have full stat blocks; the rest have quick lines. Each entry notes what the person wants, what they are hiding, and what happens to them if the characters do nothing. Remember that the characters’ own names are on the place cards, and that every person in this list will, sooner or later, want to know why.

The Keepers of the House

Absalom Thimble, the Innkeeper

A big, soft, slope-shouldered man of sixty-one with the family’s pale lashes and small chin, an apron that has not been fully white since the Thin Rising, and a voice like a warm spoon. Absalom has kept Thimble Cross for thirty-eight years and has never in that time turned anyone away, because he cannot. He loves the work. He loves the moment a cold traveller’s face changes at the smell of his pottage. The charter does not feel like a curse to him; it feels like who he is. That is why the famine breaks him. A host with no food is a contradiction his body cannot hold, and from Day One his hands tremble when he passes the empty pantry shelves. On the night of Day One he digs up his mother, Old Mother Ivy Thimble, and on Day Two he serves her, and weeps in the kitchen while the guests ask for more.

Absalom Thimble — Keeper of Thimble Cross

Hepzibah Thimble, the Keeper's Wife

Small, upright, sixty, with her ruined right hand held against her apron like a folded bird. Hepzibah runs the house: the linen, the rooms, the ledger of who sleeps where. She is the family’s memory and its law. She is also Absalom’s sister, a fact she has never spoken aloud in her life and will defend with a carving knife. She regards the charter the way a priest regards scripture. The family has suffered for it for two hundred years; therefore it must be holy. When Orrum’s table appears she polishes it, every morning, with beeswax, and cannot say why.

Hepzibah Thimble Threat 3 · Flesh 11 · Guard 11 · Attack +4 (carving knife 2) · Armor 0 · Dread 0 (Hearth-Bound, as Absalom)

Linus Thimble, the Son

Thirty-four, heavy-handed, quiet, a good farrier and a bad liar, with his father’s build and his mother’s eyes. Linus has always known that he and his sister are expected to marry, because there are no other Thimbles left, and because the Clausewright’s opinion is framed in the parlour. He has been trying for ten years to find a way to be content with it, and he very nearly has, and that frightens him more than the expectation itself. Linus discovers his father’s crime on Day Four, when he finds his grandmother’s wedding ring in the bottom of the pottage pot. He kills Absalom that night in the cellar with the cleaver his father taught him to use. Afterward he sits with the body until dawn and holds its hand.

Linus Thimble Threat 3 · Flesh 15 · Guard 13 · Attack +6 (farrier’s hammer 3, or cleaver 3) · Armor 1 · Dread 0 (Hearth-Bound)

Dorcas Thimble, the Daughter

Twenty-nine, sharp-tongued, tall, the only Thimble who reads anything but the ledger. Dorcas has read the charter every night since she was fourteen, looking for an exit clause, and there is none. She wants out: out of the inn, out of the blood, out of the marriage the parlour wall has arranged for her. She is the person most likely to ask the characters, quietly, to help her leave, and the person for whom leaving is least possible. If she crosses the station’s boundary stones without the charter being released, her body will break. She knows this. She has worked out precisely how badly. She has decided she might be willing to find out.

Dorcas Thimble Threat 3 · Flesh 12 · Guard 13 · Attack +4 (bread knife 2) · Armor 0 · Dread 0 (Hearth-Bound)

Playing the Thimble Curse

The Thimbles’ inherited curse should stay in the corners of the eye. The players learn it through the sameness of their faces; through the ledger that lists Absalom and Hepzibah as born to the same mother; through the framed Clausewright’s opinion in the parlour with its phrase “the blood kept narrow, the line kept whole”; through the single wide bed in the family wing and the second one beside it that has never been slept in; through Dorcas looking at her brother across a room and then looking away. Never make it explicit. Never make it a joke. It is a family that has been doing a terrible thing to itself for two hundred years because a dead woman wrote a kind clause badly, and the most frightening thing about it is how ordinary they have made it.

Warden Josse Haverick, of the Rim Road Company

Forty-four, lean, a long jaw shaved blue each morning in cold water whatever the weather, an Oathener of minor Tongue-line blood who speaks the way all Oatheners do, slowly and in conditionals, with all the exits built in. Haverick holds Thimble Cross for the Company. He swore before the notary Jessamy Quill, in Tacit, to “hold this station for the Company until relieved, keep its peace, and keep its ledger true.” Sworn in Oathen, the promise travels with him. He cannot abandon the station; he cannot falsify the ledger; he cannot fail to keep the peace without his body coming apart to match. He is honest because he has no choice and decent because he chose it. He is the closest thing to law at Thimble Cross, and he is trapped there more completely than anyone except the Thimbles.

The Convoy

Cullmaster Hedley Brawn, of the Board of Plenty

A vast, courteous, beautifully dressed man in plum wool and a waistcoat with forty bone buttons, all straining. Brawn is a Gut-line cadet and a career officer of the Board’s quietest department, the one that decides which vagrants, debtors and troublemakers are assigned the dusk shift in the far fields. He eats constantly and without hurry, from a lacquered box of candied fat he keeps in his coat, and he speaks of the Reaping as a farmer speaks of rain: something to be planned for, measured, and directed where it will do the most good. He is not cruel. He finds cruelty wasteful. He believes, sincerely, that the Reaping can be steered, that a field which is fed one chosen person at dusk will not take a random one at midnight, and he is, horribly, partly right. From Day Two he proposes a dusk roster: each evening, one person will go out on the marbled ground and stand there, and the rest will be safe. He will happily draw up the roster. He will not put himself on it. He has a Board warrant that says he need not.

Teamster Abel Crumm, of the Renderers' Union

Fifty-two, square, sunburned in a country with no sun to speak of, with the Fatlands’ hunger behind his eyes and a teamster’s habit of counting things twice. Abel has driven the Chute road for thirty years, and he has always known some barrels are notched, and he has always decided not to ask. He is kind to his drovers, generous with his pipe, and on the first evening he stands the whole common room a round of pear spirit and says “Lack keep away” with real feeling. On the night of Day Two he opens barrel 31 and finds, in the brine, a forearm with a tattoo he paid for himself: a sheaf of wheat and the name ROBB, for his sister’s boy, who went to work the dusk shift in Low Tilth last Carving for a debt of thirty lacks. He is found in the cold store on the morning of Day Three.

Abel Crumm Threat 3 · Flesh 15 · Guard 12 · Attack +4 (pry-bar 3) · Armor 1 · Dread 0

The Drovers

Six Renderers’ Union drovers travel with the convoy, all Fatlanders, all perpetually, quietly eating. Big Oona Harl is the oldest, a woman of fifty built like a dray-horse who sings field hymns and loves Abel Crumm like a brother. Nib Furrow is eighteen, freckled, on his first run, and so hungry he chews the leather of his own reins; he is first on Brawn’s roster. Gus Haslet and Tam Pettle are cousins who argue about everything except food; Walt Sallow is silent and missing two fingers; Lise Trotter, kin to the drover Sal Trotter, does not name the cattle. The convoy’s twenty-two oxen stand in the yard, and on the second night, when no one is watching the stable, some of them stand on two legs.

Convoy Drover Threat 2 · Flesh 12 · Guard 12 · Attack +4 (goad or knife 2) · Armor 1 · Dread 0

The Poacher and His Prize

Kale Dragoman, the Poacher

A long, sallow, rangy Fatlander of forty with a black beard trimmed to a point, a fine Vigil-glass spyglass on a chain, and the easy manner of a man who has found a trade that suits him. Kale hunts the Unfed across the border for the Blank trade. He takes them alive, because a living Blank fetches four times a dead one at the surgeries where blank blood and blank organs are sold to the nobility. And he feeds them well on the road, cooks for them himself, tender things, warm things, because his buyers prefer a plump specimen and because, he says, there is no reason to be unkind. His captives find this the hardest thing to forgive. He travels with two hired men and a wheeled iron cage. Kale is witty, morally weightless, and good company, and he will try hard to be liked, because people who like him are easier to sell things to.

Refrain Dole, the Tablebreaker

She is thirty-three, Unfed, and she has put an axe through two hundred and six of Orrum’s tables. Kale took her on the Hungry Lane a week ago with a cosh behind the ear while she was splitting a laid board near Wanting, and she has been in his cage ever since, eating his cooking because the alternative is to be force-fed, and hating every sweet mouthful. She is gaunt in the way of her people, with cropped black hair, the knuckles of a woodsman, a bruise across her temple gone green, and the Unfed’s pride in her chin like a fist. She is insufferable. She tells the characters exactly what their ancestors did and exactly how damned they are, and she corrects their grace. She is also funny, fearless, and the only person at Thimble Cross who knows how to survive the Host. If the characters treat her as a person, she will teach them: never thank a chair; walk into the wind when you smell bread; stand with your back to the door; say “No, thank you” three times and never a fourth. She is, by design, the person the players should come to care about most. She is the most likely volunteer for the ninth chair.

The Travellers

Lady Vellum Serrat, of the Second Table

She travels as “the widow Serrat, a dealer in lace,” in grey mourning silk with a black lace veil that hides a slim bit of gilt wire across her tongue. She is in truth a Tongue-line noble of Tacit, Cut 4, fifty years old, deep in the Appetite and fighting a compulsion to swear that the bit holds in check. She speaks rarely, in exquisite conditionals, through the wire, so that every sentence comes out faintly lisped and glittering. She is a member of the Second Table, whose one idea is that the gods, when they have regrown, should be eaten again, and she has come to Thimble Cross deliberately, following the Hostwatch reports of tables laid at Rim Road inns, to see one of Orrum’s tables up close and take its measurements. She carries a cutwright’s tape, a silver carving set wrapped in oilcloth, and a letter from Wont Bellamy of the Abstinent. She regards the Host as the only whole god left on the Table and therefore the only unspoiled meal. She is calm, curious, and the most dangerous person in the building.

Lord Casimir Hollowe-Vane, the Secretary

He travels as Vellum’s secretary, a quiet young man in a scholar’s coat, with heavy grey gloves he never removes and a habit, which he cannot stop, of closing things: lids, shutters, books, the inn’s doors behind people who meant to leave them open. He is in truth a cadet of the Hand-lines of Sallowreach, a distant cousin of the Left Hand of the Court, Cut 4, thirty-one, and well into the Course. Under the gloves, under a second pair of lead-lined mittens, his hands are grey and cold and have seven joints to each finger. What they touch finishes: a candle, a conversation, a person. He left Sallowreach because he could not bear to be useful there. He is gentle, frightened, well-read, and would very much like someone to hold his hand without dying.

SecretHe came to Thimble Cross hoping that if he sat at the Host’s table, his hands would be fed something other than endings. He has told no one, not even Vellum.

Sister Clemency Voide, of the Purgation

A tall, bony woman of forty-five from the red highlands of Cradlewrack, in a sackcloth habit belted with a string of pewter basins that clink when she walks. Her teeth are worn to stubs by bile, her knuckles calloused where she has put her fingers down her own throat ten thousand times, and her voice is the warmest thing at Thimble Cross: low, kind, patient, with a midwife’s certainty in it. The Purgation believes the gods can be thrown back up. Clemency’s own branch believes it must be done by the highest bloodlines first, since the god sits thickest in them, and that the Host, the uneaten god, came to this place because the guests are full of eaten god and it can smell them. She preaches fasting, bleeding, and purging in the yard each morning, and by Day Four the hungry drovers have begun to listen, because she is the only person offering a reason for what is happening. She is also, under the Regrowth of her own land, suffering the false labour of the Appetite, cramps that bend her double on the stairs, and she believes it is the god trying to come out of her.

Sister Clemency Voide — the Emetic
AttributesHand 2 · Gut 2 · Lung 2 · Eye 3 · Tongue 5 · Caul 4
Cut & RegrowthCut 2 (Cradlewrack) · Regrowth 4 (the Appetite: false labour) · Hunger 6

GiftsThe Sermon. When Clemency preaches to a crowd, she rolls Tongue + Persuade; anyone listening who does not beat her result with Caul + Resolve is swayed for a day, and will take her side in any argument. Purge. She can make a willing or restrained person vomit up what they have eaten in the last day (no roll); this removes the Laden Taste and 1d6 Hunger, and costs 1d6 Flesh.

Purgation Converts (drovers and guests swayed by the Sermon) Threat 1 · Flesh 10 · Guard 12 · Attack +3 (lancet or knife 2) · Armor 0 · Dread 0

Merrit Sloe, the Bail-Girl

Nineteen, freckled, wiry, with salt-cracked lips, a gap-toothed grin, and a wooden bail-bucket on a cord across her back, painted with gulls by someone who loved her. Merrit is from Lowmark. Her mother walked into the sea when Merrit was twelve and walked out again six weeks later, calm and courteous and heavier, and tucked Merrit into bed that night with a stranger’s hands. Merrit left home at sixteen and has been walking east ever since, as far from the sea as the Rim Road goes, earning her passage at Company inns by bailing Brinehollow travellers who are too old or too ill to cough the night’s tide up for themselves. She is cheerful in the deliberate way of people who have decided to be. She is the first to make friends with Refrain Dole, through the bars of the cage, by trading jokes for jokes. She has started to stand at the west windows at night, where the gold light of the Fast lies across the marbled fields like a tide coming in, and she does not know why.

Merrit Sloe — the Bail-Girl of Thimble Cross

Courier Benedetta "Bell" Lisle, of the Vigil

Twenty-six, quick, angular, with a courier’s narrow saddle-hardened body and the bruised, lidded, enormous eyes of someone who has not slept in her life. She carries a sealed leather dispatch case under the Warden-Prime’s lidless-eye seal, addressed to Envoy Castellan Dray at Lastgate, and she rides the Rim Road the long way round because the Fast is shorter and nobody crosses it. She also carries six vials of rouse that should have lasted the journey. They are not lasting. By Day Two she is blinking, losing seconds on her feet, waking in other parts of the room; by Day Four she is seeing the Seeming, the shared hallucinations that every Vigil citizen comes to in the end, and the Seeming here is a tall figure stooping at the windows and a dead family laid out at the table eating, and the Seeming is catching. She asks one of the characters to be her nudger, to keep her awake by any means, a pinch, a slap, a pin; it is the most intimate thing she knows how to ask. She knows that if she sleeps, wherever she lies down, she will go to the long room with the eye in it and not come back.

Courier Bell Lisle — Rider of the Waking Post

It contains the Warden-Prime’s offer to Sallowreach: to buy the secret of Keeping, so that the citizens of the Vigil may be killed and kept upright, and never need to sleep. Bell has decided that if that is the future, she would rather go to the long room now.

The Steward

Welcome Ardent, Steward of the Host

He comes out of the north on the third night, along the Hungry Lane, walking on ground the marbling melts away from: a tall, very thin, very tired man in an old-fashioned black coat and a long apron, with a napkin over his arm and a wooden box of cutlery under it. He looks perhaps forty. He is six hundred and some. He was the first of the Unfed ever to accept the Host’s invitation, at the end of the Thin Years, and he was the only guest who was ever offered a position instead of a chair. He walks a mile ahead of Orrum and lays its tables, and he is polite, gentle, scrupulous, and so exhausted that his voice sometimes stops in the middle of a sentence and has to be restarted, like a clock. He arrives to find a table already laid, without him, and he stands in the doorway of the common room for a long time with his hand over his mouth.

Welcome Ardent — the Host’s Steward

SkillsCraft (laying a table) 6, Lore (the Host) 5, Persuade 4, Rites 4, Instinct 4, Resolve 3

GiftsIn Service. Ardent cannot be killed while the Host walks; he can be hurt, and it hurts him, and he apologises for bleeding on the floor. Laying the Place. Wherever he sets a cloth, a table follows. Relief. Ardent can offer his position to another. Anyone who accepts, in so many words, becomes the Host’s steward from the next dawn, and Ardent is free (see Ending Two).

Ox of the Convoy (on two legs, unobserved) Threat 2 · Flesh 18 · Guard 10 · Attack +5 (trample or bite 4) · Armor 1 · Dread 2

The Places of Thimble Cross

The Bend and the Approach

The road comes up out of the south between low hedges gone white, and for a mile you think it is snow, and are glad of it, because snow is clean. Then your boots begin to slide in something that is not ice, and your horse will not put its head down to it, and the smell reaches you: cold dripping, a butcher’s slab in the morning, and under it, faint and impossible, new bread. Ahead, where the road bends west, stands a grey inn with seventeen chimneys, and only one of them is smoking. Beyond it, to the north, the land goes gold, as if it were late afternoon in early Carving there, though it is noon in the dead of Lack here. The white stops at the edge of that light like a tide.

The marbling covers the Rim Road for six miles south and three west; travel out is Grim 18 on Lung + Wayfaring by day and impossible at dusk, and the Reaping walks the road. North, the Hungry Lane runs into the Fast, and the ground there is bare and warm wherever the Host has walked. The characters will realise, if they test it, that the safest ground in the region is the god’s road.

The Yard and the Convoy

A cobbled yard behind a seven-foot wall, crammed with eleven wagons drawn into a ring. The oxen stand head-down, breath steaming, and do not move when touched. The barrels are stacked under oiled canvas: forty-four oak casks bound in iron, each stamped with the Chute’s mark struck over twice, thirteen with a small knife-notch beneath. Marbling lies thickest here. By Day Three it has grown veins up the wagon wheels.

Under the canvas the barrels sweat. A slow pink brine beads at the staves and runs and freezes into soft white whorls on the cobbles. When the wind drops you can hear them settling, a creak and a long wet shift, the sound of something in a hammock turning over in its sleep.

Search (Eye + Search, Hard 14) finds the notches. A Fatlander, or anyone with Reckoning 2+, can see that the notched barrels are heavier than pork should be. Laying a palm on a notched barrel at night (Caul + Instinct, Hard 14) reveals that it is warm.

The Common Room

A long, low, smoke-darkened room with a flagged floor, three tables of scarred pine, a great hearth carved with the founding motto, and a row of west windows looking toward the Fast. From the morning of Day Two it holds a fourth table.

It runs down the middle of the room where no table was, dark wood polished to the depth of still water, so long the lamp at its head and the lamp at its foot cannot see each other. The cloth is white the way bone is white when it has been boiled clean. There are nine places. Nine plates of thin cream porcelain rimmed in gold, each with a folded card. Nine chairs; eight of them pulled out a hand’s width, as if for someone about to sit. The ninth, at the foot, is pushed in square to the table, its back to the lamp. Down the centre: a loaf, broken, steam still rising from the break. A dish of butter sweating gold. A tureen with its lid on. The room is warm for the first time in two days. Nobody is standing near the hearth. Everyone is standing near the table.

The table cannot be moved: it is not heavy, it simply does not go. Axes split it (Refrain’s axe always does; others need Hand + Labor, Hard 14) and it is whole again the next dawn, with fresh bread. The food is the Host’s; eating any of it makes the eater a guest, and the eater must sit at their own place before dawn (Caul + Resolve, Grim 18, each hour to resist). The bread is never cold. Its smell reaches every room in the inn, and every character who passes through the common room hungry must roll Caul + Resolve (Hard 14) or gain 1 Hunger.

The Place Cards

There are nine cards. Eight bear names, in a fine, round, careful hand that each reader recognises as the handwriting of someone who loved them: a mother, a grandmother, a first teacher. Fill the eight with every player character’s name (correctly spelled, including any secret or childhood name), plus, in order to reach eight, Merrit Sloe, Linus Thimble, Lord Casimir Hollowe-Vane (under his true name, which exposes him), and Absalom Thimble. For three characters, use all four; for four, drop Absalom; for five, drop Absalom and Linus. The ninth card bears no name; see the handout.

The Kitchen and Pantry

A stone-flagged kitchen with a hearth big enough to roast a pig, copper pans on hooks, and a pantry of sixty empty shelves. On Day Two the great pot hangs over the fire with the pottage in it. A character with Stitching 1+ or a Fatlands upbringing who examines the pottage’s meat (Eye + Search, Hard 14) can tell it is not mutton and not pork; on a Grace, they find a small gold ring with an inscription, A.T. to I.M., kept.

The Cellar and Cold Store

Steep steps down to a vaulted cellar of casks and racks, and beyond a heavy door the cold store, where meat hangs on hooks in winter. From Day Five the cellar floor is marbled, and the white climbs the barrel-staves in veins. Abel Crumm is found in the cold store on Day Three. Absalom Thimble dies in the cellar on the night of Day Four.

The Guest Rooms and the Long Room

Upstairs, nine narrow rooms off a single corridor with thin plank walls, and at the end the Long Room, a dormitory for drovers. Here Merrit walks every morning, knocking, calling names. The west-facing rooms are the warmest, and the Fast’s gold light lies across their floors all night, and those who sleep in them dream of being invited.

The Family Wing

A locked door off the kitchen opens onto the Thimbles’ rooms: a parlour with the charter framed under glass beside the Clausewright’s opinion of 488; a plain room with two beds, one wide and worn and one narrow and never slept in; Dorcas’s room, stacked with books on Oathen law. Searching the parlour (Eye + Search, Routine 10) finds the family register, which tells the attentive reader everything about the Thimble blood without saying anything at all.

The Stable and Kale's Cage

A long stone stable, its floor marbled from Day Three. At the far end, under a tarpaulin, Kale Dragoman’s cage: iron bars, a wooden floor with straw, a slop bucket, and Refrain Dole sitting with her back straight and her eyes open. Kale’s men take turns sleeping across the door. Picking the padlock is Hand + Filch, Hard 14; the key is on Kale’s belt.

The Smokehouse

A squat brick tower across the yard, black inside with three centuries of smoke, hung with iron hooks and racks. It is where Sister Clemency performs the Ninefold Purge on Lord Casimir on the night of Day Five.

The Little Graveyard

Behind a waist-high wall, nine stones for nine generations of Thimbles, the oldest, Hadley’s, carved with a single word: Welcome. The newest, Old Mother Ivy Thimble’s, set in Carving. From Day Three the marbling lies across it. On the morning of Day Four three graves are open: Ivy’s dug down from above by a spade, and two older ones, Hadley’s and her son’s, broken open from beneath.

The Toll House

Haverick’s post: a stone hut at the gate with a bell, a strongbox, a crossbow rack, and the station ledger on a lectern. The ledger records everything the warden sees, and he cannot make it lie.

The Week Before Tablenight

If the characters do nothing, this is what happens. Every event below can be prevented, delayed, or made worse.
